reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: I’m reading Michael Benson’s book on the making of 2001 and recently visited the Museum of the Moving Image exhibit about the film, so I had to finally watch this sequel. It’s such a strange effort, in that it feels almost nothing like Kubrick’s work even though it takes place in recreations of several of his sets, and features several members of his cast (along with a lead character from his film played by a new actor).

reviews.author: ChrisStuckmann
reviews.text: Doesn’t get the respect it deserves. Aside from the use of Also sprach Zarathustra, Peter Hyams almost completely avoids callbacks or blatant homages. He doesn’t even attempt to recreate the iconic HAL 9000 closeup. Instead, he smartly uses Clarke’s source material to craft a sci-fi film that’s entertaining enough for general audiences, but heady enough for the intellectuals who want something to chew on.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: deciding to follow up one of the most perfectly crafted and purposefully enigmatic films of all time with a willfully expository science-laced procedural thriller is undeniably a bonehead move, but if you can somehow divorce this from its predecessor it remains pretty sturdy and frequently exciting. Hyams rarely worked with great material but he was always a first-rate carpenter. he's got a great cast on his hands here (i could watch a whole movie of Roy Scheider, John Lithgow and Helen Mirren just kicking it on a spaceship together doing astronaut stuff) and he gets a lot of visual mileage out of kit-bashed spaceship interiors and sly reframings of Kubrick's designs, although as gorgeous as the analog FX spectacle is here it's unsurprisingly far less seamless than that of the pioneering film it follows.

reviews.author: CJ Probst

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A very literal-minded adaptation of the sequel novel to 2001 which unfortunately takes everything cosmic, poetic, and ambiguous about Kubrick's adaptation and tries to simplify it so that it can fit snugly into a Cold War procedural; the way things cleanly wrap up with HAL and the monoliths and then sign-off by stating the message strikes me as particularly egregious. However despite this inherent flaw baked into it as a sequel the practical mission sequencing and mystery storytelling itself (where the characters go over all the tech hardware of the previous film to figure out what went wrong and learn lessons about international scientific cooperation in the process) is actually fairly engaging on its own terms, the cast is obviously putting in good work, and Hyams brings his usual good-looking widescreen shooting and analog craftsmanship to it.

reviews.text: Sergio Martino directs his cheap and less interesting version of Escape from New York featuring a bit more sci-fi and sleaziness but lacking in fun and Kurt Russell’s charm. There’s some good campy humor, though nothing that had me bursting with laughter. Performances are fine, but again, no one really stood out for me.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: not the most exciting post-apocalypse jam; for that you should look to Castellari. but characteristically bleak for Martino, and of course almost hysterically cynical. also (and this will probably sound ridiculous) the judicious mix of obvious sets and thinly disguised location work resembles nothing less than Abrams' STAR TREK movies. i have a friend who basically calls this Spaghetti CHILDREN OF MEN. he's not wrong.

reviews.author: Joachim Andersson
reviews.text: 2019: After the fall of New York us my absolute favorite of the cycle of Italian post apocalypse flicks that swarmed the market after Road Warrior was released. It has everything you need. A decent pace, graphic violence, an Oliver onions score and of course, Big Ape. The action sequences arent half bad either and sure, some of the sets might be a bit on the cheap side but we do get some good location footage. All in all, essential viewing for fans of Italian exploitation.

reviews.text: Joe D'Amato cranks up the sleaze and violence in his second post apocalyptic movie of 1983 next to 'Endgame'. This one delivers almost non-stop action in a bleak future that's ruled by biker gangs and dystopian neo-nazis. The cast is awesome and includes Italian exploitation favorites such as Al Cliver, Sabrina Siani (both of them re-unite from 'White Cannibal Queen'), Hal Yamamouchi, Donald O'Brien and a much too small role for Geretta Geretta. Sadly George Eastman is not around but he at least provided the story. If the story itself was just a little better and had more of a main character this could be a classic for the top 3 of Italian 'Mad Max' rip-offs.

reviews.author: Cliff
reviews.text: At 114 minutes, this documentary about the history of the Topps chewing gum company's best-loved (and most controversial) trading cards might run a little long, but it's surprising just how much there is to say and to learn about the history of the little 8.9 x 6.4cm cartoons.

reviews.author: Carlo Vanstiphout
reviews.text: Garbage Pail Kids barely registered a blip on my radar growing up. I think they only released the first series in the French-speaking part of the country when I was like, five years old? Finding out about them later in my life it was one of those "where has this been all my life" moments similar to the one I had when I first saw The Simpsons pop up in video games, well before the actual cartoon started airing here. So watching this on a Sunday morning with Michelle made me pretty happy. You get a lot of insight from everyone who worked on the cards, the way the franchise went from being counter to consumer culture after its resurrection, and there's even a chunk dedicated to the fascinating shit show that is the GPK movie. Really flew by.

reviews.author: Saint_Hooligan
reviews.text: Fun trip down memory lane. Tells you everything you want to know about the cards from day one. You'll hear from the artists, the reason GPK look like Cabbage Patch Dolls, the sales, the lawsuits, the cards that were banned and even the cast of the movie, (wish those interviews were longer). If you're an 80's kid or even just a fan of trading cards you'll fine entertainment here. The full story is all here if your a fan or an 80's pop culture junkie.

reviews.author: Paul Senior
reviews.text: Pretty standard pop culture doco. Talking heads, photos and interviews about an 80s phenomenon.

reviews.author: Janne Widmark
reviews.text: Watching this I could SMELL what it was like to open one of those packages as a kid. And I loved them. Even though it might not show in my art these days they sure inspired me to draw back then. And I remember hearing about the death of Jay Lynch in 2017 and how it felt like I had been hit by an Adam Bomb.

reviews.author: PlooplePop
reviews.text: Assuming you weren't of a certain age at a very particular time in the mid-to-late '80s, this documentary does a decent job of explicating just how huge Garbage Pail Kids were. Because I can imagine that it may be inexplicable to those who didn't experience the phenomenon first hand. And if you were a youth at the time when GPK was A Thing, you will likely be enthralled for at least a stretch of this deep dive.

reviews.author: Jason Alley🏳️‍🌈🐻
reviews.text: If you’re of a certain age, you know Garbage Pail Kids. Like me, you probably have fond memories of collecting those cards (the more morbid and disgusting the better), and of feeling like you were getting away with something and seeing something you weren’t supposed to see. Like MAD magazine around the same time, these cards made me feel like a rebel and like I was getting a joke that was meant for adults. It was a thrill!

reviews.author: Dan Gorman
reviews.text: Pretty in depth look at something very close to my heart; feels too long at two hours but if you're into this stuff you're gonna like it for sure.

reviews.author: Auteur
reviews.text: Certainly not a doc to change the world, but an effective piece of anecdotal pop-nostalgia from my childhood, mostly as it gives faces to the behind the scenes talent responsible for my very first collectible. The initial context is invaluable as it traces GPK's predecessors, and actually had me scouring the internet for jpegs of Topps' Civil War cards and Wacky Packages, two sets I had never heard of before. The inside scoop on the Cabbage Patch lawsuit, and the subsequent redesigning of the characters and waning popularity is fascinating as well, as I guess none of that stuff was really important to my ten-year-old self. The eighties were a special time in many ways, and GPK as they were…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Bava unleashed. There's a greedy motive as guide, a terrific location, at same time setting and reason for the murder spree, and so much comes and goings the plot is rendered useless. So what Bay of Blood has going for it are hacked bodies into a horror tableux. Bava's cinema entire reason of existence presented in a very large canvas as the movie doesn't has to pretend to function as anything else. What set Bava into such radical direction is hard to know, but I've always assume this movie is something of game of upmanship, after Argento pushed giallo into pure murderous gaze with Bird with Crystal Plumage, Bava can only take the plunge into a more essential take of the same, there's nothing left but murder and what Bava's art can make out of it.

An abrupt goodbye left much unsaid, questions unanswered, and emotions unexpressed. Consequences of sudden separation echo through a young girl's life. Confusion, sadness, and grief are the primer tone of this film, we see a young girl struggling to understand the sudden absence of a father's love. Dreams of a life filled with paternal love lay shattered, like broken seams that had once held the fabric of her world together. Coping expectedly becomes a leitmotif, and recurring melody in this journey. Though there's still a gentle cadence of newfound faces and whispered connections they offered, the capricious winds of change continue to gust, uprooting blossoming friendships with abrupt departures.

reviews.text: Laaaaate Style here, and what’s most remarkable is that Chabrol still manages to make another variation on provincial bourgeois perversions feel fresh and new. Ludivine Sagnier is amazing, and the audience never doubts that she’s in possession of her agency, even as she’s constructed as a victim by cultural convention. Magimel and his family almost remind me of a late Visconti take on the rotting upper class.

reviews.author: Dubthrone
reviews.text: Chabrol takes aim at two dominions of the rich, the old industrial money that enables generations of inherited wealth to sink into complete decadence, and second, the cultural rich, the artists and intellectuals who debase themselves on the altar of money and soulless cynicism (plaudits to Chabrol for including himself as a defendant in this judgement). By this duet, the film’s titular heroine is divided, brought to you by the luminous Ludivine Sagnier, as Gabrielle Deneige (or, as the subtitles call her, Gabrielle Snow, probably to emphasize the symbolism of the name). Benoît Magimel and François Berléand play the respective rich suitors. Unfortunately, the mens' characters are, as written, given far more heft and dramatic range than Sagnier’s Gabrielle can ever hope for. It’s Chabrol, so hey, it’s very cool, but it’s too ill-balanced and tone-deaf to overcome its mechanical shortcomings.

reviews.text: I’m glad movies like this are allowed to exist. No doubt it’s a mess, but it’s a warm, earnest, funny mess, its anarchic sensibility a perfect framework in which to explore how excruciating and wonderful the romantic comedies of our lives can be. Boyle and Hodge deconstruct their subject from the ground up, with supernatural elements representing the narrative of Love and two erratic protagonists eager to play both the Reality and the Fantasy versions of their story. McGregor and Diaz are charming as hell, and the ultra-‘90s soundtrack rips (a chaotic chase sequence scored by R.E.M.’s pummeling “Leave” is everything I didn’t know I needed). The title is apt: there’s absolutely nothing “ordinary” about the choices made in this film.

reviews.text: The true story of a French resistance fighter who broke out of the notorious Montluc prison in Klaus Barbie's Lyon, where 7,000 men where executed during the German occupation. Bresson does this thing where he never shows any of the prison guards' faces or gives them names or any discernible personality or character. The film remains in tight focus on the main character's face and especially his hands. His captors are abstracted, their cruelty and oppression is never dramatized or given a face or name, we just hear the clink of their keys, the shuffle of their feet, a barked order to stop talking, and the staccato of machine gun fire as they execute another prisoner. The grinding routine and…

reviews.text: A biographical prison escape "thriller" as a formally stripped-down, meticulously-detailed process of human resilience in the face of historical deprivation and isolation. Bresson displays a truly singular and astonishing level of commitment to avoiding all sense of easy, contrived melodrama and instead using every tool at his disposal to achieve a rigorous purity of internal expression as an accumulation of simple, concrete physical action and gesture. The locked-in visual/sonic spatial perspective is particularly masterful; teaching us right from the opening scene to become sensitive to his subjective sight lines, method of thinking, and direct unexaggerated experiences which have been written and directed by men who shared it in real life. reviews.text: As a realistic, breathtaking, influential and heart-pounding recount of a true POW story, it is a shining triumph. Bresson's style of constantly moving from one relevant event to another and letting images speak while assigning a great importance to silences and facial expressions confirms the truth hidden in the phrase "in simplicity lies complexity". Your complaint is that the title sells away the ending, right? Bresson has never cared about the outcomes; instead, his humanity testaments focus on the struggle of life itself given a set of circumstances. That's why he's misunderstood: not all people have fought for their lives even once.

reviews.text: Definitely heading into the realm of Freddy as broad trash-talking weirdo which does mute some of the scariness but the premise of preying on personal anxieties/histories/fears through dream imagery is still incredibly strong and this still manages to take Craven's surreal exploration of adolescence's first exposure to the dark, rotting underbelly, the sickness lurking just beneath the surface of the American suburb and lean into the subtext about abuse and mental health in very effective ways. Not to mention Chuck Russell's impulse towards playfully absurd images and tangible, textured body horror made him about as perfect of a choice for this group-therapy-through-horror-fantasy-setpieces material as there likely was.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: Now THIS is MY Freddy Kreuger: an aggressively foul-mouthed, snide, shit-talking, cheeky bastard who creatively & individually tailors his kills and spouts iconic one-liners as he terrorizes a bunch of vulnerable, insecure kids. Every Freddy after this is just a more wackadoo version of the same thing, but to me this is the peak of the character, with the marionette kill probably being my favorite of the whole franchise. The plot itself is more deeply elevated here too, using the “boogeyman” as a parallel to depression, suicidal thoughts, and self-harm and making our characters feel like real people that we actually know and sometimes are. The “our weaknesses make us stronger” schtick has always been a little too silly and on-the-nose…

reviews.text: casts nature as mysterious, tangled but carefully deliberate, and casts reformers combating totalitarianism as potential ghosts, the past returning to claim its place, the dead returning to vanquish their living betrayers. Hu famously continues to restore to film from Chinese literature the female knight, another piece of the past that now points forward. and the male hero finds his strength only after he sleeps with her and meets the Abbot; the power here is sexual, literally balls to bones, naturally emanating from within. the villain, corrupt and unseen, is a eunuch; his power is baseless, empty, founded on lies. sex vs death. the film folds themes in so gradually that you truly float down the river without ever seeming to get wet.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: It's probably a good five minutes before we see any human beings in A Touch of Zen - before that it's the title sequence, then some close-ups of insects in spider's webs, and various shots of water, trees, light, nature at rest. It's like a soft prayer before the story begins, and it's your first clue that this is no typical kung-fu action movie, containing almost none of the genre's usual concessions to audience attention spans. Even when the action does start up, it's pretty removed from the expected Shaw Bros. athleticism, instead punctuated by long stretches of patient waiting in between the jump-cut-aided fight choreography, just outside physical reality as we (think we) know it.

All this, even though the federal organisation Abacus supposedly stole from actually made a profit from their dealings with Abacus. The big banks, who actually defrauded the people and the government, were presented deals where they would pay a fine and then escape criminal charges. reviews.text: There is a whole lot of daylight between "this bank was unfairly punished when other banks weren't because it was small and served an immigrant community" and "this bank did nothing worthy of being punished", and the film seems completely unaware of that gap, or indeed actively working to erase it. The exact same qualities that make Steve James a great director of documentaries about human life make him much too credulous for this material, and the film ends up being so wildly lopsided and blatant in its sympathies that I find myself much, much more suspicious that the bank at the center was up to bad shit than I ever would have if it had been treated with more coldness and cynicism.

reviews.text: Yesterday's film and fellow Best Documentary Oscar nominee - Last Men in Aleppo - suffers from the exact opposite issues as Steve James' Abacus: Small Enough To Jail does. Abacus' focus is undeniably tight, but it doesn't carry the scope needed to make it fully engaging. It glances at some engaging, timely themes of xenophobia and prejudice but it struggles to broaden its horizons far enough. Small-scale and intimate - probably to a fault - Abacus is a fine but ultimately forgettable documentary.

reviews.author: Matthew B.
reviews.text: Following the financial crisis of 2008, the only company to be criminally indicted was a small Chinatown bank, Abacus Federal Savings Bank. While all of the larger banking firms were deemed "too big to fail," Abacus--a small, family-owned bank founded by the Sung family in 1984 to serve the needs of Manhattan's Chinese immigrant population--was "small enough to jail," and became the perfect target for those looking for someone to punish for the sub-prime mortgage fiasco of 2008.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Adam Resurrected is a strange one in Schraders filmography and not one I was totally expecting since it turns out to be a holocaust related film but instead of being serious and more grounded instead offers a surreal and sometimes comedic outlook and while at times sort of brilliant but mostly jarring and tonally inconsistent. The film tells the story of Adam Stein, a former German-Jewish cabaret entertainer and Holocaust survivor who resides in a mental institution for other Holocaust survivors in 1960s Israel, the main thing that works here is Jeff goldblum’s performance and it’s such a reward to see him go to a more serious performance again since he’s phenomenal balancing a line of trauma and manic charisma…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: By far the weirdest movie Schrader was ever involved. It is too literary a concept and it is arguably tasteless, but remarkably consistent and it follows its premise almost as far as possible (while throwing even more strange detail). It is really hold together by how straightforward Schrader is willing to treat it and by Goldblum remarkable performance which makes perfect use of pretty much every one of his excessive tics.. It is along with The Fly his finest work and the film deserves to be better known as a showcase even if one ends up concluding it is a crazy ill-conceived idea.

reviews.author: Paul Schrader
reviews.text: Let me rebut Tony Scott's absurd assertion in this review that it is "bold" to cast non Jewish actors in Jewish roles. There once was a golden age of Jewish actors and cinema--but it is gone, gone, gone. Financiers much prefer non Jews as Jews just as they prefer non homosexuals as homosexuals. I know, I've done both. I tried to cast Rupert Everett as a gay escort in The Walker but was rejected. I disastrously went with Woody Harrelson. When I cast Jeff Goldblum as a camp survivor in Adam Resurrected I was begged by my Israeli producer to go with Gary Oldman.. It is the opposite of bold to cast non Jews as Jews. It's business as usual.

reviews.text: ADAM RESURRECTED demands greatness in every direction, but regrettably only delivers a mere shadow of what's expected given its meritorious component parts. reviews.author: Dante
reviews.text: It’s... a Nazi petplay slash transspecies movie from the writer of Taxi Driver. More unbelievably bizarre shit from Paul Schrader. Worth mentioning that he didn’t write this and it was in fact adapted from an Israeli novel from the 60s which just makes me wonder why the fuck it exists. Could conceivably be “entertaining” depending on how much you like Jeff Goldblum and/or Willem Dafoe (although Dafoe is sadly very underutilized) as actors but nonetheless a truly perplexing picture. If one movie of his were most characteristic of the version of himself that Schrader presents on Facebook it would probably be this one.

She was excellent. This movie is so heartfelt and has so much soul and when you really dig deep there are fantastic life lessons that young people need to really learn scattered all throughout. People need to fail, people need to experience life and all it has to offer, and people need to accept who they are and not expect to be the most famous or the greatest in their field or the most talented. Overall, this is a fantastic film that after 5 watch throughs I feel comfortable giving a 5/5.

reviews.text: Alan Rudolph’s emotionally deranged screwball comedy from Hell. Here lie hardboiled yet literary dialogues full of double entendres, rampant innuendo, but also subtle visual gags and physical performances, all highly charged, unnervingly horny, increasingly uncomfortable and tense until its fever pitch crescendo-climax of apocalyptic pain (the sky literally darkens and Julie Christie scream-sobs like a newborn). reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: One thread that stood out on this watch: A quiet but brutal critique of television to rival the far louder satire of Network, which was released the same year. The film repeatedly shows televisions, mostly around the Washington Post newsroom, presenting a counterfactual narrative of the Nixon administration that stands in complete opposition to the one assembled by Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein. While they search for the facts, the Post TVs mostly regurgitate the Nixon party line and publicize their “non-denial denials” of the latest Post story, propagating an illusion of a moral, lawful President unfairly attacked by a politically motivated newspaper and its agenda-driven journalists. TV obscures the truth while newspapers expose it, an idea neatly encapsulated in the final scene where Nixon is inaugurated on television in the foreground, while Woodward and Bernstein pound away on their typewriters in the background.

reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: The final 10 minutes feel truly momentous and hardly anything else does. Crowe and Denzel toe-to-toe, trading sweeping proclamations about the past and the future, refugees from their chosen lifestyles connecting to reroute their destinies; Josh Brolin splattering a sun shield with blood after pressing his Smith & Wesson to his chin; Frank Lucas exiting prison to the perfectly synced sound of 1991 Public Enemy, facing a new world order all alone. I love the idea of Ridley Scott’s merciless sense of grandeur and Harris Savides’ scratchy, naturalistic camera building a slick-scummy vision of ‘70s New York, but there’s something sort of perfunctory about the way it plays until the final 10. I kept thinking about what it would be like…

reviews.text: Something that usually goes completely ignored that I would like to focus on is Ruby Dee’s arc as Mama Lucas, specifically how the relationship between Frank and his mother may be limited in terms of screen time yet still struck me as one of the more powerful moments in the film. Her character is used for two reasons: to show Frank’s love for his mother and how she might be the only person who can strike him deeply on an emotional level. The main drive of the story shows how he becomes the outlet for crime within his neighborhood. The murder, robbery, and most notably, drug trafficking were ways in which he expressed his menacing persona.

reviews.text: I've circled that poster for a while, even though I knew it wouldn't have anything to do with the content (although I hoped it might, at least a little). What I hadn't done was educate myself a bit about its status as a failed TV pilot recycled into a movie, nor about the number of familiar faces involved in the project. Annihilator/Executor is both a mess and a blast, with a very strange but striking narrative structure, where its protagonist, who is unaware of anything around him, finds himself surrounded by robotic beings who surely have a plan and powers, but aren't much smarter either.There are more than decent action and chases, montage sequences with Bowie music, and a slightly pessimistic vibe surrounding the figure of the false culprit mixed with a sci-fi adventure that never crystallizes as it should, but it's still frustrating how it lingers unfinished.

reviews.author: Curtis
reviews.text: Meet Richard Armour (Mark Lindsay Chapman), a newspaper editor whose girlfriend, fellow reporter Angela Taylor (Catherine Mary Stewart) goes on a Hawaiian vacation and comes back...changed. It turns out she and her friend Cindy have been replaced by secret robot doppelgangers called dynamitards, for reasons which would have been disappointingly revealed in a post-peak season 4. Running into sculptor and good Samaritan Layla (Susan Blakely), Richard will have to navigate a world that thinks he murdered his cybernetic girlfriend as he tries to track down the other passengers of Trans Northern Air Flight 508 in search of mystery-solving answers.

reviews.text: Precedes both Maurice and Dead Poets Society, and despite being lesser known than those two, it was a clear and important influence on both. It's less poignant and doesn't delve as deep into its themes and characters as those two, but it offers a really interesting portrayal of British boarding schools in early 20th century—how homosexuality was extremely common, despite being seen as both just a phase & dangerous and punishable. The way they would openly talk about desiring other men, but without a sense of community or camaraderie because the system in place and its enablers stopped them from forming those bonds, from being loyal to one another, because all they could ever do was save their own skin.

reviews.text: Emily Watson delivers a knockout performance in a show that offers a fresh take on the rape-revenge genre. Probing the ethical, emotional and legal complexities of a rape's messy aftermath, Apple Tree Yard is as relentlessly thoughtful as it is entertaining, and while there's a dubious voiceover that betrays the show's origins as a novel, it parcels out cinematic suspense without ever losing steam. To that end, the final episode (which is mostly an extended courtroom scene) will leave you breathless.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Arena" is a 1989 science fiction, creature film directed by Peter Manoogian. Manoogian, a director from the seven-director ensemble piece that is "The Dungeonmaster" (1984) also working on other Empire efforts such as "Eliminators" (1986) before continuing down this road with this effort. He also translated past Empire to the Full Moon side of things, directing "Demonic Toys" (1992) amongst other novelties. "Areana" is an interesting piece within the set, but in a strange translation of things it easily becomes one of the greatest films in the set. Set upon a very clear effort of energy placed upon the sleeve of things, "Arena" starts off as having a heavy lacquered element of goofy bad "Star Wars: A New Hope" (1977)…

reviews.author: Ziglet_mir
reviews.text: A delightful rich-person-gets-humbled story sprinkled with man-child syndrome and alcoholism. But of course there is also the romance with the most unexpected blue collar woman (Liza Minelli) as well as one of the greatest friendships between a butler and his employer. I never really thought any one could match Foster Brooks' drunken stupor act, but here is Dudley Moore, plum-pickled extraordinaire, and HILARIOUS. The character of Arthur puts Moore's talents in the spotlight with frenetic comebacks and his high-level piano playing. Like all exceptional comedies, there's a massive emotional payload waiting until the final act and Moore is certainly a guy who can carry it all on his back. I think my qualms are how Minelli doesn't totally fit or match Moore's energy, and how some of the focus gets away from the Gielgud-Moore relationship. Overall Arthur is 100% quotable, absolutely endearing, and something perfectly pleasant for an easy night of movie watching.

reviews.author: Gh0stman
reviews.text: At Any Price is a superb rural melodrama that's morally and dramatically complex and is oddly unappreciated. With two excellent performances by Efron and Quaid, the film revolves around the duo's father and son relationship and each character's desire to excel in their respective fields, race car driving and farming. Both men quickly find themselves in dilemmas that challenge their prospective futures and their self-images. It's intelligently made by Ramin Bahrani and under his guidance, the film avoids easy cliches and answers. Perhaps the real reason why critics and audiences didn't take to the movie was because of its dubious depiction of Americana culture and the agriculture business. Its story shatters the fantasy of the American Dream so many hold dear.

reviews.text: Rodney Dangerfield plays Thornton Melon, an uneducated, self made millionaire who enrolls in college in order to support his son, Jason, played by Keith Gordon. Jason is unsure whether he wants to remain in college. Thornton becomes super popular at school, cracking jokes and throwing wild parties. Meanwhile, Jason is trying to fit in with his classmates and wants to make the swim team. Back to School is a very entertaining 80’s comedy. Dangerfield is hilarious throwing out his famous one liners right and left. Sally Kellerman plays Dr. Diane Turner, a professor Thornton falls for. The rest of the supporting cast is very good, including Robert Downey Jr., Sam Kinison, Burt Young, Adrienne Barbeau, Ned Beatty, M. Emmet Walsh, and Paxton Whitehead. They all get a chance to shine and Dangerfield’s character is so likable, you can’t help but root for him.

reviews.text: It would appear that some actors and directors go together, as Forrest Gump would say, like peas and carrots. Richard Widmark and John Sturges only made two Westerns together, and that's a real shame, because both of those films are excellent. This film from 1956 kicked it all off, and The Law and Jake Wade from 1958, in which Widmark co-starred alongside Robert Taylor, was the other collaboration between two skillfully talented individuals who each brought something special to the table. Sturges' best work arguably came in the form of his Westerns, but Widmark was known as a man who cut his teeth in noirs, before branching out into different genres with enviable success, and there's a hint of noir…

reviews.text: I love when films touch on subjects that aren’t discussed onscreen as often as they should be. The time period surrounding WWII was perhaps the most profound era in human history, mostly due to how unanimously it affected every area of the world. There were thousands of impactful themes that came out of it and, naturally, a select few rose to the forefront of the film industry, which allowed them to live on for generations through public consumption. However, many other themes were left mostly as memories or as things to be learned only through history textbooks. Luckily, some films at the time did choose to acknowledge less “popular” concepts, and I appreciate when I can stumble upon them; Judgment…

reviews.text: There is a point in Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call - New Orleans where the absurdity hits a boiling point and it goes from an OK police procedural to an absolutely nutso character study. I would imagine most people would consider that moment to be when Nic Cage's Bad Lieutenant, Terrence McDonagh, watches two imaginary lizards cavorting on his coffee table while conducting a police stakeout. For me, that moment is laughably absurd, but the real launchpad into Cage/Herzog hysterics is the scene where McDonagh reveals himself to two old biddies and threatens their lives, all while standing in a corner, nonchalantly shaving. Everything after became an increasingly bizarre and increasingly enjoyable journey into this madman's schemes.

reviews.author: Scott Anderson
reviews.text: Occasionally, I just want to sit down and watch a film, any film, as long as it fits into a specific genre. I might say "I'm in the mood for a comedy" or "I could go for a kick ass Sci Fi right now", and then I walk over to the wall o' film and find exactly what I am looking for to whet my appetite. As the clock struck midnight and a new day began, I realized what I was looking for at the moment. reviews.text: Somewhat mixed on this half-fearless, half-conventional attempt to approximate an artist flourishing before our eyes. But there’s flashes of beauty and invention. Schnabel demonstrates an elevated and urgent sense of portraiture as Basquiat begins a mural canvas set to “Flamenco Sketches” before quickly making way for a quick-cutting montage as “White Lines” blares, in less than 30 seconds. It’s such an economical, elegant explication of Basquiat’s style and process within the bounds of a 25-year leap in Black American music. Super refined and intentional, and the kind of movement only a movie can communicate.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Julian Schnabel’s tribute to his friend and fellow painter Jean-Michel Basquiat is less a conventional biopic than an impressionistic, sensory immersion into the much-mythologized downtown-Manhattan art world of the 1980s. Jeffrey Wright, in his first lead film role, stars as the visionary artist whose rise from graffiti tagger to art star forces him to confront the glare of sudden fame, along with racism, his own struggles with addiction, and the difficulties of being self-determining and free in America. Bolstered by an ensemble cast that includes a sublime performance by David Bowie channeling Andy Warhol, Schnabel’s directorial debut—presented here in the filmmaker’s own luminous black-and-white remastering—is a profoundly expressive elegy for a radiant life cut short.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Maybe I need to pay more attention, but I feel like this didn't really tell me all that much about Basquiat's life? His (well, a) personality is present, and it has moments where it feels compelling, where you see a spark of someone you want to know more about. Those moments, though, never go further, and the parade of familiar faces and characters are little more than cameos that provide little context. I don't know what Basquiat was actually like, but it seems unlikely that he was so... devoid, disconnected, that his art and his life weren't somehow more strongly bound, that the experiences we see could not be somehow more connected to the art we see. reviews.text: Decided to revisit this in light of going to see the new live action film tomorrow. I'm not sure I ever actually saw the entire OVA growing up, though I was well aware of it, and had certainly seen some of it. It's a flawed piece of work, adapting two volumes of the manga in two brief episodes, totaling less than an hour. The pace is thus rushed, and the dialogue full of exposition. Nonetheless the core concepts and style make it very enjoyable and impressively poignant in it's final moments. The art is great, packed with violence and detail, and the score is pretty killer too. It's no surprise that it made the impression it did, even in this sample sized format, and I'm really looking forward to seeing the new film. It's simply exciting to live in an age where this sort of niche media can be adapted and put out at such a large scale.

reviews.text: Beyond Rangoon, directed by John Boorman, is a film that ambitiously seeks to blend political upheaval with personal redemption. Set against the backdrop of Burma’s 1988 pro-democracy protests, the film follows Laura Bowman (Patricia Arquette), an American tourist who inadvertently becomes embroiled in the country's violent struggle for freedom. Arquette’s performance as Laura is commendable. She brings a raw vulnerability to the role, portraying a woman grappling with grief and loss after the murder of her family. Her journey from passive observer to active participant in Burma's turmoil is compelling, even if the script doesn’t always give her the depth she deserves. Arquette’s portrayal is a reminder of her range, yet the character’s development feels more like a series of plot…

reviews.author: Lara Pop
reviews.text: My first Joe D'Amato and I'm kind of speechless. Buio Omega encapsulates the two words that serve as the epitome of Italian horror films: sick tenderness. This film is one of the most visually merciless I've seen and yet it is one of the most tender, in a perversely twisted way, of course. There is everything here: gravedigging, cannibalism, adult breastfeeding, preserving a dead body, chopping off limbs and dissolving them in acid, having sex next to a corpse, passionately kissing said corpse... and yet what lies underneath the film is a twisted tragedy about a man who can't get over the death of his love. This combo shouldn't work but I'll be damned if Joe D'Amato doesn't pull it off. Add a hypnotic Goblin soundtrack to the mix and you have yourself the sickest brew of 70s Italian sleaze. Can't wait to see more from the guy.

reviews.text: Everything in Big Fish feels, well, big. In Bloom's stories the greens are greener, the whites glow, the camera never stops moving. When the camera isn't moving we are in some strange angle. Whether that be in the corner of a house, looking directly down at the subject, or perhaps perfectly symmetrical with everything else in the frame. Every moment in Bloom's life feels bigger than it actually is. Unlike Forrest Gump (because the comparison feels inevitable) these moments aren't historically significant, but they matter a hell of a lot to not only Edward Bloom, but those who helped along the way.

reviews.author: Jacob
reviews.text: All the BROCKHAMPTON music videos have been great -- Billy Star is so much more. It's clear that Kevin Abstract loves movies, and he has a real talent for making them too. The narrative here is just strong enough to give these 20 minutes momentum, but it's also intentionally limited for the sake of the music. Transitions between story and song feel surprisingly natural, and the songs generally succeed at progressing the narrative on at least a thematic scale. The heavily saturated colors are to be expected, but I really was surprised by how gorgeous the compositions were. It's a difficult feat to shoot in public spaces and make the lighting look that good. Above all else, Billy Star manages to be expertly crafted while feeling effortless and full of life. Easily one of the most vibrant short films I've seen in a while.

reviews.text: One of my personal favorite slashers. Love the frequently moody wide-angle compositions, patient camera moves (and zooms!), artificial glow of the Christmas lights, and quaint lived-in hangout quality to its performances (actually quite funny with a crowd!) that really makes you notice the silence of its eventual bare soundscape when the girls start disappearing and bodies piling. The sheer quiet intensity of its cross-cutting, split-diopters, and (post-Giallo, pre-Halloween) POV imagery nearly send Christmas caroling and ringing rotary phones into the realm of the metaphysically terrifying... Love the killer's eye poking out of the closet, the shot of the swinging hook cutting to the sorority house mom being yanked up into the attic, the glass unicorn kill, the iconic "the call is…

reviews.author: Holli
reviews.text: i went in a expecting a fun, campy, christmas time slasher and instead got one of the most bone chilling horror films i've seen in ages. not because of the actual murders themselves, but because of the abuse, control, and manipulation the characters undergo - something too many women face from men in their life. that feeling of never being safe, not even in your own home or in your own body. this could have very easily been a misogynistic mess, but instead it's a feminist piece of work that subverts all conventions associated with the treatment of women in that subgenre. one of the best horror films i've seen in a while.

reviews.author: David W
reviews.text: When I was 12, I accompanied my father and older sister to a Drive-In double feature of Blood Beach and Zombie. Zombie made a deep impression and prompted me a couple years later to seek out (at our local video stores) as many “Euro Horror” films as I could find to rent. Blood Beach made no impression whatsoever, except in the form of ennui. So, multiple decades later, what reason could I possibly have for rewatching a film that nearly bored me to death on its first release? I honestly don’t know. But what’s done is done. I accept full responsibility for the consequences.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: Around the midpoint of BLOOD SHACK, Carolyn Brandt takes a somnambulistic midnight stroll. The wind whips her hair. The moonlight catches her eyes. The dark blue sky outlines her path. It’s poetic, chilling, and beautiful, like the climax from I WALKED WITH A ZOMBIE combined with the artsy minimalism of Roberta Findlay’s A WOMAN’S TORMENT. This scene is at odds with the rest of the movie, which jams together mundane narration, ill-fitting music cues, and The Chooper’s baffling attack scenes. But that’s why I love it. reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: Roberta Findlay certainly has a solid directorial hand/eye at work in this this low-budget sorority haunted house slasher. Well-constructed shot transitions, indirect lighting, solid composition, all are hallmarks of a sensibility at work that makes this look far better than most movies of its period and format. What happens when a bunch of pledges are made to weekend in a fake haunted ex-brothel which is an actual haunted ex-brothel? The girls all have realistic, grounded personalities, and their exploration of the house proceeds organically and coherently, as the movie's narrative linking past and present unfolds. The camera moves from from room-to-room as the pledges do, frequently lit ambiently with flashlights, adding to a sense of discovery. The focus is frequently…

reviews.text: BLOOD SISTERS is in a long line of sorority slashers (THE INITIATION, THE HOUSE ON SORORITY ROW, BLACK CHRISTMAS, HELL NIGHT, etc.) and while it doesn’t add anything new to the sub-genre, it does have dialogue that is actually more in line with how young women actually talk to each other. This is because the script was written and directed by an actual woman, horror legend and classic New York City curmudgeon Roberta Findlay. Even after the passing of her husband and long-time collaborator Michael Findlay, she continued pumping out horror films. She wrote, directed, produced, composed, and shot at a time when there were painfully few women working in the genre. While her movies still have plenty of nudity…

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: It's a shame that Franco never made another slasher film, because Bloody Moon is pure, fractured perfection. Literally beamed in from some German-Spanish galaxy completely foreign to our own where everyone looks and dresses perfectly, where boarding schools are at hotel pools and where the killer isn't the one that's into incest. Nothing makes sense: knife wounds move from scene-to-scene, and a woman tells the killer to take off the mask that he was never wearing. The music alternates between partially-diagetic AM gold guitar licks, Throbbing Gristle outtakes and half a dozen amazing original songs (yes, they're on Spotify!). Nobody could shoot sleaze like Franco. I want that one girl's Grace Jones sweater SO BADLY.

reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: As they say in the movie, “Suffering is good for pleasure!” Produced to cash in on the first American slasher wave and directed with grace by Jess Franco, BLOODY MOON is the apex of Spanish slash-trash eloquence. It contains incest, disco-synth dance-offs, beautiful landscapes, an unforgettable decapitation scene, and a little kid who gets run over by a Rolls Royce. Visually exotic and rarely conventional, this movie deserves a place in your perverted heart. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: By the middle of the 1960s it was undeniable that the baby-boomers were on the rise and the World War II generation was on the decline. While many in the older generation responded to this phenomenon with fear and aggression, others found it fascinating. Having already completed a trilogy of films (L'avventura, La Notte and L'eclisse) in effort to understand his own generation's ennui, 54 year-old Italian filmmaker Michelangelo Antonioni decided it was now time to see what gave the younger generation angst. The resultant film Blow-Up, is a beautiful synthesis of plot and theme. The character of Thomas has a hole inside himself which he desperately wants to fill. He is also a good pick for a sports movie because sentiment is so low among his preoccupations but not even he can redeem the soft ending in Ron Shelton's not-good script. reviews.text: For a while in the early 1980's, John Badham had something of a lock on the half-baked paranoid tech thriller, making War Games, Blue Thunder and Short Circuit within a few years of each other, dealing with AI-directed nuclear war, militarized policing and battlefield robotics respectively. Blue Thunder, in particular, is a strange admixture of the voyeuristically sleazy and the politically naive in that police surveillance of citizenry to satisfy the hungry male gaze is kinda OK, but the same activities applied toward a political agenda are a real no-no. In the 1980's, police helicopters were a tangible manifestation of domestic imperial oppression, especially in Los Angeles, where they were used to hem in and control poor predominantly non-white neighborhoods…

There is a conspiracy thrown in for Roy to try and uncover but who cares about that when you have helicopter chases under low bridges, explosions, police cars being destroyed, and 1980s computer technology. reviews.text: Such a shame so few understood this movie. Even when the title kinda gives it away. It doesn't matter what event happened (or why), this is a film purely about how 2 people react in different ways to that event. One person acts practically (the male) and the other acts emotionally to it. The guy doesn't realize the devastating effect the loss of friends and family is having on his girlfriend as he's just happy the two of them are still together. The realization comes to him like a hammer to the head however at the end. I thought this was a fantastic film that stripped away everything from the apocalypse down to the bare bones. No zombies, no gangs, no explosions, or explanations. I'm pretty sure it's never been done like this before. Btw, BOKEH is a photographic term meaning to have things out of focus. Now you know. reviews.author: K. Austin Collins
reviews.text: The carnage here is essential. So is the humor. The laid-back bullshitting of the first set of cops is what initially caught me; Vaughn's ability to colonize a space with his height is another high point. The prison half of the movie is an incredible descent into one of the weirdest, most shit-streaked visions of hell I've seen in recent memory--which is another reason I don't need a backstory. The willingness to break a guard's arm to get sent to a max security prison, only to hold that prison hostage until you're sent to live among the most damned of its prisoners, says more than any language, or plot, or fabricated insight could say. And the images speak for themselves, too: the vast moral and behavioral gap between the earthen dank of that last prison versus the bright sense of spaciousness and opportunity in The Fridge, with its YMCA-friendly cops who compliment the size of your dick, is pretty incredible.

Craig Zahler had already proven with his debut film Bone Tomahawk—shocking everyone with the way his restrained, novelistic approach to style and writing eventually gave way to grindhouse carnage—he’s definitely a filmmaker to watch out for, and probably a psychopath. Brawl in Cell Block 99 is no different, his still, detached style and rigorous pacing this time applied to a noir-inspired, apocalyptic descent into the American prison system. Vince Vaughan stars as Bradley (not Brad, Bradley) Thomas, a quiet, composed man in the body of a giant, who—after he’s laid off from his towing job turns to drug-running to take care of his wife and unborn child—when a drug deal goes violently wrong is blamed and blackmailed…

Para mejorarlo aún más, Wim Wenders toma su cámara y retrata la melancólica historia de la agrupación 'Buena vista Social Club', conformada por estrellas olvidadas del son cubano, como Compay Segundo, Ibrahim Ferrer o Rubén González, algunos con edades cercanas al centenario.

Y un día decidí verla, y lo que vi, fue la mejor película que vi ese mes y uno de los mejores documentales que he visto en mi vida.

reviews.author: Steven Sheehan
reviews.text: With the re-opening of relations between Cuba and America along with the death of Fidal Castro and the last tour for the Buenos Vista Social Club planned, releasing a sequel to the 1999 Oscar nominated documentary appeared to make sense. Renowned documentarian Lucy Walker was eager to bring her passion for Cuban music and culture to the project by connecting the political history of the country with the music, an element sorely missing from the first film. Unfortunately the version we see now is not the film Walker wanted to make due to significant changes made in the final cut that were taken out of her hands.

reviews.author: Alejandro Riera
reviews.text: A far superior documentary than Wenders' enjoyably hagiographic and, let's face it, promotional documentary; yet it also works as a perfect complement to it. "Buena Vista Social Club: Adiós" offers historical and musicological context to these musicians' lives and their late career success. And when it comes to archival footage, Lucy Walker certainly struck gold when digging deep in Cuba's TV and film archives. My favorite, without a doubt, is every single piece of footage featuring the Cuarteto D'Aida (founded by sisters Haydee and Imara Portuondo), especially one where they sing a really catchy jingle for Winston cigarettes. Kudos to Walker for giving the man behind the Buena Vista Social Club and the Afro-Cuban All Stars, Juan de Marco González,…

reviews.author: Maxwell Linge
reviews.text: I'd thought that I was watching the doc that was released in 1999 but this is, in fact, a follow-up production. It has clips from the 1999 one about the assembling of the artists but adds to it with clips from their successful tours in many cities, including a session at the White House. The deaths of some of the musicians is covered as well. On this note, it's incredible to see some of them performing at high calibre at such an old age, particularly Ibrahim Ferrer's voice that still seems lively just before his passing at the age of 78yrs.

reviews.author: Tomasina
reviews.text: Going back to Cuba to visit with the sensational (and elderly) local talent almost 2 decades after they became internationally known. The film starts a little slow, but it doesn’t take too long and there is the “mojo”! If you love the music or miss the stars from the original film and concert it’s a must-see. It is more informal than the first film, but it is as astonishing and moving as the 1999 documentary. (in time: the “Adiós” is not a figure of speech, there are actual goodbyes) 🙏💐

reviews.text: The title suggests a valedictory follow-up to Wim Wenders’ 1999 documentary, and director Lucy Walker (The Crash Reel) does offer some of that. It’s also several other different things at the same time, which makes for a sporadically entertaining missed opportunity. For the first hour, Walker mostly offers context for the celebrated 1990s gathering of legendary Cuban musicians orchestrated by Ry Cooder, including details about the artists’ lives and behind-the-scenes rehearsal footage. That makes it almost more of an expansion of Buena Vista Social Club than a sequel, covering a lot of the same ground but in more detail—not much of which is as interesting as just listening to them play. Eventually Walker focuses briefly on vocalist Ibrahim Ferrer, and…

reviews.text: Bullet Ballet should be considered in the pantheon of perfect film names. A highly stylized symphony of violence where the level of violence goes on a meteoric rise as the film progresses. In a world that is as bleak as the monochrome that it's shot in, the downward spiral of all the characters involved is seemingly avoidable but seldom avoided. Shinya Tsukamoto has created one of the grittiest looks at extremely detached and hopeless individuals. The closed spaces, the narrow alleyways, the dead ends - claustrophobia runs wild in Bullet Ballet. The claustrophobic imagery is an assault to the senses. And it's oh so good.

reviews.text: There are queer films that reify queer identity, films that celebrate it, films that honor it, films that depict it, and films that examine it. There are films that denigrate it, exploit it, deride it, misrepresent it, or use it simply as a superficial sheen over straight stories. And then there are films that don't so much depict queerness as they depict homophobia. I don't mean they are homophobic films; I mean they focus more on the homophobia than the identity, humanity, or reality of queer people. And usually, these films end up being coarse gay misery films or tired cliches.

Director Daniel Barnz must have seen something of purpose and pertinence that separates Cake from any run-of-the-mill drama, but his notions fail to become tangible. The film is deprived of any distinctive potency, themes and bonafide creativity but is inundated with insipidness and insubstantiality; feebly vocalizing its meditation on....life? Grief? Absolution? I'm not sure what it aims to be, but Cake's ambition regrettably remains equivocal.

reviews.text: We're really in the golden age of physical media right now, with niche Blu-Ray companies releasing better and better editions of worse and worse movies. God bless Severin for reaching deep into the barrel, scraping the bottom, finding Joe D'Amato's rip-off of Caligula (1979), and releasing it in a handsome, extras-packed box set alongside Bruno Mattei's Caligula & Messalina. The disc contains two cuts - a 95-minute bowdlerized version, and a 121-minute cut with a lot of hardcore sex scenes. Though 121 minutes is entirely too much time to spend on something like this, I opted for the longer cut anyway, because if you're going to watch this you might as well watch it.

reviews.text: watched Justin Decloux's live-stream of the 35mm director's cut that Pyun's widow had digitized - and it is wildly different and vastly better than the theatrical cut. (also different than the cut that Pyun self-released like 12 years ago.) It's beautiful and moody and somber, there's barely any action until the end, the score is lovely, it makes the Red Skull feel... tragic. Lot of stuff that feels jarring or bizarre in the theatrical cut is given context and coherence here. It's also not in chronological order, about 20 minutes longer, and certain scenes are swapped out with alternate versions. Whole vibe reminds me of that bit in The Winter Soldier where Steve Rogers in present day tries talking to old Peggy, and she completely forgets their conversation by the end of the scene. Loved this.

Red Skull, in particular, is so much better served by this cut. A genuinely moving arc! Matt Salinger is much better served by this cut, as well. He’s still not great but working the past and present around each other gives him more personality. You definitely understand why they cast him. Some shots where he’s a dead ringer for Steve Rogers, as drawn by Howard Chaykin. So much on this movie's mind, too: Disaffected yuppies as henchmen, far more anti-war than most modern blockbusters, a president willing to tank the economy to save the environment. It's kind of remarkable.

reviews.text: Located in the dusty stretch of hell that lies between homage and pastiche, Mickey Keating’s “Carnage Park” is a lean, mean, motherfucker of a movie that confirms the young director’s outsized potential but fails to follow through on his most explicit promise. A twisted “true crime” story that’s heavily indebted to Quentin Tarantino and boasts all the historical validity of “Inglourious Basterds,” this gnarly gore-fest opens with the kind of reckless, apocryphal declaration that’s only made by geniuses or kids too young to know any better: “The film you are about to see is perhaps the most bizarre episode in the annals of American crime.” That’s a mighty big gauntlet to drop at the feet of an unsuspecting audience, but “Carnage Park” nearly lives up to its own hype — at least for a little while, anyway.

reviews.text: It’s got a good sun-baked, sweltering look, and I like Ashley Bell, but all in all this is pretty fucking obnoxious. And the choppy, mannered, non-linear, deliberately disorienting way they’ve edited it makes it incoherent: we lose track of what’s happening, and when, and where everybody is in relation to each other. Most importantly, though, we stop caring. At about the 55-minute mark (of an 80-minute movie), I realized that I’d tuned out completely, so I whipped out the cell phone and started playing my little word search game until the credits rolled. reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: On paper, a structure that compares vigilante groups on either side of the U.S.-Mexico border makes a lot of sense. But in practice, the scenes in Mexico (where a vigilante group called the Autodefensas springs up to protect locals from a drug cartel that is intimidating and murdering the populace) are a lot more compelling than the ones in America (where a bunch of right-wingers patrol the border to little effect). It feels like director Matthew Heineman recognized that too; after early scenes establish a back-and-forth structure, the Americans fade into the background while the leader of the Autodefensas, Dr. José Mireles, becomes the main protagonist. Massive respect to Heineman for his fearless work in the field, but if he'd applied an equally bold approach in the editing room and cut the U.S. scenes entirely, he'd have an even stronger documentary.

reviews.text: These days the most violence I experience is all the pushing and shoving everyone does to make sure they get a seat on the train at the end of the work day. On the other hand, violence sizzled and cracked all around me like an exposed live wire on the loose when I was growing up. My suburb might have looked liked it was lifted straight out of the set of a Spielberg movie, but we lived on the periphery of one the most crime-ridden centres of my city. Gang and drug-related beatings, stabbings and shootings laced every day life with a slither of fear that was ever present.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A playfully broad, kitschy 90s hard-boiled film noir pastiche set in an alternate 1948 Los Angeles where Lovecraftian supernatural horror runs casually rampant. Produced by Tales from the Crypt era HBO and directed by future Goldeneye and Casino Royale director Martin Campbell, this actually has fairly handsome production values for a TV movie: great charmingly artificial period production design/costuming, wonderfully exaggerated and colorful lighting choices, some goofy and surprisingly gruesome 80s creature feature puppet FX including gremlins, werewolves, a gigantic Old Ones finale that looks like the Rancor from Star Wars meets The Blob.

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: Pretty much junk food for Lovecraft fans with Martin Campbell - who gave us both Goldeneye and the very overlooked No Escape - turning in inspired noir-kitsch that feels more like the product of Full Moon than HBO. It's impressively gory, has goofy puppet effects to spare and doesn't lean too hard on the Lovecraft lore - it honestly feels like one of those FMV PC games turned into a feature length movie, which probably means nothing unless you played Night Trap and/or Under a Killing Moon a lot in the 90s.

reviews.author: Daniel Reifferscheid
reviews.text: In which first time director John Boorman takes the already quite avante garde template of Richard Lester's Beatles films and, hitching his wagon to the Dave Clarck Five (a fascinating case themselves - once as big as the Beatles, now not even in the top100 of most famous 60's hit makers), uses it to portray a cold, grey England that is anything but swinging. A skeletal plot based around Dave and his girl evading some authority figures is the only concession towards the genre in a film featuring an abadoned holiday resort, a couple straight out of a Pinter play and hippies so burned out you'd think this was made in 1975. Lord knows what the teenyboppers made of all of it.

reviews.text: Chaos is a pretty basic and mostly forgettable cop action thriller that's heavy on the obvious twists and fairly light on having a believable or realistic plot, even if it is somewhat enjoyable junk. Most of why it is fun is due to it having a solid cast who take their cookie-cutter roles and inject a bit of life into it. There's also a few decent action sequences to liven up the mechanical storytelling and the final twist that's pretty easy to predict for the kind of movie this is. The bigger problem is just that the whole thing is kind of completely unremarkable in every way, since Chaos is the kind of action movie that, while watchable enough, you'll probably forget about five minutes after finishing it.

reviews.author: jrhovind
reviews.text: Relic from a very specifically earnest chapter in the history of indie American filmmaking, a sad-sack tour back and forth across Chicago that can never shake its clearly stage-bound roots. All manner of 90s indie stars get their turn in the backseat, and yet none of the vignettes amount to much more than a doodle (unless Laurie Metcalf’s brittle yuppie getting head and then going on her way is supposed to have something to say about anything beyond itself). The whole thing feels like the product of an especially low-stakes writers’ workshop; finally aiming for something like poignancy with Julianne Moore’s troubled client at the end of an already long day, achieving just another variation of its own moody little miserabilism.

Some of them I've absolutely loved, and some I was left thinking "what was the point?" but I guess sometimes not having a point is the point.Some are comedic but most of them have this mundane feeling, a sort of melancholy "is this life?" kind of attitude. reviews.text: A heady psychosexual drama that’s steeped in dense anxieties and rich European glamour (the film was partially funded by Chanel), Olivier Assayas’s latest finds the French auteur at the very top of his game. Combining the acute professional paranoia of All About Eve with the existential crisis of Persona, Clouds of Sils Maria stars the remarkably accomplished Juliette Binoche as Maria Enders, a fading star who’s agreed to be in a revival of the play that made her famous as a young ingenue. This time, however, Maria isn’t performing the part of the seductive teenager awakening to the power of her sexuality; she’s playing the older woman who’s wrapped around the girl’s finger. Retreating to the Swiss Alps with her unfailingly honest assistant (Kristen Stewart, a deadpan revelation), Maria begins a rehearsal process that will force her to grapple with the presentness of her past.

reviews.author: Martin
reviews.text: Collective:Unconscious is the rare anthology film where each segment is equally strong. Held together by dream logic, it connects universal, primal fears (loneliness, social humiliation, motherhood, death) and familiar forms (black and white 'art film', music video, teen drama, '90s game show, horror film) with the bizarrely specific details personal to each dreamer/director. At the same time, we don't dream in a vacuum; across all the segments there are undercurrents and sometimes overtones of social critique along gender and racial lines. It is a wholly unnerving, disturbing, even profound insight into the subconscious, an experiment I hope will be repeated.

Money quickly runs out and the pair gradually get roped into a sordid lifestyle of prostitution and porn. Walker's tone is all over the place, almost like he's undecided if he wants to make a bawdy sex romp or the grim cross-cutting sequence of everyone hitting bottom in BOOGIE NIGHTS. Likewise,…

reviews.author: CJ
reviews.text: Pete Walker's sexploitative look at the emptiness of "swinging" London is impressively dark at times, for the genre (and a far cry from your usual nudge-nudge Robin Askwith fare) but, in a way, it's this almost kitchen-sink realism that lets it down a little. There are never any great consequences within the slight narrative and while Askwith and Janet Lynn play their parts - naive teens from the countryside, visiting London and getting sucked into a world of vice - with a degree of charisma and charm, the film never quite fully lifts off for me. Part of this may be thanks to the BFI Flipside collection releasing many more superior movies of the era that show the dark side of London's sex industry. As skillfully shot as it is, this certainly doesn't hold a candle to the haunting likes of Lindsay Shonteff's Permissive.

reviews.author: Cliff
reviews.text: It may be a sexploitation movie starring Robin Asquith, but he hadn't by this point found his screen personality. That's not helped by what seems like a strict adherence to the dialogue written in Murray Smith's screenplay; everyone speaks with the same voice, with the inexperienced actors sticking to the lines instead of tweaking them to fit their characters. It's also jarring how many opportunities for comic misunderstandings and double entendres are ignored, but that's okay because as a viewer you can make your own jokes.

He is just so good at the dead-eyed, "foully and berserkly rich" pretty boy surface asked of him here; an indifferent specter navigating a world where "the logical extension of business is murder", amused by the chaos that circles his removed comfort…

Remarkable (for me, at least) only because I caught the ending of this as a child while visiting a friend's house, and the walk home thereafter (alone, down a short stretch of rural road--hey, it was the '80s) terrified me more than the actual movie. I'd been wanting to identify this movie for literal decades and had accepted that I'd either misremembered it or had seen it and failed to recognize it, until I downloaded this film on a whim (thanks to the Saul connection, whose books I devoured as a teen). And while this movie isn't exactly worth waiting forty years to see, it's gratifying to know that it actually exists, and pretty much the way I remembered.

reviews.text: An electric chamber piece that couldn’t more perfectly complement “Dunkirk” if Christopher Nolan wrote it, “Darkest Hour” is as rousing and ferocious as Winston Churchill was himself. It’s also a hell of a lot more controlled. Unfolding with the clockwork precision of a Broadway play — director Joe Wright has always been at his best when he’s been at his most theatrical — this tightly coiled retelling of Churchill’s first days in office is more than (yet another) passionate appeal to our collective goodness, it’s a deliciously unsubtle testament to the power of words and their infinite capacity to inspire.

My close friends who I've discussed history and/or politics with (usually drunkenly) have experienced what I'm going to dub "the Churchill conversation" which is where I basically argue that Winston Churchill is the most overrated person in history. To put my argument succinctly: he was elitist, stupid, immoral, and (most importantly) usually wrong. He did terrible things throughout his entire career but just so happened to do the right thing during World War Two (and was helped by many factors outside his control).…

reviews.text: A bleak world of widespread rapacity, lying, and self-delusion, where each character's path constantly reveals itself, and John Schlesinger doesn't manipulate emotion or overdramatize, expressing each person's tormented soul with a delicate beauty and unshakable truth of feeling. The characters' actions and motivations are completely described by them in straightforward and direct conversation that is neither contrived nor judgmental. Darling jumps between bright and dreary, pondering the cost of deception and the anguish of attempting to build a reputation for yourself when you don't have anything, acting more as a broad social allegory than anything else.

reviews.text: Diana Scott is a glamorous woman who has no limits, however her independence and lack of containment is a limit within itself. Her life consists of roaming around the streets of London, fooling with men, and getting glimpses of whatever job she wants, but she is in a constant state of boredom despite this intense freedom. The relationships she puts herself in - whether they’re long or short - always feel dry, which is a subtle way that John Schlesinger critiques both femininity and masculinity. The ability she has to present herself as a model is an unprecedented way to cover up the difficulty and emptiness of her personal lifestyle. At one point in the film, she becomes a literal princess, yet her sentiment is unsatisfactory. When under control, she’s unhappy, when in control, she’s bored

The classy type of anthology stories of ghosts and other weirdness (golf!), complete with a compelling wraparound and a crazy final few minutes.

reviews.author: Tony the Terror
reviews.text: I watched this because I love horror anthologies and because one of the segments is set at Christmas. All of the segments were fun, but unexpectedly it was the wraparound that I found most interesting. This guy comes to a country house and meets a group of people and realizes they are all part of a recurring dream he’s been having. He listens to stories from each of the guests before the dark part of his dream starts to come true and that is where we get some seriously creepy scenes including a life size ventriloquist dummy coming after the poor guy.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Dead of Night, the original horror anthology, depicts five tales of terror, cleverly wound around a central wraparound story following a man with a recurring nightmare. The film has a lot of class and is very "British" in the traditional sense. The stories are all rather tame but they are entertaining in their own right and the film has good variety - including ghosts, premonitions, a ventriloquist dummy and a man getting wound up by a dodgy mirror. The film has definitely dated but there are a lot of ideas and imagery here that would go on to influence huge genre films later on. Of course the stories vary in quality and everyone will have their own favourite - I would say that the film saves the best for last and the dummy sequence is by far the standout.

reviews.author: Lara Pop
reviews.text: Dead of Night was a pleasantly drifting experience. It carried me on its placid waves of 1940s style gothic horror it offered in each of its ghost story sketches, but then came the last anecdote with Michael Redgrave and his dissociative personality disorder pre-dating Hitchcock's Psycho but with a ventriloquist's dummy instead of a mother figure, and the pleasant drifting all but turned into a nightmare. But then, luckily, I woke up. Or did I...?

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: “Andy’s home. Some boys never come home.” The grief of a family and the guilt of a country. Self-inflicted national tragedy leading to domestic decay. Post-Vietnam destruction of the American ideal. A home broken by our own inability to accept the repercussions of our actions, the fate we thrust upon our children, and the façade shattered by horrors we never thought we’d have to face. It’s “The Monkey’s Paw” mixed with A24 elevation and EC Comics pulp, sprinkled with the blood & sweat of a rookie Tom Savini and oozing an atmosphere so cozy and worn-in that you cower in unassuming fear whenever something happens that’s as shocking as Andy strangling the family dog in front of a bunch of kids. It’s a fucking vibe and a half—one of those movies that gives your soul goosebumps and makes you hang your head in shame.

reviews.text: Please remember that the American invasion of Vietnam--following French occupation--was an act of imperialist war that was a vile genocidal attempt at conquest in the name of suppressing the rights of the Vietnamese to self-determination. You can argue all you want that the draft somehow mitigated the level of culpability of American soldiers, but the My Lai Massacre wasn't an act done under coercion. PTSD in returning soldiers and certainly the lack of support or medical care for them after they stopped being weapons of the empire is an aspect of the capitalist treatment of non-bourgeois people as disposable. reviews.text: 'Deathdream' (also known as 'Dead of Night') packs the anger, grief, and confusion of an entire era into one 88-minute film. And it does so without the weight of self-importance that so many of our modern, more prestigious, and socially minded horror productions tend to bear. As Travis Crawford succinctly puts it, what makes 'Deathdream' and other classic 1970s horror films so effective is that the earlier productions “deftly handled themes of great importance, but in a way that only serves to give their work more emotional resonance and power.”

reviews.text: "Deadly Friend" is something of a reverse "Short Circuit" (1986). As the "Short Circuit" is centralized upon a plot where we take a weaponized robotic killing machine, and a bolt of lightning injects the humanistic sensibility into things, "Deadly Friend" takes an element that was once very human and turns it into the killing machine. There's not really much wrong with creating a story like that if its dynamic, but the wayward process of the story doesn't really garner any fanbase attachment. As a result, the film becomes unique in that is a side note for major horror master, Wes Craven, but even Craven has gone on to say that it was one of his worse films in production. Regardless…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Disconnected" is a 1984 slasher directed by Gorman Bechard. Recently watching his film "Psychos in Love" (1987) and being enamored by its clever narrative build, I ventured to his film prior, "Disconnected". "Disconnected" was also his first film, holding a lot of the same raw energy as "Psychos in Love" but even more unrefined in its presentation. The unrefined element also aids into its interesting cohesion of story, as there is an easy-to-follow story but yet the film feels purposely done with unanswered questions, like Bechard intended things to be that way.

reviews.text: A testament to Stuart Gordon's skill as a director is that this was shot back-to-back with From Beyond (on the exact same sets!) but the atmosphere here could not be more different. Which he should have, he's pretty good at it.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: A movie with a happy family moving into a nice two story home in a leafy neighborhood that gradually darkens the tone as you find out more about them. The most shocking stuff is the way the kids' more sinister sides come through. With Dennis Weaver and Valerie Harper you're thinking it's going to be lightweight and it's fun and riveting to watch that expectation blow up. It focuses the daughter Mary played by Robin Ignico, whom you can see on the poster on the burning bed. You can't get enough of Robin as this goes on. It's like that with the film, too because of how weird it feels and how well it succeeds. A 1982 made for tv masterpiece.

reviews.text: "Doom Asylum" (1987) is a complete horror schlockfest directed by Richard Friedman. In that vein of things, the film is utterly and completely full of cheesy gore but is self-aware in its intentions to be an over-the-top goofy presentation, rather than some other horror films that hold an energy of being so bad that they are good for accidental reasons. There are many other films that induce some sort of comedy within horror, all situating a tonal balance to directly works according to the narrative. In this subgroup, things like "Return of the Living Dead" (1985), or "Killer Klowns From Outer Space" (1988) are easy acknowledgments that bring this energy, which "Doom Asylum" walked me down that road a bit.…

This very colorful group consists of an indecisive hunk, his girlfriend whose mother died in this same place 10 years earlier, a flamboyant black guy, a nerdy baseball fan, an all-girl rock band trio, and Kristin Davis from Sex In The City (as the daughter of two psychiatrists). There’s also a killer in the asylum who has become a monster after miraculously surviving a car crash on the road outside ten years earlier.
