reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: My idea of a 1931 movie is something like Dracula or one of those early Garbo talkies - static camera, awkward dialogue, millions of rats, etc. - but this has the visual acrobatics of a silent movie, opening on an extended POV shot for no particular reason and very rarely letting up from there. It matches nicely with Jekyll's rationale for his experiments, that he performs them because he can, paying no heed to conservative reservations about how these things just aren't done. It's safe to say that the filmmakers don't take their ostensible moral, about how there are things one just doesn't do, seriously.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Hyde's treatment of Ivy is textbook abuse, so much so that at its most harrowing the scenes between them begin to seem less like a horror movie and more like some Lynchian, surreal exploration of an abusive relationship. But this time around I was struck by how clearly the social hypocrisy surrounding Jekyll is subtly but unmistakably emphasized, and how Hyde's insane possessiveness and domineering are a difference of degree rather than type from the behavior of Muriel's father. Hyde is a scientifically created distillation of Man's evil nature - what's Dad's excuse?

reviews.text: David Wain's A Futile and Stupid Gesture from a couple of years back was a very good screen adaptation on the birth of National Lampoon and the two guys most responsible for its success, Doug Kenney and Henry Beard. It charted the concept, their backstories, and the drug and alcohol dependency that drove them apart and cost one of them their life. It focused also on the rise of certain comedic actors who went on to international success on the back of the National Lampoon branching out into radio, theatre, and eventually cinema. Nothing was off-limits for the magazine, they'd satirise everything from politicians to corporations, celebrities to Religious figures, everyone was fair game.

reviews.author: Jim Morrow
reviews.text: My first experience with National Lampoon was junior year in high school when there was a copy floating around the commons area. That was where all of us dorks, geeks, hippies, trash, and social rejects hung out, so no surprise that 90% of us probably became subscribers. The issue I first saw was "Nostalgia," which had the first iteration of the 1956 High School Yearbook parody that later became Lampoon's first (I think?) special issue a couple years later. That was during the heydays of Kenney, Beard, Miller, Hendra, O'Donoghue etc., so the writing was brilliantly sophomoric, and absolutely spot on hilarious. It stayed that way for five or six years, and I rarely missed an issue.

reviews.author: Paul Schrader
reviews.text: "Dying of the Light," a film I wrote and directed, was taken away from me after the submission of the Director’s Cut (June 2014). Grindstone Pictures and the producers wanted a generic Nick Cage video-on-demand film, while my editorial instincts were pointing toward something more interesting. Grindstone recut, scored, and mixed the film without my input. Subsequently, actors Nicholas Cage and Anton Yeltsin, executive producer Nic Refn and I distanced ourselves from the film. Because we were threatened with lawsuits if we spoke ill of the Grindstone version, our protests took the form of wearing T-shirts bearing the “non-disparagement” clause that prohibited public statements. For now, that’s the only photo I’ll include on this web page. I remain hopeful that someday I will be allowed to finish the film.

reviews.author: Paul Schrader
reviews.text: I'm in the process of editing. I'm trying to use disruptive visual and sound techniques to fit the subject matter. After a second cut I've come to realize that if you do something a little odd no one notices. Subtlety doesn't cut it. Viewers are so used to seeing "wrong" visuals (out of focus, miscomposed images, jump cuts, bad continuity) that they correct the errors in their minds, hardly noticing them. Perhaps this is the result of multitasked viewing and reality TV. Now if you want a viewer to notice something isn't the way it is supposed to be, you have to be OBVIOUS about it. Repeatedly.

reviews.text: This was a fantastic film. I would call this a mix between E.T. and Chronicle. The plot is very similar to that of E.T., kids find alien, alien needs help, kids help alien, government tries to find alien, alien escapes with kids help and goes home. What made this different was the cinematography, which was similar to Chronicle. One kid, Tuck, obsessively videotapes everything, and this leads to several different cameras, being handled by the kids, and creates a very amateur feel. There are also some interactions with other technology, such as scenes from Youtube, and Google Maps. While it is amateur, it still fits perfectly with the film. The plot and cinematography mesh together to create a wonderful beginning, that is augmented by the music and acting. While the ending is bittersweet, I feel it is exactly what this film needed.

reviews.text: On the extras on the Arrow blu ray, part of the Mexican trilogy box set, Robert Rodriguez explains the technique of in-camera-editing. When you are on a very tight budget - this movie is made for $7000 - and shooting on film, you must make sure you don't cut too much film on the editing table. Film is expensive. The same technique is used by low budget masters, like Michael J. Murphy and Andy Milligan. Thanks to this movie, Robert Rodriguez made it to Hollywood. However the works of other low budget filmmakers, who never came near Hollywood, feel somewhat more personal compared to El Mariachi.

reviews.text: Early on the morning of December 21st, 1970, Elvis Presley rolled up to the front gate of the White House with a letter for President Richard Nixon. The King of Rock n'Roll wanted a meeting with the leader of the free world — more specifically, he wanted to be sworn in as an undercover narcotics agent. Presley delivered the handwritten note to a befuddled guard, who passed it up the ladder until it reached H.R. Haldeman, the infamously flinty Chief of Staff. By sunset that evening, Elvis was standing in the Oval Office, posing for a snapshot with a smiling President Nixon. Of all the images in American history, that (now easily Google-able) photograph became the most requested picture in the National Archives. It sounds like an interesting story, but Liza Johnson's asinine "Elvis & Nixon" will shock you with how little you care.

For foreign productions from the 70s, Ōshima's pictures look exquisite, and Empire of Passion is no exception. The film certainly has that 'new wave' aura to it; not surprised at all to find out it's a French Argos Films co-production. A relatively simple tale about guilt and punishment, elevated by it's 'kaidan' format, and directorial vision. Not as life-changing as In the Realm of the Senses, but I'm still excited to check out even more Ōshima films.

reviews.text: Alejandro Jodorowsky creates an autobiographical film about his beginnings in the avant-garde art scene in Santiago and his struggle to break free from parental oppression in order to unleash his creativity. True to his style, the Chilean director delivers a bizarre and imaginative piece of work about a fragment of his life that unfortunately feels excessive in its artificiality, eccentricness, and even superficial in its introspection. Poesía sin fin is a simple story full of the infinite resources that abound in Jodorowsky's filmography, which at this point feel dated, redundant, tired, and seem to indicate that the director has nothing new to offer. A reflective, nostalgic, rather narcissistic, and very tedious film, but one that possesses a truly poignant ending that, in a way, almost makes the journey worthwhile.

reviews.text: A giant hovering rock appears out in the desert, is some kind of alien spacecraft but doesn't initiate contact, so scientists, military, government and a much deeper cast than you'd think from a Sci-Fi Channel TV movie converge on the site to find out its true nature. "Stargate" and "The Abyss" are what it was primarily compared to at the time, but beaming in from the far-off future of 2021 as I am now, my first thought was Villeneuve's "Arrival". It's a mystery box that they proverbially open a little bit at a time, forcing in a couple gratuitous action scenes for the jarheads watching, before revealing important lessons about mankind.

reviews.author: UltimateMovieRankings
reviews.text: A low budget science fiction film that borrows heavily from Stargate, Aliens, The Abyss and many other much better science fiction movies. In this one David Keith plays an all knowing scientist that is brought in by the government to figure out what a huge ice cream cone shaped rock from space is doing landing in the Far East. Turns out the ice cream cone is 4 billion years old and is here fix Planet Earth. Movie is filled with bad special effects, some pretty weak acting and some very low budget sets. Final thought: This is one to avoid.

Then an American character angrily tells a Chinese diplomat "Bhutan is an independent country!" only for the diplomat to calmly respond "So was Nepal." Uh... Mister Screenwriter? Did you mean Tibet? Did nobody bother checking these things before filming the movie? Did James Hong just let this slip through intentionally because he thought it was funny? Idk man

Still, for a Sci-Fi Channel original, the concept has potential (if frustratingly paced) and the CGI sequences, even given its age and budget, are pretty damn impressive at times. Sadly, as hard as it tries, too many elements are mismanaged to make the film worthwhile aside from being a relic of a time before 'so bad it's good' became the predominant goal (sought for but oh so rarely found) for this kind of Blockbuster shelf-warmer.

They're all up there in terms of being genuine genre titans, but one man seems to have been confined to being considered an afterthought, a certain John Sturges, a man who, in my humble opinion, has delivered thrillingly entertaining Westerns time and time again. So he didn't make as many as Ford, but when you consider Sturges had The Magnificent Seven, Gunfight at the OK Corral, Last Train from Gun Hill, Backlash (which I've just watched as a double-bill with The Law and Jake Wade), and…

reviews.text: John Sturges‘ first foray into somewhat bigger budgeted filmmaking is hampered by an unsatisfying script that doesn’t make very much out of a potentially interesting concept.The setting is a remote fort in the Arizona desert that doubles as a Union stockade for captured Confederate soldiers during the days of the Civil War. This scenario was actually handled better by Robert Wise three years earlier in Two Flags West and incomparably better later on by Sam Peckinpah in the flawed but magnificent Major Dundee. Here the Confederate prisoners just stand around most of the time in the hot sun, whistling Dixie, while a few of them hatch ineffectual escape plans.William Holden is the uncompromising Union Captain, who’s disliked even by…

reviews.text: my brain has been so exhausted for the past few days that i haven't had the bandwidth for anything substantial, but i looked at my stack of unseen blurays and realized that a john sturges movie might be just what the doctor ordered. there aren't really any theoretical ideas in a sturges film, no concept beyond the premise, no division of text vs. subtext, he is a director of pure immanence in the sense that it is all about figures positioned in a space and there is zero political or spiritual horizon that divides them except for the basic rules of mortality and the ideological necessity of the genre he is working in (war picture, western, etc.)

reviews.author: Daniel88
reviews.text: Leave it to John Sturges to turn what could have been a highly generic 1950s Western, with an all too familiar plot and setting, into one with memorable and thrilling action set pieces. Admittedly, the first half of Escape from Fort Bravo contains all the tropes your average B-Western, but that is hardly Sturges’ fault. It are especially the final 30 minutes, which for some reason remains a vague early childhood memory when I first watched this one on television, that are a testament to his ability in turning this sort of miniature siege sequence into a great long action sequence without becoming repetitive (which is so often the case in similar 1950s and 1960s ‘Cavalry’ westerns).

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: Having recently watched a couple of westerns that try to treat Native Americans sympathetically but run up against the genre’s limited ability to do so, I found it kind of refreshing to turn to a western that doesn’t bother. The Mescaleros in this film remain mostly faceless plot devices that allow nominal enemies (Union Captain William Holden and the Confederate prisoners he’s trying to return to the titular fort from which they’ve escaped) to set aside their differences and learn to trust and respect each other. It’s certainly not enlightened, but the simplistic nature of the plot enables director John Sturges to prove his skill at handling action sequences.

Immediately at face value, I thought for sure I was going to get some courtroom novelty element based on title and poster art, but that element is basically non-existent in entirety. This isn't a make-or-break element of things at all, but I will argue that if this film instilled a bit more of a gimmick…

reviews.author: Josiah Morgan
reviews.text: Lovely little film examining fragility and sterility, one mind-boggling shot at a time. Hogg simply observes for almost two hours, never interrupting the flow of naturalism and concision within her work - nothing lasts too long but we have enough time to survey each image entirely. One perspective-altering shot right near the beginning is a static shot as a woman draws her own face whilst looking at a two sided mirror, we see the shot from the front as the second side of the mirror reflects abstractions of space and area, motion bouncing every which way. Communication is a foreign object to these characters but intimacy is something they're all too aware of, consistently forced to acknowledge another's presence without…

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: Joanna Hogg's Exhibition is a fascinating film that demands a lot of its audience, but rewards the effort. It's essentially a three hander. D is a performance artist, currently unemployed, who potters about, trying to connect with her husband, H. He's a successful architect, a bit short-tempered and prickly, spending his days in the upstairs study, rolling about in his designer chair on the hard floor like storm clouds brewing. The third player is the house itself, a modernist inner city haven, all glass, and concrete, with big windows onto a courtyard and a view over the noisy neighbourhood.

The hastily recruited team receives no proper training and sets off. They navigate various tissues and organs—the lungs, brain, ear, and lymphatic system—and are attacked by white blood cells at the film’s climax. The story is inventive and interesting. They try on archetypes as if they were wigs or jewelry, with even Banderas' strung-along photographer in a constant state of flux between hopeless attraction, smug condescension and vicious hatred. When I mentioned I'd rewatched this film on Twitter someone said that the movie is good up until the first time Rebecca Romijn speaks, but aside from the pithiness of the line, that notion ignores all that she does. This is the best modeling gig of her career, a collection of poses and gestures in which she can be whomever the men she…

reviews.text: A horny whirlpool of twinned, mirrored, repeated images, never abandoning the audience's perspective but meticulously constructed to meddle with it. A less defensive extension of a lot of what BODY DOUBLE was up to. As De Palma films go this is practically a tonic.

reviews.author: Jude
reviews.text: De Palma goes to Europe and, for the first time, gets really interested in metaphysics: the nature and transference of souls, the encroaching inhumanity of the image as tool and telos, salvation through chance and meaningless structural coincidence. seven years later and no time has passed at all, instead it feels like a different movie collided with this one and some tiny crucial piece got lost in the confusion (but it is wonderfully, gorgeously regained in a dream). some of Hitchock’s influence has been traded in for Eurosleaze’s stumbling towards glorious abstraction, for the better: De Palma has never been freer even at his trashiest. a bathtub overflows and it fills the Seine, seven years later and in a dream

What everyone does in this movie doesn't really make sense, exposition comes in streaks, gore barely comes at all, tempo shifts are clunky, etc, but none of that fundamentally derails Fender Bender. You believe these guys experience something that shakes their understanding of the world. Robert Patrick in particular, as a good guy for once, is just killing it. I wouldn't call it a horror film, as much as I wanted to include this in my on-going horror marathon, but the scene of actual horror is up there with anything produced in the 90s. Nightmare fuel. Better than the best X-Files episode. And Fire in the Sky is still one of the coolest, most evocative movie titles of all time.

Yet this stripped-down unpretentious actioneer essentially amounts to an 87-minute freight train of Donnie Yen badassery and effortless awesomeness, even if the film can't decide if Yen or Louis Koo is the main hero. It is probably the last Arthur Penn movie people would likely watch because it is an Arthur Penn movie, amusing considering it is very dominated by writer Steve Tesich and openly conceived as sort of follow up to his earlier hit Breaking Away. At times, Four Friends suggest a midwest liberal version of Millius Big Wednesday, but nowhere…

Penn is certainly older than the characters here but much of his New Hollywood work spoke to the tensions and failed idealism of the sixties so there is interest in seeing Penn return now with more critical distance. reviews.text: There’s no pleasure in trashing a film as humanistic and well-intentioned as Freeheld, but just because anyone would agree with its message doesn’t mean this glorified Lifetime movie does a worthy job of conveying it. The story itself, based on real-life events that transpired in Ocean County, New Jersey, during the winter of 2005, is a beautiful paean to love, dignity and progress. It begins when Laurel Hester (Julianne Moore), an eminently capable detective who has spent 23 years on the force and roughly 45 years in the closet, commits herself to a much younger woman named Stacie Andree (Ellen Page). When Laurel is diagnosed with terminal cancer, she naturally wants to pass her pension benefits to Stacie so her partner can continue to live in the home they bought together, but local law doesn’t acknowledge same-sex unions. Cue a courageous legal battle that precipitates—and accelerates—a sweeping change across the country.

Hitchcock was a genius of manipulation, though, and FRENZY is a film where I actually enjoy being pushed around while watching it.

reviews.author: Joe A
reviews.text: In 2009, Apatow’s name was synonymous with comedy, largely due to the fact that his name was attached to seemingly every major studio comedy, ask anyone around that time who directed Superbad and their answer would probably be Apatow (people still think this). So by time his actual third feature rolled around, after the explosive success of Knocked Up and 40-Year Old Virgin, many people approached Funny People expecting some variation of the raunchy comedies that circled the drain into something more insightful, except it wasn’t. Instead it was 146 minute black comedy about a comedian reckoning with death. The outcome? Middling reviews and a true financial failure, his first since he penned Walk Hard: The Dewey Cox Story (a brilliant film).

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Classic British gangster film without which Guy Ritchie could not exist and Quentin Tarantino would be significantly different. Michael Caine is precisely as sympathetically psychotic as the best of Scorsese's villain-protagonists. Impeccable pacing and escalation. Some interesting framing choices including an abundance of obstructed close ups (vaguely reminiscent of Wong Kar-Wai). Classy parallel editing especially between a speeding car and a sexual encounter. Controversial film about the tragic irony of vengeance which pushed the boundaries of on-screen sex and violence. A bit slow and convoluted, but rewarding for attentive audiences.

reviews.text: If made another "Heavy Metal", it'd probably not be too dissimilar thematically from the hyperviolent, super-sexualized "Godkiller." Genre veterans Lance Henricksen, Bill Moseley and Nicki Cline lend their voice talents to this futuristic motion-comic which follows a teenage boy navigating a demolished earth as he tries to secure an artificial heart for his dying sister. There's plenty of blood and sex and alien weirdos. Frankly, if they had decided to go with a completely fluid-animated or (gulp) live-action format, it might have just collapsed under it's own extreme concepts. I liked it, but the abrupt ending with "To Be Continued" preceding the credit-roll was jarring, plus it suggests the intention of more to come - Four years have passed since that promise was made...

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The African-French soldier shows them his pictures, and they turn him away. They just ignore him, and in that simple moment, Renoir's film transcends from a simple morality tale, rises above its themes and critiques of politics. It almost silently reveals its awareness of the depth of humanity's flaws as even the heroes in this melodramatic war story can't be the paragons of acceptance or fellowship that Renoir clearly believes humans can be. He spells it out a bit later, showing the parallels between the French and German aristocrats, the antisemitism and classism of the German officer, the antisemitism of the French officers, and so on and so forth. Bonds form between the prisoners, bonds that ultimately prove a salvation of sorts for them, but in a single moment he says that we have a long, long way to go.

reviews.author: Wesley R. Ball
reviews.text: Frodo Baggins playing the piano while Lloyd Dobler keeps a silent sniper rifle trained on his head. A taut, confined thriller with a gimmick in the vein of Phonebooth, Grand Piano is a decent and competently made thriller that actually manages to deliver its thrills fairly well and frequently. Sweeping camera movements and some brilliantly strategic camera placements provide some pretty breathtaking cinematography, and the beautiful designs only complement this further. It does feel like a slow start, with some seemingly unnecessary setups that don't provide any really satisfying payoffs, but when the film is focused on its psychological tension, that's where the story really manages to shine.

reviews.text: "Gunfight at the O.K. Corral" is a 1957 western directed by John Sturges. The film is a romanticized version of the events that took place within Tombstone, Arizona in 1881. Featuring a notorious gun battle between Wyatt Earp, his brothers, and Doc Holiday versus the Clantons and McLaurys, it's one of the major events told in something of a folklorist stance within the mythos of the wild west. Much of this was due to famous lawman Wyatt Earp living to something of an old age, residing his end days in Los Angeles, California, and passing on his tales to the right personalities just before his passing. As a result, Earp's and Holiday's legacy really birthed them into being two adventure…

reviews.text: Gunfight at the O.K. Corral exists in a weird movie space for me— you probably know the one — where you enjoy the film but still feel let down by the end product. On paper, this movie is made for me. Directed by the John Sturges, produced by Hal B. Wallis, and starring two of the biggest movie stars of their era, Burt Lancaster and Kirk Douglas, who portray two of the old west’s most legendary icons, Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday, respectively. The supporting cast is stacked too, featuring the likes of a baby-faced Dennis Hopper, John Ireland, Lee Van Cleef, DeForest Kelley, and, one of my personal favorites, Jack Elam. So far so good right?

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday are stock characters in the Western Commedia dell'arte That makes Gunfight at the O.K. Corral more interesting in the context of a tradition than as a stand-alone. This includes not just the GOAT, My Darling Clementine or Sturges’ own reworking, Hour of the Gun, but Revisions and modern Huckleberry visions.

reviews.author: Dale Nauertz
reviews.text: It pisses me off that the 1980s has been reimagined as some kind of capitalist utopia, where profits were sky high and business was booming. My parents are dairy farmers, and I remember the 80s as a time when my parents were scared of losing their farm because dairy prices (paid to the farmers) were at an all time low. Family farms all around us were going under. People were being foreclosed upon. In my experience, the 80s were a time of incredible financial insecurity. Small towns were going extinct as the factories and farms that contributed their life blood closed or moved to another country. Don't just take my word for it, listen to a Springsteen or John Mellencamp…

reviews.text: "Gung Ho" is a 1986 film directed by Ron Howard. The film stars Michael Keaton in the central role as Hunt Stevenson, a former automobile plant foreman who has been tasked to save his auto plant which has closed for months. This is a boom or bust endeavor for Stevenson and his town, as the automobile plant provides most of the jobs for the town to exist. Good news comes rather quickly as Stevenson's trip to Japan to find a buyer went successful, but now that the Japanese company of Assan Motors is in charge, there is a major contrast between East and West working conditions.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Obviously, the racial politics of a 40-year-old movie revolving around the interactions of American factory workers and their incoming Japanese business overlords are going to age questionably at best (stop being so racist, George Wendt!). However, the overarching message of working together to achieve a sense of mutual respect and well-being is probably the most fantastical element in '26. Even more unbelievable is how well-crafted this dramedy for adults is, as Don Peterman brings a bunch of that FLASHDANCE blue collar chic to the proceedings and Michael Keaton is tossing out every comedic performance tic in the book. Plus, speaking as a guy whose dad is from this region, Clint Howard actually looks like a dude from one of those dying Pittsburgh factory towns, though I'm not really sure what that actually says about my people. Anyway, fun movie that I probably hadn't seen since it played eight billion times on HBO back in the day.

reviews.author: Connor Carey
reviews.text: While admittedly some of this hasn't aged very well and it's a bit too long for its own good, Gung Ho is a good old fashioned feel-good screwball comedy that has a rocking soundtrack, a surprising amount of heart and all the cheesy 80’s montages you'd hope for in an underdog story like this. Michael Keaton is super charming and likeable in his role, and this really makes me yearn for him to do another full-on comedy in the future. It's nothing great but it's a lot of fun and pretty overlooked. Michael Keaton and Ron Howard make for a great combo. Their 3/3 as far as I'm concerned.

Starring Elizabeth Perkins and Kevin Bacon as dueling newspaper columnists who become a couple and, then, TV personalities, the film offers contrasting moments the duo's history, differing based on who is telling the story. The concept is intriguing, but its execution can be flimsy; and enjoyment of the work overall may be dictated on its protagonists' ability to generate appeal. Enjoyably, Perkins and Bacons charm throughout and lead the film to a comfortable landing.

It’s just too bad the film drags as much as it does in the second act. None of the kids are especially likeable (by design), and since the viewer spends most of the runtime with them, the movie gets a bit taxing when nothing much happens for long stretches. reviews.author: Karl Janssen
reviews.text: This appears to be an episode from a Hercules television series, perhaps a pilot that was never picked up. Hercules (Gordon Scott) is an itinerant do-gooder who uses his godlike strength to assist those in need. Sidekicks Ulysses (Mart Hulswit) and Diogenes (Paul Stevens) are his traveling companions. The great Gordon Mitchell has a guest appearance as an evil pirate. The production values are really quite good for its era, with beautiful sets, two ships engaged in a naval battle, and a giant rubber sea monster. The story is fast-paced, never boring, and unlike many peplum films, makes logical sense. Though half the length of a feature film, this TV production is better than many of the sword-and-sandal epics that have graced the big screen. Too bad the series was never picked up.

reviews.text: "High Anxiety" represents to me the moment when Mel Brooks started to "lose it" in a sense. Whilst it's a nice tribute to the films and style of Alfred Hitchcock, satirising a handful of his classic films such as "Vertigo," "The Birds," and "Psycho," It doesn't have the blistering social commentary of "Blazing Saddles" or the hilarious belly-aching laughs of "Young Frankenstein." In a sense, it feels like a generic spoof film that's lacking any sort of depth. The film does contain some funny moments that brought about a couple of chuckles, but nothing much beyond that.

reviews.text: "It's amazing what you can do when you don't have to look at yourself in the mirror anymore." (It most assuredly is not.) Now I can see it's very much a Paul Verhoeven movie, using the H.G. Wells story to affirm his jaundiced view of human nature-- who we really are when we're accountable to nothing but our basic instincts. The film sets up Kevin Bacon's character as an arrogant, aggressive, morally compromised person from the very first scene, and comes to the not-unreasonable conclusion…

Wells The Invisible Man for the trashy, crass R-rated 90s sex-criminal thrillers mainstream studios were briefly interested in putting legit budgets into ($95m?!) post-Basic Instinct. Interesting to think about the fact that this is probably Verhoeven at his most reined in by the execs (and by the bad kind of moronic, unsubtle screenwriting that flattens many of the ideas/characters inherent to the source material) and yet it's still operating at a level of astonishing craft, leering eroticism and unpleasant violence that are unmistakably him. reviews.text: I watched Hollow Triumph for Joan Bennett. She delivers. The film is a gritty, low budget noir with a very contrived plot. Paul Henreid stars as John Müller, a recently released criminal mastermind who’s already plotting his next big heist. He assembles a crew to knock off a corrupt casino owned by Rocky Stansyck (Thomas Browne Henry) but when it goes sideways John and the remainder of his crew have to flee town to hide from Stansyck and his men.

reviews.text: There were a lot of films that appeared in the late 1940's that were known by more than one title, depending on which market they were released in, and this film from director Steve Sekely is one such anomaly, known here on LB as Hollow Triumph, but also as The Man Who Murdered Himself, and in the US as The Scar? A film I'd bought when looking for old Joan Bennett dvds for my collection, this intriguing little film noir crime film was just what I needed after the bad taste that Mr Malcolm's List had left in my mouth, and sometimes I do wonder why I watch modern films at all?

reviews.author: Raphael Georg Klopper
reviews.text: The most ludicrous of premises with one of the most forceful and stylistically rich executions a proper Noir classic you could hope for! Hollow Triumph, or better yet The Scar, is a blunt mix of implausible pulpy plotting sold under a tight moodier existential Noir tale that will both leave you shaking your head in denial to some of the ideas regarding change of identity, while finding yourself immersed in a state of thrills for the sadist fatalism of Noirish dark B entertainment.

reviews.author: covkate
reviews.text: I think I'm in the minority with such a high rating* (and maybe I've been a bit over generous) but I enjoyed this a lot. There is some absolutely preposterous plotting but to be honest I don't mind that when it's such a riveting yarn and so well told. There's some fabulous lighting courtesy of John Alton and the pacing is tight. I really enjoyed Paul Henreid's over-the-top performance as the slick, arrogant Muller, and Joan Bennett is great as the beautiful Evelyn, whose bitter backchat hides a vulnerable heart.

reviews.author: mumblecorgi
reviews.text: Hollow Triumph, also known as The Scar, is one of the most perplexing films I've ever seen. Though wonderfully shot by John Alton, this uncanny, demented movie features a few of the strangest choices I've ever seen a director make. First, our villain John Muller, played with sufficient intensity by Paul Heinreid, puts together a crew to rob a gambling house. While he makes away with $60,000, the rest of his crew gets pinched. Now on the run, he happens upon a psychoanalyst named Dr. Bartok who looks JUST LIKE HIM -- except for one thing: the good doctor has a long, narrow scar on the right side of his face. Muller decides to impersonate him as a cover, even…

reviews.author: Daniel Martines
reviews.text: Hollow Triumph is a noir classic from filmmakers Paul Henreid and Steve Sekely whose cinematography tells the story of thief John Müller trying to steal the identity of a psychiatrist after a failed attempt to stealthily rob a casino. Noir films from that era often have well-defined characteristics in terms of their photography and acting, but this film has become one of my favorite noir films because it presents a well-defined idea that, although is different from the common characteristics of the most well-known noir films, still provided a captivating experience. .The film has an interesting relationship with its characters not repressing themselves in relation to the stereotypes shown, the film even reminded me of Spielberg's Catch Me If…

reviews.author: Kunga Sagar
reviews.text: Further proof that filmmakers tapping into nostalgia can lead to favorable results. This is one of the finest coming of age films of the 80s, made by the man who brought us testosterone epics such as Point Blank and Deliverance. To say that a film as delicate and emotional as Hope and Glory came from the mind of John Boorman speaks to his talents as an artist but also how much this story meant to him. It’s his life, and it was those formative years that brought him immense joy, despite a literal world war around him. It’s the beauty of seeing everything through a child’s eyes, there’s a purity to even the most juvenile of actions, yes throwing rocks…

reviews.author: Mark Cunliffe 🇵🇸
reviews.text: John Boorman's masterful semi autobiographical tale of growing up on the home front in WWII is a stunningly authentic and affectionate evocation of the period and a fitting tribute to those that helped preserve the way of life we enjoy today. It also ranks as one if the finest British films of the 1980s. Utterly memorable, each frame returned me to my childhood in that decade when I watched it with my family and also, perhaps surprisingly given the occasionally mature content, in junior school as a way to teach us kids about the children of a previous generation.

reviews.author: Richard
reviews.text: My dad’s parents never really spoke about the war. They were both 18 when they entered their respective air raid shelters in the early evening of 14 November 1940 and, when the all clear finally sounded after 11 sleepless hours of continual bombardment, they emerged to find a scene of utter devastation. The city of Coventry had been razed to the ground. In their working-class neighbourhood, homes nestled alongside munitions factories, industrial units and metalworks, and they all burned together. The Nazi propagandists were so pleased that they coined a new verb to celebrate their achievements: “coventrieren” or “to coventrate”.

Corral. Another case of some great actors giving great performances but I have to doth my cap to Jason Robards(Doc Holliday) for being so acerbic and charming. This 1967 film from director John Sturges covers familiar ground for us Western fans, and familiar ground for Sturges too, given that he directed a heavily fictionalized version of the events at the OK Corral in Tombstone 10 years earlier, with Burt Lancaster playing Wyatt…

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: "Hour of the Gun" is the revenge driven aftermath to the famed gunfight at the OK Corral. It's a violent 60s western with no real heroes. James Garner's Wyatt Earp is just about as cold-blooded as Robert Ryan's Ike Clanton. There's no Clementine in this film to lend some softener to its harsh fabric. However, the cinematography captures some beautiful outdoor scenes of the west, so that kind of adds beauty to the cold-blooded vengeance. It also features a couple of courtroom scenes that illustrate something about a the role of the legal system in trying to find justice through due process. William Schallert's Judge Herman Spicer is an interesting part of this saga. There's some interesting shifts in jurisdiction that make the killing either legal or not. John Sturges tried to get to the bottom of this famous story. The movie "Tombstone" is definitely more color-driven and richer, while this one just kind of gets it done.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: You have to ask yourself why this particular slice of the history of the West is so heavily mythologized, especially by Hollywood. Why put so much money behind the bloody gang war between the Clantons and the Earps? I haven't delved into the histories as much, but from what I have read and seen, there are always a few hints here and there as to the materialist view of things - monied interests were behind each side; this was a capitalist conflict of some kind. The Clantons are treated more poorly in the mythologizing, which begs a lot of questions. The descendants of the Clantons have famously spoken out against the Earps.

So, you're expected to know the history of what transpired in town just before the shootout, but primarily for iconography reasons. The myths and legend-building didn't stop with the shootout, but continued on with more bloodshed than the original shootout.

Jason Robards is great and James Garner is solid if a little dry, but Kilmer and Russell are definitely the gold standard of those two characters.

reviews.author: Rakestraw
reviews.text: Three years in the making, Matthew Wade’s How the Sky Will Melt has the distinction of being an extremely rare piece of cinema for its time. A feature-length filmed on Super 8 released into a cinematic landscape overcrowded with digital films upon digital films. reviews.text: Feature-length films shot on Super 8 are extremely rare beasts these days, which makes ‘How the Sky Will Melt’ quite a special feat, particularly given its half-dreamed delirium quality. The hyper-grainy aesthetics provided by the ‘outmoded’ format are not merely a gimmick – on the contrary, they actually make you believe that you are watching a lost, dusted off artifact from the past. Strengthening this illusion is the great, throwback-to-the-80’s production and costume design by Sara Lynch (also jumping into the lead role), as well as the sinister synth-heavy score composed by Wade himself, and most probably inspired by the work of John Carpenter.

Essentially if a woman was promiscuous or unfaithful she'd be branded a Madame Bovary / Pan Jinlian and socially ostracized.

reviews.author: Evan Morgan
reviews.text: I'm a Feng Xiaogong novice so it's possible that there are treasures to be mined from his previous blockbusters and I'm just ignorant of them, but based on reputation alone I did not expect this. Even without the silhouetted frame, I Am Not Madame Bovary could reasonably lay claim to possessing the most distinctive mise-en-scene of any wide release this year, certainly if we're just counting films likely to draw big crowds. It's dioramic and lateral in a way that should satiate Wes and Kitano cravings, but it's also maybe the most successful melding of Hou's middle-career middle-distance style with (somewhat more) conventional storytelling? A rather heady brew, but somehow it gels.

reviews.text: Sports pornography and erotics. Watching Icarus is like being sitting on a nuclear bomb. Icarus (Greek Myth) represents the story of every fallen athlete (Lance Armstrong). Lance was a machine. And the doping was just one part of him being, essentially, this spectacular, single-minded athlete in pursuit of greatness. He could fly and he kept pushing and pushing. When he finally got caught, it wasn't about science; it was about the enemies he made during the journey in his sport. That's essentially the story of Icarus. You can fly, but if you get too close to the sun your wings are going to burn. This is not about cheating. This is about learning about the truth. Truth is the new banned substance. And during times of universal deceit, telling the truth becomes a revolutionary act.

reviews.author: Borgnine
reviews.text: This movie stars Ernest Borgnine as Tzar Nicholas II of Russia on yet another submarine journey, this time to the north pole to retrieve a downed McGuffin, apparently shot in real time. No joke this mildly interesting spy tale comes complete with an overture, intermission, entr’acte, and exit music like it’s the fucking Ten Commandments or some shit. Anyway, Borgnine is a an expat Russian now working for the Americans who wishes to spend his free time inspecting the nuclear reactor, to which genius commander Rock Hudson happily obliges him and does everything but show him the damn blueprints. Also along for the ride is Number 6, whose loyalties are also questionable, though I can say no more, that would be telling. It all culminates in an epic showdown on a foam covered Hollywood set, where all the forces converge on an ultra sensitive Russian space thermos secured with a 3-digit briefcase lock. Be seeing you!

reviews.text: Director John Sturges often gets overlooked when people start to discuss influential directors within a particular genre of film. Sturges' Westerns are what drew me towards his filmography in the first place, with The Magnificent Seven, Gunfight at the OK Corral, Last Train from Gun Hill, The Law and Jake Wade, and Backlash all fabulous films in their own right. Sturges' filmography is one that's ripe to be re-evaluated, and that's exactly what I've decided to do over the next few months by picking off a few more than I've never seen before, starting with Sturges' Cold War espionage thriller, Ice Station Zebra.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: I have a soft spot for 70mm roadshow films of the 1960s, especially those that, like this one, aren’t entirely successful or even suitable for the format. What should be a taut espionage thriller that moves along so quickly you don’t stop to dwell on the gaps in its story’s (or characters’) logic ends up being a bloated pseudo-epic that, in its second half, keeps drawing attention to its own limitations. Yet the crispness and clarity of Daniel Fapp’s cinematography is immersive, and the time director John Sturges takes to tell the story allows us to get a sense of what life aboard a nuclear submarine during the Cold War might have been like. reviews.text: In My Country opens with a Black South African asking members of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission if there can be justice for the victims of apartheid without exacting vengeance on that brutal system’s perpetrators or its white beneficiaries. The answer to that question, of course, is “yes.” By definition, revenge is not justice, as several of the foundational texts of world literature (the Torah, the Oresteia, etc.) teach us. But that doesn’t make restorative justice any more satisfying to most human beings, who seem predisposed to think of fairness in terms of retribution. Nor does it make accepting a friend’s or a family member’s direct — or one’s own indirect — complicity in systemic injustice any easier to come to…

You know about the "twin films" phenomenon? Deep Impact/Armageddon, Dante's Peak/Volcano, etc. The connections between Elah and Old Men transcend the very idea of "twin films." They are "conjoined twin films." You could even swap words within the titles and it still works. In the Valley of Old Men. No Country for Elah. It's a spider's web.

Who thought that was going to be a fun and entertaining premise? It's an externalization of the pain of giving birth. Instead of taunting the crew with their imminent demise, she is usually sobbing and begging for help, right up until she murders them. It might have had more of an impact or purpose if I could tell any of the characters apart, I gave up and just call them all Garys and Kates. It's inexplicable to me…

What starts out as a shipwreck drama soon morphs into an ominous horror film, before becoming an adventure, dipping into wild fantasy and then making its way back to some kind of sci-fi horror and ending up as an adventure again. The main influences seem to be The Island of Dr Moreau and The Creature from the Black Lagoon, with a sprinkling of Lovecraft on top, as are launched into a plot involving an isolated island full of hostile aquatic creatures and the paranoid lunatic that presides over it. It's a mess really, but there's so many great ideas that it never fails to be entertaining. The…

reviews.text: Certainly not the most comforting film to watch right now as it’s about 4 couples quarantining themselves from the imminent lethal threat of a contagious chemical outbreak, but the relevance is what made me want to watch it again, and I loved it. A pitch perfect black comedy that examines several different approaches to grief in both a relational and personal context. A stellar script, a stellar cast- it feels like a stage play turned into a film and I’m honestly shocked it isn’t. That’s the UT touch, baby! I also find the ending to be such an inspired choice that left me confused as to the thematic implications on my first watch, but I don’t think I cared as much this time because it’s just so good.

reviews.author: Deckk
reviews.text: 100-word review: A delightful surprise that finds dark humour in its unique premise. What starts as a seemingly mundane gathering quickly unravels into a comedy of errors as the characters grapple with personal revelations amidst a looming catastrophe. One of the film's strengths lies in its ability to deftly shift tones, blending jokes with moments of genuine tension and introspection. Director Todd Berger crafts a witty screenplay that keeps you engaged while exploring the dynamics of relationships under pressure. The ensemble cast delivers performances that enhance the film's quirky charm. It's a Disaster stands out for its sharp dialogue and clever satire.

reviews.text: I think it’s pretty well established by now that Terry Gilliam is a director who won't make my favourites list anytime soon. For some reason or another, I really struggle to invest myself in his films. I don’t know if it's down to the absurdist humour or the surrealist narrative structures that he uses in his latter films, or if it’s an amalgamation of both these issues. With all that being said, I seem to connect more with him as a director when he’s playing in the medieval-style sandbox, and that’s the case again with one of his earliest features, "Jabberwocky."

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: It took me about 15 minutes to realize that Terry Gilliam’s first film with a sole directing credit (he previously co-chaired directing duties with Terry Jones), wasn’t going to work. Jabberwocky is a quasi-brutal Middle Ages comedy with the affable Michael Palin as the American-named Dennis* Cooper (har-har) who makes a pilgrimage to the “developed” province. Mistaken for a prince, he has an encounter with a princess; we look at an eager Palin to pounce on some opportunity. His smile is sorta funny, but we wait and wait for him to say something funny and the script offers nothing.

reviews.text: I can’t believe I’m saying this, but the acid-psych-funk jazz in this movie works. Guitars scorch solos, basses twang, and cymbals crash while a body is dragged across a hallway and hidden in a bathtub, which definitely no one will find. JANIE is a movie for those who have a strong tolerance for jazz improvisation, tongue-kissing, and exploitative twists. This is not a movie for those who require bras. The directing credit goes to Jack Bravman, but he claims that Roberta Findlay did the directing (as well as the cinematography). In other interviews, John Amero, the Findlays’ longtime collaborator, claims that Michael Findlay directed the film. It’s hard to say who directed what, but I think it’s safe to assume…

reviews.author: theironcupcake
reviews.text: I love a good mystery. Today's conundrum: who directed the softcore serial killer feature Janie? Was it Jack Bravman (later director of the Adam West-starring horror flick Zombie Nightmare), whose name is credited on the finished product? Was it cinematographer Roberta Findlay (who additionally appears in a small but significant role), as Bravman later said in an interview? Or was it Michael Findlay, who also shows up in the film, and was the actual director according to one of Janie's sound recordists/production managers, John Amero?

reviews.text: It's rare to come across a film about a drug addict that isn't About Addiction. Though FH (short for the cruel nickname "Fuckhead") eventually kicks the habit, the film doesn't treat this as the catharsis his character was working toward all along. He's the same person on dope as he is off of it: sincere, compassionate, and lovable. Unlike basically every other film about a heroin addict, his drug use and criminal activity doesn't override his vibrant personality. It's actually dismissive to call this a film about a heroin addict; it's a playful, earnest, sometimes heartbreaking, and often hilarious character study of a man surrounded by tragedy.

reviews.author: Julian (Seeking Film)
reviews.text: The Old Oak was a particularly disappointing retirement feature from famed critical British filmmaker Ken Loach, in part because its well-intentioned but ultimately saccharine angle on its hopeful message felt like it could very well have come from anyone. This was especially notable in contrast with his preceding two masterpieces that could only have come from a lifelong ally of the struggle, bitterly fed-up with the innovative new ways in which the working class continues to be tread upon. But it turns out, it only took going back one film further to find Loach once more exploring his ever-present social concerns with a lighter touch.

reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: Whether it's a period drama like this one or a contemporary piece like The Old Oak Ken Loach is true to his convictions; the quest for freedom, equality and justice, his sympathy for the struggle of the working class, and the importance of unity and community are constants in his filmography. In Jimmy's Hall we are taken to 1930s Ireland, in the midst of the Great Depression, the open wounds of the Civil War, and the religious fanaticism of the Catholic Church, to honour the communist leader Jimmy Gralton. Although at times slightly Manichean, there is no doubt that the British director films with passion and is aware that his themes are universal and still very much relevant to our present.

reviews.author: Midwest Movie Madness
reviews.text: While I appreciate DC doing a shared universe with their recent animated offerings, I'm very thankful they keep producing side projects like this. Gods and Monsters is a refreshing change of pace which harkens back to the classic Bruce Timm animations from the 90s. In this universe, Superman is Zod's son, Batman is a literal vampire (and Kirk Langstrom no less) and Wonder Woman is a scorned warrior whose background I won't spoil because it definitely surprised me. Gods and Monsters is full of twists and surprises that some may groan about but I found it exciting. This is no reboot, rewrite or re-do, just a good old fashioned original story in an alternate timeline.

reviews.author: TyTy
reviews.text: I usually can’t stand when alternate versions of iconic heroes are just turned into straight-up evil because it feels lazy and overdone, but Justice League: Gods & Monsters completely flips that trope in the best way. These versions of Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman aren’t villains, they’re flawed heroes who genuinely believe they’re doing the right thing, even when their extreme and lethal methods start crossing lines. I really loved how the movie gives them unique twists on their origins while still keeping the core traits, morals, and personalities that made me fall in love with these characters in the first place. Watching them slowly question their own actions and grow as characters made this version of the Justice League way…

Granted it wasn't as entertaining as Crises on Two Worlds, but it was still fun seeing the alternate darker Justice League trio that this one was about, and it's easily another DC animated flick that I like and am ranking fairly highly.

reviews.text: If we define an auteur as “a filmmaker with a recognizable style and consistent themes across their body of work,” then Amir Shervan is absolutely an auteur. I didn’t need to watch Killing American Style’s credits to know it was directed by the same dude who made Samurai Cop. They share so many of the same visual tics and narrative preoccupations: Grimy L.A. locations (several of which appear in both movies), psychotic criminals, crotchety police captains, svelte women in bikinis who almost never go swimming, violent shootouts, quirky dialogue, graphic yet weirdly unerotic sex scenes, and Robert Z’Dar.

To confuse matters further, the original Zombi was meant to be a sequel to Romero’s Dawn of The Dead and was titled Zombi 2 upon its release in Italy. reviews.author: Matthew B.
reviews.text: Knife Skills, an Oscar-nominated documentary short film, is a valuable reminder that everyone deserves a second (and, if needed, a seventy-second) chance. The film follows the ambitious project of Edwins restaurant in Cleveland, OH. With a staff comprised almost entirely of ex-convicts, Edwins is a culinary school and restaurant that specializes in second chances, empathy, and compassion. Watching the restaurant team take on this ambitious goal--and change lives in the process--is empowering and special. An entertaining documentary on a noble business pursuit, Knife Skills is a solid documentary short, even if it doesn't quite match the quality of the best of this year's crop.

reviews.author: Andrew Motte
reviews.text: Thematically a deeply flawed work. It answers none of the questions viewers may have, such as: Why a French restaurant? The restaurant owner was also deeply unlikeable and clearly performed for the camera.

reviews.author: Lise
reviews.text: The subject matter was fascinating. An ex-con creates a training restaurant for other ex-cons. The beauty of it is that they aren't flipping burgers here; they are learning French Haute Cuisine, and that's what is so admirable. They are being treated like real human beings who can learn beyond what they might see as their limited capabilities. They aren't just learning to cook, they are learning to be chefs, and I love what that does to their aspirations and confidence.

But the program itself is thriving and going strong, offering not just a marketable skill but hope to those often forgotten and written off by society.

reviews.author: Ken Rudolph
reviews.text: Edwins Leadership and Restaurant Institute is a highly rated French restaurant in Cleveland, Ohio. What distinguishes it from others is that it makes most of its hires from released prisoners who attend a rigorous cooking school, and then work at the restaurant after graduation. This documentary short follows the activities during one school term of several ex-felons. It also tells the moving story of the emotional and dedicated manager and founder of the restaurant, Brandon Edwin Chrostowski. This is a fine example of a good-works documentary, well shot and edited. As a "foodie" doc, it isn't quite up to the best of the breed...the food looked luscious, of course; but the focus was on the people and their struggles to succeed and not recidivate. That the project works, for the most part, is evidence of its admirable purpose in helping ex-prisoners return to civilian life and become productive citizens.

reviews.author: ChrisStuckmann
reviews.text: I admire this film. To say there’s nothing else like it is an understatement. It feels staunchly against all Hollywood norms of its era, and certainly those of today. It’s no wonder that studios at the time became antagonistic with Shyamalan’s attempts at bold and original films. I’ve always viewed 2006-2008 as the period when Hollywood began gravitating toward IP and proven roadmaps, distancing themselves from unique voices and innovative stories. Lady in the Water arrived at the tail-end of a time when every weekend held a new, modestly-budgeted original film. I’ve got nothing but respect for artists who put their heart and soul into their stories, rather than giving in to the machine. If you ever want a fascinating look at the production of Lady, read The Man Who Heard Voices by Michael Bamberger.

reviews.text: As always, this rating is a reflection of my experience with the film, not its broader political significance. Fayyad showcases and potentially exploits the suffering of the Syrian people through some incredibly brutal and horrific images, and I can't deny the power of documentaries like this -- Last Men in Aleppo has inherent worth as a representation of violence so often ignored as a means of calling out irresponsible, apathetic government. I'm glad it exists, but from a filmmaking standpoint, it does not package its material well. It's such a strange feeling to be horrified and bored at the same time. Even with a somewhat shorter runtime, the poor structure and sequencing just makes this 90 minutes of unpleasantness that didn't culminate in much. I'm glad if this movie frustrates governments, but as a viewer, it didn't do much for me.

reviews.text: Jean Vigo was one of those rare pioneering geniuses of cinema, envied for his mind by new waves of filmmakers. His short filmography, essentially consisting of Zéro de Conduite and with only one feature-length film, L'Atalante itself, not only profoundly influenced French cinema but also drew an irreversible rupture with the traditional paradigms of his time. Vigo made no concessions. His anarchic sensibility (inherited from his father), his almost instinctive intuition for cinematic lyricism, and his ability to fuse the everyday with the dreamlike place him in a singular position within film history. It's no exaggeration to say that, with this film in particular, he established a new horizon for French poetic realism, anticipating, to some extent, modern cinema itself.…

I watch the enigmatic L'Atalante and think that cinema might well explode.

reviews.text: Jean Vigo’s L'Atalante is a measured and mature glimpse at the everyday conflicts of married life. It's perplexing to think that this, and the small handful of other movies which make up his filmography, were largely neglected by the late thirties, and only proceeded to be rediscovered after World War II. Vigo manipulated harsh and cold shooting conditions to the advantage of the production to formulate a movie which appears staggeringly modern in its thematic authenticity, although it sadly developed in him becoming ill. And although this is less surreal than his other work; this is probably his masterpiece.

reviews.text: I had always passed this by back in the day, as it always looked like a cash-in on other more popular fantasy anime, like Record of Lodoss War. Just recently I realized it was directed by Ryutaro Nakamura, who went on to direct classic anime series such as Serial Experiments Lain and Ghost Hound. This sparked my interest in checking it out, but sadly it was everything I always expected it to be. In the realm of fantasy, RPG-esque anime, this doesn't quite cut it. Everything about it is pedestrian and the only thing that stands out is how some of the characters can shape-change into beast-like forms. Otherwise, you've seen all of this before, and likely in a lot better form (like the aforementioned Record of Lodoss War). It doesn't help matters that the animation is pretty flat and does little to grab you. Not terrible, but completely forgettable.

reviews.author: Ethan Vestby
reviews.text: Marcello Mastroianni plays the prince of an unnamed European country who moves to his father's London townhouse only to be alienated by the elite sex parties and such. He gradually turns his telescope to the tenement across the street and finds himself spying on its numerous black tenants. Initially felt it was going for a filmmaking metaphor about 2019 A24 movies or whatever, but the picture actually builds up to a climax that I would describe as like Chaplin meets Zabriskie Point (some weird shit was in the air). Maybe a tad "ill-conceived" but full of so many deranged images and tonal shifts that I couldn't help but kind of love it. Boorman really might be the weirdest director to ever find mainstream success.

reviews.text: A half decade before Cannon really got going, this was Golan and Globus' first real attempt to crack the U.S theatrical market. Yes, it shamelessly wears its influences - everything from the first two GODFATHERS all the way back to '30s Warner Brothers gangster flicks - on its sleeve and is driven by plot rather than any depth of understanding for its characters. That said, if you take this as a deluxe b-movie potboiler, it's tons of fun for fans of gangster fare. Golan's direction shows impressive confidence, creating a lavishly designed period feel on a modest budget and packing the running time with plenty of shootouts, assassinations and tough guy posturing. Curtis makes up for the thin nature of…

reviews.author: Lisa Marie Bowman
reviews.text: Menahem Golan's first American film, Lepke is a gangster biopic that hits all the usual points. It's a bit slow but there's a few good gangland executions and Tony Curtis is believable, if not particularly compelling, in the lead role. Blustery Vic Tayback is all wrong for Lucky Luciano, a gangster who was famous for his calculating nature. It's not as sordid as one might expect from a Golan film and that's ultimately the film's main flaw. It's well-made and has its moments but, in the end, it's a little boring.

reviews.text: I've never actually read any of Bret Easton Ellis's novels (I intend to), but I sure am a fan of the films that are based on his work. AMERICAN PSYCHO, THE RULES OF ATTRACTION and LESS THAN ZERO are all weirdly compelling stories about the lives of the wealthy, white, and vacant, most of them made with the perfectly ironic backdrop of the sparkly, shallow 1980s, amid a jungle of neon-lit nightclubs and cocaine-smeared mirrors. Even though most of the characters are always junkies, preppies, hustlers, and even murderers, all three films are unexpectedly emotionally involving, none more so than this one.

reviews.text: Feels like something you catch late at night on TV at your grandparents' house, about thirty minutes in and you either get scared and turn it right off or watch to the end if you're cool. Really difficult vibe to capture but it never once falters. Really special lead performance. "Is she actually cRaZy!?" is one of the hardest notes in the world for an actor to land and so for Zohra Lampert to not only nail it but to make it this compelling is something else. She never resorts to tics or Jared Leto style "mom! Look! I'm acting! Mom! Over here! I'm acting! See?" swings, she's just insanely present and nobody else is really matching her so you feel trapped with her in her own mind. Beautiful.

reviews.text: Эд Соломон, сценарист "Билла и Теда", "Людей в черном" и "Ангелов Чарли", писал сценарий для своего "серьезного" режиссерского дебюта более 20 лет. Видимо, именно столько выводится из организма развлекательная голливудская зараза. Но в этой вялотекущей благостной драме нет ничего оригинального. Сиделец откидывается после 20 лет тюрьмы и хочет получить прощение у сестры убитого им при ограблении подростка, который ему иногда является. Билли Боб Торнтон с седыми патлами проявляет чудеса актерской сдержанности и спит на ходу, а остальные хорошие актеры честно отрабатывают свой хлеб. Единственное, что понравилось — заснеженные трущобы Монреаля и бойкая Кирстен Данст, единственный островок жизни в океане клишированной тоски.

This cost $20 million (and admittedly failed to make it back) and stars consummate pros Danny DeVito and Holly Hunter, two actors who are so routinely excellent that we take them for granted. They’re also not box office powerhouses, but once upon a time, Living Out Loud was the kind of film that would get a theatrical release and people would happily go out and see. reviews.author: PacificNil
reviews.text: "Redwing - Flucht vor den schwarzen Droiden" stammt von Roger Christian, dem Regisseur, der 15 Jahre später den nicht minder qualitativen "Battlefield Earth" drehte. Christian lernte unter George Lucas und fungierte als Set Designer, und gerade das Set-Design, in Zusammenspiel mit der Beleuchtung, gefolgt von der Musik aus der Feder von Genesis-Mitgliedern, werten den Film auf. Der planlose Filmschnitt, die öden Charaktere und die langweilige Erzählweise bei einem eigentlich interessanten Stoff um Aufstände von Zwangsarbeitern auf einem fernen Planeten im Jahr 2084 mindern das Vergnügen. Trotzdem hoffe ich auf eine Kinosichtung eines Tages, da die Aufnahmen der Raumschiffe und der Riesengefährte eindrucksvoll, geradezu bildsprengend sind und die DVD bestenfalls für Röhrenfernseher geeignet ist.

reviews.author: Ewan Munro
reviews.text: This is a strange film: it's bleak for sure, but the film seems somewhat ambivalent about the bleakness, as if 'oh that's just part of life in modern China'. It may well be, of course (and "films dissecting China's modern experiment in capitalism" is as much of a genre these days as "films dissecting the American Dream", I suppose), but that doesn't change the fact that the leading leady, the wonderful Fan Bingbing, gets raped by her boss and then her husband, but she seems to soften when she has a baby. Sure there's some karmic balance in the end (I won't say what), but it doesn't change her difficult circumstances, exploited in a menial massage parlour job, taking grief from both sides. The camera wobbles all over the place, with a sort of faux-Dardenne brothers style, but it's not badly put together as a film, I was just left feeling unmoved.

reviews.author: AgeWithoutDecay
reviews.text: The strength of this film lies within the perspective that the director brings to the subject matter, through writing and directing. Exploring the toxic patriarchy, sexual assault, sex work, marriage, and motherhood through the lens of a female, Chinese director is enlightening. The film is painful to watch, with its realist form seeping through every shot, even in its dreadfully real-time moments of sexual assault. But this is not a masterpiece by any stretch. I just don’t know if the film feels worth it. The narrative is interesting and has strong messages, but something about the whole portrayal just feels very bleak and self-defeating. Or maybe that was the point. I’m not sure. But if you’re looking for an excruciating watch about the underbelly of contemporary Chinese society, this is worth seeing.

Very seldom do I remember seeing a couple exude as much contempt and resentment as Zhenya and Boris; he seems more concerned about keeping his job and taking care of appearances in a conservative society; she is eager to escape and begin a new chapter in her life away…

reviews.author: Kevin Y
reviews.text: A soulless husk of a film that so desperately wants to feel cold and punishing, yet struggles to match its aesthetics to a substantial foundation. It undercuts its own story right from the beginning, moving from a beautifully devastating silent shot into an almost torturous, overlong departure from its essence. The initial decision to spend so much time on the characters' new partners, paired with the bland social commentary on technology and the political climate, creates such a complete miscalculation of pacing and style until the film descends into apathetic drivel. Like with (the admittedly better) In the Fade, this is a subject matter and style that's right up my alley, but the execution of it all is so deeply frustrating and disengaging (in a bad way) that the performers are left holding an empty bag. Or a full trash bag, however you look at it.

reviews.text: Probably my favorite film adaptation of Macbeth I've seen so far, and it's probably due to its closeness to the original and its unflinching realism and brutality to its period. It throws away theatrical grandeur for this realism and allows for some great landscapes as well as a gritty, grounded, savage world. Even the cinematography and cast are perfect, especially the latter, who deliver the grand nature of Macbeth all too well. Overall, it's a grand and unique vision filled with memorable imagery, realism, and despair, and is a genuinely great watch.

reviews.text: Oi! Oi Oi! - Tim Roth pulls a frightening face like a rampaging cur in Alan Clarke's 1982 Made in Britain, in which various social workers try for 70 minutes to drive the notoriously destructive Roth out of his nonsense. The climax is a 10-minute monologue by one of the well-meaning officials, who laconically tells the devilishly grinning Roth what the rest of his life will be like if he doesn't get his swastika-tattooed bald head straight. The 16-year-old keeps going and actually ends up in jail in the last three minutes of the film. A quick blow from a rubber truncheon makes the situation clear to the angry young man - in the final shot, Roth's face freezes between childlike fear and raging hatred.

It doesn't moralize its subject at all, and Tim Roth's mesmerizing turn as Trevor is both victim and aggressor. How the institution, which is meant to rehabilitate, is part of his anger nails down its point even harder. It's a bleak watch and it remains bleak until the end, but its message is clear throughout. reviews.text: This film is like a box of chocolates; you never know what to expect. I mean, you have a picture that would normally feature and be made by a low-level actor and director that everyone would probably forget. And yet, you have Richard Attenborough directing a film written by William Goldman, composed by Jerry Goldsmith, and starring a deranged young Anthony Hopkins in a dual role as this pathetic puppeteer and the voice of this diabolical puppet whose banter is all pure gold. It's bizarre, disturbing, and amusing; it's a film that, in a rational world, would never exist, but here it is.

reviews.author: Adam Nayman
reviews.text: Joseph Breen didn't like this movie, which begins and ends with its protagonist attempting to assassinate Adolf Hitler; this tells you everything you needed to know about Joseph Breen (as if we didn't know it already). The movie is very good, of course. Transposing the predatory metaphysics of The Most Dangerous Game into a wartime zeitgeist of occupation and appeasement—and making sure that his fellow Germans were depicted as unflatteringly as possible—Lang crafts a rousing continental chase picture with multiple layers of intrigue (including the malevolent comedy of manners encoded in George Sanders' casting and performance as a British huntsman). It also keeps its anti-fascist sentiments in view throughout, as dramatic texture rather than subtext.

reviews.author: Jon M.
reviews.text: A film made by a real expatriate. More than that - a film made a truly stateless person, who owes no allegiance to any country, who knows betrayal and sees it everywhere. Germany is full of Englishmen; London is full of Germans. The only film of its era not given to the lie that the two are, in the last instance, morally distinguishable. This is probably Lang's most technically perfect film in the period after M, even if it is hampered by Joan Bennett's brutally bad Cockney performance. The ending feels obligatory and false - we can't believe it for the same reasons we believe Casablanca, which is on this count its opposite.

But the pace really drags it down today and the performances are campy at best. We all know how space works now and it isn’t this. Gregory Peck is pretty amusing as the unflappable NASA flight director and the astronauts aren’t far behind. Richard Crenna tries to provide level headed leadership in the capsule and James Franciscus sweats a lot. Gene Hackman aims for the fences as the astronaut who can’t handle…

reviews.text: The sleepiest of space dramas, Marooned apparently did big business simply by opening a few months after the Apollo 11 moon landing. It won the same Visual Effects Oscar that 2001: A Space Odyssey took a year earlier, but the legacies of these two films could not be more disparate. While Kubrick's stunning, interpretation-friendly masterpiece is still revered with religious zeal, the melodramatic Marooned might be best known for its treatment on Mystery Science Theater 3000 under the title Space Travelers.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: There are two very different explanations for why “Marshall” — ostensibly a biopic about Thurgood Marshall, the first African-American Supreme Court Justice of the United States — isn’t really about Thurgood Marshall so much as it’s about a shaky Jewish lawyer who Marshall once coached through a case. The first (and more generous) of the explanations is that the world could use an inspiring film about different kinds of discriminated against Americans joining forces to fight the prejudice that betrays the promise of the nation they share. The second (and more sincere) of the explanations is that Hollywood still believes that white audiences need an entry point to stories about people who don’t look like them, a Virgil to take them by the hand and guide them — safely and without implication — down through an inferno of intolerance and then out the other side.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: For a deeply satisfying movie that hinges on a career-defining performance from one of modern cinema’s most fascinating stars, Ridley Scott’s “Matchstick Men” has a strange way of falling through the cracks. Released to a tepid response in September 2003, this slippery tale of a con artist with a guilty conscience was too much of a tweener to find the audience it deserved, and — much like its twitchy protagonist — was also conflicted about swindling people out of their money. For a major Hollywood film that climaxes with a bare-assed Nicolas Cage running around an L.A. parking garage, its “B” Cinemascore is borderline miraculous.

The film plays a lot like a cross between Blade Runner and Network, the dark grungy aesthetics contrasting with the cheeky comedy and sardonically approached subject matter. While Channel 4 may have ordered this to provide a veritable prologue to introduce a character, yet in every regard this film benefits from a lot of care and craftsmanship. reviews.text: Whoo mama, this Redbox rental about winged kids escaping an evil science lab is a stinker. Traditionally I spend the Christmas holidays watching awful movies with my camp-loving sister, and she insisted on this one because she read the first book in James Patterson's series, and wanted to see what it looked like on the screen. She is now apologizing to me profusely. Even by "man, I want to laugh at a really cruddy movie tonight" standards, this was a snooze. Weak acting, awful dialogue, sleepy editing, repetitive action, and a plot that only makes sense if you have a 10-year-old's understanding of science, explosives, guns, psychology, and corporations. And the flying special effects are basically Birdemic's bird effects superimposed over posing teenagers. There's a drinking game in here somewhere. I recommend this rule set: Have six drinks and don't watch the film at all.

No, I selected "McQ" last night because I wanted to see John Wayne, so old his character can barely get out of bed in the morning, his toupée clamped down on his head tighter than screws, still kicking ass with a badge and a gun in the early 70's—and that's exactly what I got!

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: As I mentioned back when I watched Brannigan, John Wayne reportedly felt that turning down the chance to star in Dirty Harry was the biggest professional mistake of his later years. Brannigan and McQ were Wayne’s attempts to correct that error. Alas, neither was as successful as Wayne’s westerns of the period. (True Grit and The Cowboys had done well at the box office.) So Wayne returned to the saddle for his last two films, Rooster Cogburn and The Shootist.

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: If McQ had been made 20 or even 25 years before its 1974 release, then I might've been able to buy John Wayne as a Harry Callahan-style maverick cop but because it's abundantly clear that he was in his late sixties, it's more difficult to accept his action star credentials by this point. Now, this is still a moderately enjoyable cop thriller for the most part (if one that's rather blatantly ripping off Dirty Harry) but it's also really hindered by the fact that I simply can't buy a 67-year-old Wayne in this role. For most of the runtime, he's just lumbering around without much energy which I guess sort of fits the plot since McQ is mostly a slow…

reviews.text: The fact that Justine smiled all throughout her wedding night (1 hour of cinematic runtime) but smiled her only REAL smile with a little boy asking about magic caves (2 seconds of cinematic runtime) tells you more about depression and unhappiness in general than the most precise psychological analysis ever could. Because all we ever need is a magic cave where we can hide out together with those who understand us. The cave won't protect us from the all-consuming onrush of Melancholia, but it will provide a place where we can hold hands and be at peace with the world, other people, and ourselves. A home built from the tree of the collective unconscious whose branches unite at the top to form a temporary refuge against the perpetual unknown and unknowable: Melancholia itself.
