reviews.author: Broken VCR
reviews.text: This high-octane nihilistic Aussie thriller is an oddball deep cut from the 90s that should be taken for a spin. It follows a toxic love triangle gone wrong set against the backdrop of suburban gear-head culture and the alienated youth of Gen-X. The production design and sound are commendable. A young Ben Mendelsohn arrives here long before cracking into the Hollywood zeitgeist. Aden Young is solid as “Psycho” Joe, his brooding rippling into his brilliant work in the series Rectify nearly a decade later. And Tara Morice is tragic as the shop-lifting Satan-worshipper caught in the middle. A pedal to the metal gem that should be mentioned among Ozploitation’s most interesting. Grip it and rip it.

reviews.author: Jack Russo
reviews.text: A suburban petrol tragedy huffing the fumes of the inevitable. These surfaces are all covered in grime, these relationships are all coated in something toxic, and Wright's aesthetic nihilism cannot picture a place beyond the callous games teenagers play with each other in their death race towards the finish line of young love fractured by broken homes. Many stunning sequences of stylistic angst pierced by the unflinching honesty of destructive people continuing to destroy themselves within the formal structure of emotional continuity, discarding sequential rhythms for pained invocations of what has come to inform the present with such a tactile remembrance - of blue paint, shattered glass, chicken blood - that these bitter memories and hopeless futures feel concurrent above all else; no geography in the final pursuit, just the metal cage of two lives caught in cyclical collision with one-another.

Romper Stomper was a genuine hit in Australia and generated some buzz overseas, but Wright never really broke out. Hollywood sees Australia (and the rest of the Anglosphere) as the farm league for promising directors and actors, who we snatch up as soon as they make a promising movie in their homeland. The film, directed by Alan Parker and penned by first-time screenwriter Oliver Stone, caused quite a stir at its 1978 Cannes Film Festival premiere but divided critics. The studio continued to lack faith in its box office potential due to its harsh themes and almost demanded a very commercialized adventure ending (that was discarded), but audiences found it a sensation anyway. The film was nominated for several Academy Awards including Best Picture and for Director Parker, and won for Best Screenplay by Stone and Best Original Score by Giorgio Moroder.

I've learnt not to mention my love of Spring Snow and The Sailor Who Fell from Grace with the Sea. I get the tension. Mishima was a brilliant writer, but an unbelievably problematic person. Politically, he stands against everything I believe in, and he is a hero to Japan's infuriating nationalists whose vans that pump awful militaristic tunes have become the bane of my Sunday mornings. reviews.text: Contrary to the preceding Mobile Suit Gundam film, the second installment, Soldiers of Sorrow, was smoothly paced, filled with character redemption arcs, and was pretty eventful as a whole. While the first film was solely focused on combat between the Federation and Zeons, the second one touched the more humane aspects of war and the process inculcated alongside it-- plagued with fear, losses, immaturities, and insecurities in order to survive. The first film started off pretty weak, hence the stakes are raised high on Soldiers of Sorrow for it to be a definitive watch among its audiences.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Possibly the textbook definition of a “low-key banger”; a character first buddy action movie that feels like it somehow escaped the ‘70s and ended up in the ‘90s. Woody and Wesley are always fun to hang out with (especially while they’re drinking pitchers of cheap beer in an NYC dive bar) and Robert Blake is just on another planet as the psycho megalomaniac in charge of the titular cash bullet. Plus, the set pieces are plentiful and rather thrillingly choreographed (not to mention reminiscent of Peter Hyams’ cop movie thrashers like BUSTING or RUNNING SCARED). Possible MVP: Chris Cooper as a subway pyromaniac, utterly terrifying as he lights up pretty MTA workers in their glass encased tombs. A weird gem from a genre workman (Joe Ruben) who has delivered straight up horror classics (THE STEPFATHER) and lowbrow tripe (GORP - which I still unabashedly love). The scene where Snipes and JLo dance? Swoon bonanza.

The dialogue is pretty heavy handed, especially when it's trying to emulate moments from better legal dramas, like A Few Good Men. The performances are a touch over the top, and the voice over narration is wholly unnecessary. Plus the courtroom proceedings are Hollywood as hell. reviews.author: Jay D 's Watching
reviews.text: Solid performances from a strong cast Slater, Gary Oldman, William Macy- particularly Kevin Bacon in a co-leading turn here, and a message film about prison conditions and inhumane punishment (Solitary Confinement and the abuse of power by prison officials) that's easy to sympathize with here, on the other hand, somewhat curious choices from the director (the way the camera spins in that early murder scene) and a script that takes ah...strong liberties with the historical record (It says 'Inspired By' and not 'Based on' a true story for valid reasons, let me just say). Hollywood doesn't make legal thrillers like they used to in the 90s, this is true, but the way this one doesn't play fair and keeps its thumb on the scales is annoying enough (the writer of the screenplay, Dan Gordon, also penned Denzel Washington's film The Hurricane, which had...similar issues) that I don't really begrudge them for stopping, at least in this case.

reviews.text: The beauty of Sophie Goodhart's "My Blind Brother" is that it isn't the jet-black megadose of cringe comedy that anyone else might spin from the same premise. This is a story that has all the makings of a Todd Solondz movie, and — in the early going — it often feels like it's on the verge of becoming one. But Goodhart, who's been preparing for this debut feature since her short of the same name played at Cannes in 2003, isn't interested in anything so savage and cynical. On the contrary, she's reached into the darkness and returned with a deeply humane and frequently hilarious comedy that laughs at the fine line between kindness and pity.

Williams), who Till was visiting at the time he was attacked. This subtle change of focus allows the viewer to experience the horror and fear of the Emmett Till murder all over again, and it is a smart writing choice. Not seeing the violence actually makes the audience feel it all the more.

reviews.author: AntoniusBlock7
reviews.text: Powerful story, and one that’s well told here. One of the great things about telling it from the uncle’s perspective is that the feeling of dread and powerlessness is amplified. Imagine laying there in the dark of night, listening for someone who may come, wondering what cruelty might be committed. We see who Emmett Till was from his perspective – just a kid, an innocent kid. Like other young men, he’s interested in having fun and flirting with women, but not in a menacing way. There is a quietness about the film that goes well with the pain of subjugation in the Jim Crow south. The inclusion of the archival footage is also brilliant.

Especially Joe Odagiri's role as Japanese colonel felt a bit degraded toward the second half. Although to me its his best performance yet still im doubtful about his character's historical accuracy. Although its a well made war film and the setpiece is great too, but its over dramactic at times and also im doubtful about this films accuracy.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: The story of Yang Kyoungjong forms the loose bases for Kang Je-gyu's follow-up to his blockbuster Korean War hit, Taegukgi (2004). Childhood athletic rivals turned bitter enemies - one Korean (Jang Dong-gun) the other Japanese (Joe Odagiri) - find themselves forced into a series of armies during the second World War. The competitive running portion of the film is compelling but sadly used as bookends for the war. The bulk of My Way is POW degradation scenes and graphic combat, perforated by bullets and melodrama. From director Kang Je-gyu (Shiri) the action was never going to be anything less than riveting, but the plotting does seem counter intuitive.

The unraveling of the Code's restrictions and a growing willingness/need to question and subvert the tropes of the noir genre made for a short period of really surprising little films. Not artistic masterpieces, but far more realistic in tone and quite a bit darker than the noirs that ruled up until, say, 1947 or so.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Absolutely loved seeing a young Ricardo “Kahn” Montalban in this very interesting Film Noir that one could describe as a spiritual predecessor to all modern crime/forensic movies and TV-shows like CSI. It was very engaging and fascinating to see a crime movie like that not just focused on police work but also the (pretty new at the time) forensic work here done by a Harvard professor who helps our detective. A good amount of tension comes from the fact that the audience knows that the evidence will ultimately lead them to the wrong man if interpreted incorrectly. Very clever writing here and great direction by John Sturges.

Throw in some romantic Tangerine Dream synth, an unhinged Bill Paxton in shades and a leather jacket (slitting throats with his spurs!) and general smokey western hangout vibe that any moment threatens to turn into a vicious and hostile piece of bloody neon horror? Hell yeah. Should've watched this way sooner.

reviews.text: Alexander Payne always injects a great dose of humor in his films and also thoroughly investigates the dramatic aspect of the main characters and their backgrounds. Nebraska certainly wasn't an exception and with its black and white format, it was a delightful, constantly funny and touching film. As usual, he manages to get the best efforts from the cast and even Will Forte, who is mostly known from his comedic work, gave a solid performance in a more serious role. Veterans Bruce Dern and June Squibb really shine here, displaying not only great comedic timing but also a nice emotional touch to their characters. Nebraska is a trip to the past, a journey of rediscovery, a story of redemption and the rebonding of father and son, being very worthy of all the praise it's been receiving over the last months.

A pointless road trip, breathing fresh life into the estranged relationship between a father and son is explored beautifully. While Bruce Dern and Will Forte deliver outstanding performances, its June Squibb who steals the show in her hilarious role. A highly satisfying watch.

reviews.author: Cat Paisley
reviews.text: I think of this little 6 minute masterpiece all the time. “Look at all that wasted space” rings through my mind almost daily. I know too well what it’s like to have such a pedestrian relationship with a father, having only one or two small activities/objects to bond over. I could imagine myself looking at that same open casket, with that same feeling: a tragic lack of connection, with only one trivial shared interest to think about. The smallness of the characters and the animated transitions speak volumes on how our main character was so engulfed - almost drowning - in his father’s interest (in this case luggage) in attempt to force a deeper bond but in the end, he feels nothing.

reviews.author: pirateneckbeard
reviews.text: This was a greasy, dark early 60's British little noir full of prickly characters hustling through there day. Richard Todd(John Cummings) plays the victim of a car theft which then he spirals to greater depths in order to retrieve it. Clearly the deck is stacked against our protagonist but not enough to make it unbelievable. Peter Sellers(Lionel Meadows) is great here as car dealer working in a criminal field who becomes more and more unhinged as it goes along. I really felt that I could feel the stakes for all the major characters and the look and pace of this film is really something. Having watched this and "Bridge at Remagen" I realized I got to see more John Guillermin films. Glad I checked this one out.

reviews.author: RetroHound
reviews.text: A story about two men backed into a corner and the confrontations that ensue. This was way better than I expected, the editing and directing in the third act was spectacular. Richard Todd's car gets stolen. He needs the car for his job as a wholesale cosmetics salesman. He's about to lose his job for missing appointments. He relentlessly starts following the trail until it leads to a vicious Peter Sellers. Sellers doesn't seem particularly vicious, until he starts to feel cornered. Then he lashes out at everyone around him. And he totally sells it, it is not overdone, it's like it just boils out of him. Whoever put this on my radar (probably 6 or 8 years ago, I have a crazy long queue) thank you! And if you have not seen it, you should add it to your watchlist.

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: Peter Sellers gets Adam Faith to steal Richard Todd's Ford Anglia...then all hell breaks loose.An interesting minor British noir from 1960 with Sellers in an unusual straight sadistic criminal role and Todd as the mild mannered cosmetic salesman driven to extremes when his job and marriage are on the line. (Apparently they were cast the other way round but Sellers persuaded Todd to swap.)Good work also from young stars Adam Faith and Carol White and nicely directed by John Guillermin with a pounding, tense score from John Barry. Really rather good.Apparently Carol White said that during filming she had affairs with Adam Faith, Richard Todd and Peter Sellers. Wow, she was only 16 when this film was made.Watched on YouTube.

reviews.author: Daniel88
reviews.text: After seeing Never so Few I am just grateful that this film didn’t wreck Steve McQueen’s career before it even got off the ground. I have always had a thing for these kind of old-fashioned war films that are low on the unnecessary subplots and affluent in action, explosions and bravado. Looking at John Sturges’ career he has always been the kind of director to deliver. He was no Hawks or Ford, but more like a 1950s/60s equivalent of Richard Donner or John McTiernan. Not the kind of filmmaker to direct the new Citizen Kane, but just fun and, in their own way, timeless action classics.

reviews.author: Deaner50
reviews.text: Nico Icon is a documentary film about the singer, actress, song writer and model Nico. Nico acted in some films early in her career La Dolce Vita and Chelsea Girls. She joined the Velvet Underground while hanging around Andy Warhol. At the suggestion of her friend Jim Morrison she started writing her own songs. Nico saw herself as bohemian and led a nomadic lifestyle. She struggled with a heroin addiction. I think the movie looks a little cheap. I wish a better director would do a proper documentary. The film jumps around time lines a bit off the top. It does have great music though. Overall it's not a masterpiece of a documentary. There are lots of talking heads and it focuses on her drug problems a lot. But it tries to explain where she came from and her dark worldview. She certainly was a one of a kind artist icon.

Sa voix est extrêmement limitée, mais peu importe qu'elle la pose sur un folk pastoral ou une ambiance de tempête post-apocalyptique, peu importe le sujet abordé, il s'en dégage un ascendant rassurant, quasi-maternel, qui laisse croire à l'auditeur qu'elle a le pouvoir de transcender et de contrôler la tristesse du monde pour l'emmener à un droit ou tout ira mieux. reviews.text: Nico has always been incredibly fascinating to me, elusive, multifaceted, complex, frustrating, a person who has lived many different lives. She was known for being cold and dull, but she lived fiercely. She was at all the right places at the right time. She was an up-and-coming model in Europe landing a role in Fellini's La Dolce Vita. She was in New York in the mid-sixties, part of the Factory scene, pioneering the avant-garde in music with The Velvet Underground. She ventured into her solo music, remarkably darker, morbid, haunting, which made her a goth icon. She had flings with Alain Delon, Lou Reed, Brian Jones, Jackson Browne, Jim Morrison, who she felt was the only one who truly understood…

reviews.author: Jack Burnham
reviews.text: An admirable effort, but an almost impossible film to make well because what comes across quite clearly is that Nico had an aversion to being truly known or understood. So the testimonials from the various down-and-outers about how she blazed through their lives are only a small part of what feels like a deeper and much more mysterious story about what compelled her towards self destruction. There are hints that she was an inveterate mythmaker, who found decline and decay glamorous in some way, easily spinning bad habits as part of the legend. But the degree to which Nico is either in control or in thrall to external forces is never clear. Perhaps Nico was never quite aware herself.

reviews.text: Opportunism is a theme of James Young’s fun but unreliable account of touring with Nico in the 1980s, Songs They Never Play on the Radio – the opportunism of musicians who need a gig, the opportunism of addicts. A sincerity about producing art never comes into it. As such, it’s no surprise to see Young in Ofteringer’s short Nico documentary (look online for scratchy copies) saying that he wrote the book for the money. The myths and images and put-ons keep obscuring the person, whoever she was – all the Teutonic stereotyping, the attraction to and repulsion from the junkie life, the scruffy Withnail and I bohemian tragicomedy of cold rooms and dirty kitchens, the unwillingness to take a good-looking…

reviews.text: Prepare to be DOHLERIZED! NIGHTBEAST follows the trail of an alien monster in a silver tuxedo as it ravages the foggy Baltimore suburbs. Cheap gore! Laser guns! Pool party padding! And the most phenomenally awkward sex scene ever captured on 16mm film. A teenage J.J. Abrams wrote and recorded part of this movie’s synthesizer soundtrack. reviews.text: the whole perverse mental apparatus of Besson is visible here; La femme(!) Nikita is very much the epitome of what his mind would produce in the following decades. Besson’s fetish object as usual: a naive (not so innocent) but wild animal. a young woman as an enigmatic beast, of violence as much as of sexuality. "girls just wanna have fun" is a sentence that Besson is aware of, being very scared of it. first she’s becoming the victim of drug addiction, through a punk adoring her, then she learns more about his world through her 'parents'. Nikita feels like an alien throughout the whole film.

reviews.text: Much like Léon (1994), Besson ambles effortlessly between the razor edge risks of a hidden life and the bigger implications of juggling the emotions of being human while operating as a machine. Anne Parillaud runs a marathon across these shifts developing a character that has the facilities inside to survive yet remains conflicted. Jean Reno shows up as a literal cleaner of bodily carnage that surely influenced Besson to pursue the actor for a now iconic similar character four years later. This leads to a fairly sedate conclusion that's not quite as impactful as the aforementioned Léon, but sees Nikita making an important decision regarding fate.

reviews.text: The concept of criminally under seen Nine Lives is a gimmicky one, but executed to understated perfection. The film is comprised of nine brief segments, each staring a woman suffering through an emotional, physical, and/or philosophical crisis. Each episode lasts for roughly 12 minutes and takes place in one single shot. The vignettes were all captured in just one day of shooting (with one preceding full day of rehearsal). No special effects, no digital trickery, just solid acting and great storytelling.

reviews.text: During the nineties, it sure was fun watching Hollywood try and figure out what to do with Ray Liotta. They really left no stone unturned, electing to place him in leading man status after the one-two punch of Field of Dreams and Goodfellas, but never really gave him a movie that didn’t come out of some executive’s dust bin. reviews.text: In relation to other 1994 movies, this has Highlander: The Final Dimension beat for decapitations and uses "Son of a Preacher Man" better than Pulp Fiction. A messy, overly long, surprisingly violent slice of modestly budgeted major studio genre junk from the mid 90s. It's basically an amalgam of Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves, Fortress and Waterworld with a cast that includes Ray Liotta, Lance Henriksen, Ernie Hudson, Michael Lerner, an especially annoying Kevin Dillon and the scene stealing, Christmas caroling Stuart Wilson as the dread-locked, decapitation prone bad guy. From the very reliable, and underrated, Martin Campbell who would give us Goldeneye the next year. No relation to - and much better than - that awful Owen Wilson debacle with the same title from a few years ago.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: “We did what we had to do,” argues one of the beautiful terrorist teens in Bertrand Bonello’s “Nocturama,” a vague and intriguingly inert thriller that waits 50 minutes before revealing “what they had to do” and never bothers explaining why they had to do it. It’s hypnotic all the same. Fresh off his emotionally extravagant biopic of fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent, Bonello has returned with another film about the seductive power of surfaces. With his previous project, he presented that idea as his subject — with this one, he sublimates it directly into his style. The result is a portrait of radical violence that has almost no resemblance to terrorism as we know it, and yet sometimes feels all more accurate because of that.

It's a film very much "of the now," not in some lame zeitgeist-y manner, but in the way it captures a specific outlook, a way of seeing. Call-backs to Dawn of the Dead and Night of the Comet aren't trite commentaries on consumerism or radicalism or whatnot, but more ambitious abstractions of an inescapable, atomized mode of experience. It's how the notion of the progressive "now" - note the alternate title: Paris est en Fête - has become warped because of individualized context. ("She was only ten when she sang this. reviews.text: A criminally underseen film from the Polish brothers, Northfork is a religious allegory that seems to tell an inverted Deluge story, where the ones who stay behind for the flood are more saintly than those who flee. Stunning cinematography features the serene Montana landscape as a quiet drama plays out in the town of Northfork. Set in 1955, a dam is soon to be built, effectively flooding the town and all its inhabits. Most have already left for higher ground, having been persuaded by a posse of gov't evacuation men, who visit the hold-outs in a series of surreal encounters.

The reflection on a boiling kettle, or on a cold gravestone. What will you find when you reflect inwards? A crisis of faith or the affirmation that angels do exist?

reviews.text: Yes, the plot is lifted pretty heavily from Vertigo (even more than Body Double), but in many ways this really is post war Hollywood melodrama done through giallo's distorted lens. So, a way of thinking about how a certain form of painting with emotion can be turned into another. Hermann's wonderful score actually feels like the movie organizing principle more than Schrader's script, De Palma's images just act towards giving the music a physical presence. Bonkers and delirious perverse, Pretty much a catholic madman movie. De Palma was lucky he did Carrie around the same time as I could easily imagine this sending him to movie jail. Lightow and Bujold are wonderful as well. Also, because Hermann convinced De Palma to eliminate Schrader's even more insane third act, this is fascinating almost experimental structured.

reviews.text: History repeats itself, first as tragedy, second as farce, for beauty is a witch. A church that becomes a tomb that becomes a cake, glimmering airport lights and a delusional happy ending, the world reduced to its aesthetic value and promptly distorted by a madman’s deranged lenses. De Palma at his most twisted, a fever dream plagued by an insanity so profound that only teary eyes and the reflection of flickering lights in their ocular globes could be able to accurately portray it. Vertigo distilled as pure madness.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Hermetically sealed within the confines of a special brand of cinephilia, one that is unable to exist solely in its own future by virtue of being in constant conversation with itself as both present and past – yet, in spite of such self-knowing reference it manages to iterate endlessly upon itself until it creates its own newness through the oldness of its obsessions (ba dum tss). Subversion, inversion, perversion become the only escape that this De Palma picture can envision, all fixations upon its parent that serves less to annul such trauma than to derive a new, contemporary one.

reviews.author: eddie
reviews.text: mentally freezing the protagonist in 1959 is a great way to start this, showing how out of time and tragically regressive the vertigo conceit is. he even talks about returning to the graceful values of the old south before the traumatic inciting incident occurs. every deviation from the template set by hitchcock's original is a further twisting of the knife, with the third act fully indulging in the sleaze that his later vertigo riffs would have on display from their opening scenes. the textures of zsigmond's gauzy photography of the film, particularly in the italian segment, lend themselves to de palma's movement to create a dream-like free and floating camera rather than the more rigid tracking shown in some of his other films. i'm sure the accent police have already remarked upon john lithgow's southern twang, but i found his caricature to be an effective stand-in for the evil industry that made him and cliff robertson obscenely wealthy.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Not so much a remake of Vertigo as an echo of it, or maybe a memory. Even Vertigo, when you boil it down to its generic plot skeleton, is a detective mystery about a guy figuring out a complex murder plot, but this goes even further by running on pure emotion - Cliff Robertson's hero never solves anything, and spends virtually the entire movie in a transfixed, wet-eyed torpor. By the end, this emotion has blossomed into possibly the best protracted slow-motion climax of De Palma's career, and maybe (if you're paying attention) his most disturbing ending.

Enyedi takes her time in establishing a mood, through heavy use of distant shots and soft lighting. Scenes drag on for so long, they become uncomfortable. Jokes hang in the air until they’re barely jokes anymore. This is all intentional, as On Body and Soul is a perceptive portrait of its protagonists’ unfulfilled emotional lives. reviews.author: Graham Williamson
reviews.text: Can you even make a movie out of On the Road? Francis Ford Coppola, who has a producer's credit on this version, tried for years, eventually conceding that the need for a period setting made it too expensive for a studio to roll the dice. He's right that Kerouac's book needs to be considered in the context of its time: back then, this was rebellion. Now, it's a gap year. But how can you make a period movie, with carefully-sourced classic cars, shop fronts kitted out with old-fashioned displays and extras wearing vintage clothes, out of a book whose defining characteristic is an in-the-moment, improvisational energy?

The nude skateboarding gag wasn't bad, but I would have cut that down some. Still pretty cool directing debut of the screenwriter behind Kevin Smith's Cop Out that has some memorable comic scenes, especially between Willis and John Goodman. reviews.text: This reeks of the quirky R crime comedies of the 90s—where a lot of effort was dumped into writing characters who were equally parts damaged and savvy but also quirkily charming to an outside observer. And mostly, ONCE UPON A TIME IN VENICE works. Willis seems to bring his career out of a deep winter’s nap and embraces his inner-naked-skateboarding private investigator. John Goodman shows up and plays along merrily with the edgy, violent foolishness. He brings a level of comedy straight man to offset some of the odd goings-on, but Goodman also lends an air of credibility to the proceedings.

reviews.text: A sturdy, sincere, deceptively complex, and sad movie. Every actor is locked in, a who's who of men (Bridges, Brolin, Teller, Kitsch) who pay the bills with IP but hunt for stories about dignified underdogs battling nature and God and their own personal shortcomings. Kosinski's sanded-and-buffed style—architected, geometric images and sci-fi-forged utopic visions—mingles in an unusual way with the inherent chaos of a film engulfed in flames. Early on, Jennifer Connelly heals a wounded horse in a not-so-subtle but helpful metaphor for the damaged men who jump into the fire for pay and honor. It's all about these guys, the Granite Mountain Hotshots, but also about the way generations support and fail each other, the way opioids and meth hollowed…

reviews.text: Special people deserve to be loved. Neil Simon excelled at creating juicy lead roles for women. Of course, that doesn’t mean any of this is attainable. Her life as a working actress in NYC isn’t depicted as glamorous per se, but it’s still extraordinary. Looking back, this feels more influential on the future of television than it does anything else. Any sitcom in the 90s would have loved to have dialogue this good. That also means that the more dramatic scenes towards the end don’t feel as authentic as they should. Maybe it’s not Terms of Endearment, but it’s a worthy comedy-drama nonetheless.

reviews.text: When I was a kid I did some pretty questionable things. Of course I knew they were wrong but I convinced myself it was fine since they weren't jail worthy offenses. I had enough sense to know, even while acting out or rebelling, there is a limit. The kids in this movie don't have limits. They shoot at a cop car with a bb gun while it's driving on the freeway. They sell drugs and use them. They point guns at cops. They destroy multiple cars. Terrorize an entire town. Set fires, and for an encore, decide to step their game up to murder, and this movie wants me to sympathize with these punks? Never, which would also be my response to whether I'd ever watch this again.

reviews.text: I love Kurt Cobain, as I’m sure many of you do. He loves this movie. “Smells Like Teen Spirit” is THIS movie. Anarchy for certain, but a study into suburban teens and a coming of age story that doesn’t follow the typical beats. Vibes of The Outsiders are prevalent for sure, with all that 70s long hair and fashion certainly setting up what would be Dazed and Confused. Young Matt Dillon was a force to be reckoned with even then, he commands your attention, but the whole gang of kids were convincing and felt like youngsters from the neighborhood. Tim Hunter co-writing this then going on to direct River’s Edge makes all the sense in the world, both are wickedly funny, but…

reviews.author: sakana1

In this case, though, on top of the vibes is some pleasant cynicism about colonialism, and white presumptuousness about non-write cultures.

reviews.text: Given the title, you might be forgiven for thinking this is a cannibal film. But given the director, you won't be surprised to learn that it's actually a porn film. It actually gets off to a good start - a sex scene but with a horror twist! However, from there it's basically just a collection of sex scenes. Apparently there's some kind of story involving a nuclear reactor floating around; but this is lost amongst a sea of boobs. To be fair, the sex scenes are generally well shot and the leading ladies are beautiful but it's all just generally so boring. There's an amusing exchange involving names but even this is cheapened when it is done for a second…

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Joe D'Amato had a unique talent for making sex movies on tropical islands that are somehow butt-ugly. When people hang out on a beach, they're always backlit. When they have a threesome in a bathtub, it's always the smallest, grimiest bathtub. Of course, ugliness is a major part of the D'Amato Touch™.

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: There aren't really any cannibals here, but that doesn't keep this from being maybe the strangest Joe D'Amato skin show that I've seen, mixing tribal disco, cockfighting, and anticolonialist politics between the requisite sex scenes. I could maybe do without the latter, but at least D'Amato isn't afraid of parading Maurice Poli around just as much as he does his actresses. I'm mostly just here for the Stelvio Cipriani score.

reviews.author: JacobGreen
reviews.text: This has always been my favorite D'Amato film and one of my favorite sexploitation films in general. It has such a unique, almost dream-like atmosphere that I find very beautiful at times. It also has tons of memorable moments, like the opening and the cannibal dance scene. And Stelvio Cipriani delivers what I think is one of his very best scores, which heightens every aspect of the film to a new level. It's also not a cannibal film as the title suggests, well, at least not in the same tradition as what most people are used to.

reviews.author: dirtylaundri
reviews.text: D'Amato teases with cannibalism and cock fights, just to let you drown in the quicksands of a tropical slow-burn soft sex / uneasy hangout / moody postcolonial horror movie. Compared to the EMANUELLE-films, the plot feels rather well-rounded, but still doesn't really go anywhere. (Mostly because the cyclical time of myth is at odds with the linear time of politics; Papaya herself is positioned as a political actor by the script, but D'Amato's camera films her like an ancient goddess sent to earth in order to punish men by fucking them to death). Anyway, the journey is the reward.

reviews.author: Steve Sandberg
reviews.text: It looks like I'm in the minority on this one. Diablo Cody's directorial debut has been met with minimal fanfare and almost unanimously negative reviews, but despite its numerous problems, I found a lot to like, both in its attempts at cultural satire and its focus on a unique group of characters. It's an ambitious comedy that tackles the divide between faith and cynicism in smart and funny ways. Paradise is often confused in its larger statements, and sometimes perilously unsure of its tone, but the film hits more than enough to make up for its many misses.

She'd taken a very specifically queer, transgender, Latino and African-American phenomenon and totally erased that context with lyrics about how "It makes no difference if you're black or white, if you're a boy or a girl." Madonna was taking in tons of money, while the Queen who actually taught her how to vogue was sitting at a table in front of me, broke. So if anybody requested "Vogue" or any other Madonna track, I just told them, "No, this is a Madonna-free zone! And as long as I'm DJ-ing, you will not be allowed to vogue to the decontextualized, reified, corporatized, liberalized, neutralized, asexualized, re-genderized pop reflection of this dance floor's reality!"

reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: God, please just let us celebrate while we're here. Let us dance and open up the world to one another. We want to live out our dreams and be the people who we always wanted to be. We'll reach for that safe place where we can exist and let everything else fall out of vision. This hyper awareness of appearance, actions and danger should rest long enough so we can move to song. An opening in a void where everything isn't pitch black so we can come out and shout who we are. We're Xtravaganza and we're proud. And we live hand in hand without the worry of a real world. Everything's a ball and we'd vogue for hours into the sunlight and walk home safely and rest like everyone else, and when dusk comes around again we'd do it once more with no fear of rejection, personhood or danger. We'd be home. If only for a moment.

reviews.text: A prog-metal concept album that takes 20+ years to listen to and is still being recorded as you are listening to it. This is the part that gets quiet and spacy and inward and mystical and stuff where people sit around fires and practice their time travel and telekinesis when not rebuilding engines or staring intently at the moon as it goes down in time lapse, hidden away for the time being, pulling the tides along with it like a bed made upon rising. The part of the album that if your friends are talking you might shush them or call their attention to the layers of sonic detail just under the surface or, not needing to be shushed, conversation lapses at just that moment and eyes fix upon some point invisible or barely manifest in this world, gradually resuming, but quieter than before.

reviews.text: With a slashed budget and limited resources, Coscarelli's filmmaking returns to the spare surrealism that made the first film so effective, furthering the interdimensional travelogue of our heroes in a way that retains the heart of the previous sequels while excising their goofier distractions. All four principals deliver their finest performances yet, and the fact that we've gotten to see them age across twenty years adds a level of genuine poignancy to the mayhem. New events bleed into old footage to make the film itself a cosmic battleground, with Mike and Reggie standing alone as the world's last bastions of good and the Tall Man preparing each wasteland and hellscape for Armageddon.

reviews.text: Wow, I was in tears for almost the entire last five minutes of this film. And it's funny, because after reading many of the reviews of Phoenix, I was really anticipating an extraordinarily executed ending, something truly special - and my god, that's exactly what I received x 1,000. Beyond the masterful suspense that the film retains throughout the duration of its runtime, it's also strong thematically. There are the obvious themes of war and the Holocaust and the notion of returning from a concentration camp, but the more abstract themes that it presents are equally as fascinating. I enjoy the way Phoenix, much like the recent Under the Skin, approaches the idea of surfaces and what is beneath them,…

reviews.text: Recommended to me by one Scott Tobias because of the ending, which he described as possibly the best of the year; the ending of this film is powerful, but boy, does it take some contrivance getting there, and it leaves an awful lot of frustrating threads dangling along the way. In particular, there's a key side character who seems more compelling and likely to produce a better story than the lead character, but she disappears offscreen late in the film, as if she had to get back to her own, better movie. But also, so much of the narrative here just didn't pass the Roger Ebert Stupidity test for me, in terms of people making choices that don't make sense, except to forward the narrative. There are a few vague attempts to explain away what's going on, but for me they weren't convincing or compelling arguments; you almost have to take the whole thing as metaphorical to buy it.

reviews.author: mrbalihai
reviews.text: The Salton Sea figures heavily in my personal history, especially during my teenage years growing up in Southern California. The Sea was a frequent weekend destination for me and my buddies. We'd ride around in VW Beetles converted into dune buggies, fish for Tilapia, and hunt ducks in the marshes surrounding the national wildlife refuge. We'd also drive to nearby Yuma, AZ, where we could easily buy cheap beer and cheap weed in order to enhance the festivities. Even back then, the Sea had clearly seen better days, and by the time the 80s rolled around, it had become a disaster zone of unbelievable proportions and we had moved on to healthier locales in which to indulge ourselves.

It’s without question that Marvel is severely lacking in the animation department as opposed to the likes of DC, and this film is proof of it. reviews.text: Sometimes I realize, especially when I watch films like this, just how much I distance myself from people with shallow thinking. Not to call them dumb, but I prefer to say their thinking is underdeveloped. It’s striking how fiercely they defend their beliefs, grounded in nothing more than theories they’ve constructed in their own minds. The irony is that everything they criticize or claim to hate is a direct product of the very system they were born into (produced by those they blindly defend). What the world truly lacks is the curiosity to imagine what it’s like not to be ignorant. I can’t believe people like this exist. And it’s heartbreaking to think that a film like this shouldn’t even need to exist — but sadly, it does.

reviews.text: Many Japanese films from the late 1990s and early 2000s explored the disillusionment, apathy, and lack of direction felt by the country's younger generations. Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Bright Future and Pulse bring attention to some of the anxieties and struggles that young people in Japan deal with regularly. Shunji Iwai's Picnic follows lost souls on a quest to find meaning and purpose in life. My introduction to director Toshiaki Toyoda's filmography, Blue Spring, is arguably one of the greatest films associated with this segment of Japanese cinema. It concentrates on similar issues but within a high school setting instead of Shibuya (Pornostar's setting). Although, perhaps most similar to Pornostar is Shinji Aoyama's Helpless, which is an unconventional yakuza film of sorts…

reviews.text: Violent pessimism washes over Toshiaki Toyoda's strikingly dingy feature debut which inventively uses one man's psychotic path of aimless destruction to shine a light on the emptiness spreading throughout an entire generation. Similarly to many other Japanese films from the time, the economic disparity and social unrest that had been simmering away in the country during the previous decade plays a crucial role in shaping the bruised outlook; for people like the unhinged Arano (played with chilling intensity by Chihara Junia), falling into a life dominated by criminality becomes the only logical option he can make as the sense of power it brings him counteracts the overwhelming apathy caused by circumstances beyond his control. reviews.text: Well, I'm not off to a great start with Roberta Findlay. This should be more fun than it is. A sleazy bit of satanic panic, with a goopy demon puppet, a satanic cult leader that feels like the actor based his performance on the Bela Lugosi Dracula, and the requisite amount of exposed flesh you'd expect in one of these things. So, I have no idea why this felt like such a chore to get through. I suspect the editing had a fair bit to do with it though. It's very narratively muddled, with events not properly transitioning into one another. There's no flow. Editing is one of those things that you almost never notice when it's done right, unless the editor is just showing off, but when it's this shoddy it can bring the whole movie down.

There is a long out-of-print release dubbed in Italian with all gore intact, and I hope someone makes a composite someday or some company (Vinegar Syndrome?) finally releases an intact English version. reviews.text: RV culture is in many ways born from the ashes of the beatnik/hippie hit-the-road-to-find-Amerikkka-and-in-finding-Amerikkka-you-will-find-yourself but even that dream was presaged and paralleled by the endless middle-class family trips taken by boomer children in Airstream Trailers, a way of making the ideal of the suburban home portable, transferable to any location, where everywhere is becoming more like where you left. When they became adults, became disillusioned with liberation and revolution, saddled with jobs, given up esoteric mysticism or folded it into a general program of self-improvement, the yearning to just get out of this place, to go somewhere, anywhere but here and never having to stop channeled itself into the luxury RV market. The RV was a home on wheels which…

reviews.text: The best metaphor I can think of for the gender politics in this movie is a scene in which Marlene Dietrich's character slyly wins some money off of a rigged roulette wheel. By all appearances to the bystanders, she's a tough, willful, risk-taking dame. What they can't see is that a man has his foot on a pedal that controls the (literal) wheel of fortune. She's at his mercy.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: very fierce gothic western, a prologue to the heist-western that would later be perfected by leone, walter hill and peckinpah, but perhaps most importantly, rancho notorious is a memorandum on dietrich's 'fallen woman' persona, becoming the emotional touchstone for a group of bad men after she's aged out of the freewheeling proto-femme fatale roles she had in all her collaborations with von sternberg; her gender-bent goddess now rules with economics instead of romance. fritz lang takes a quintessentially american genre and uses it to say that democracy is a sham, loyalty is a farce, and love is a temporary illusion.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Imperfect in the same exhilarating way that The Searchers is, as filmmakers struggle to explore themes that their chosen art form (studio film), genre (western), and its social context (1950s America) heavily limited the depiction of. Still, it can be tempting to give this thing a lot less credit than I think it deserves - it's a pretty dark and unforgiving look at two people twisted by their surroundings into monsters (in other words, a Fritz Lang movie), and a subversive take on sexual politics (this is up for debate, but I don't really buy that we're meant to accept Vern's mission as a righteous one - this is Lang we're talking about, remember).

O herói trágico luta no sentimento paradoxal de que os obstáculos que encontra na sua ação são ao mesmo tempo intransponíveis e necessários para serem superados. O conflito trágico é uma luta travada contra o que é fatal para o herói que a trava; é a oportunidade de afirmar e mostrar na ação que esta não é totalmente fatal ou não permanecerá assim. reviews.author: João Bénard da Costa
reviews.text: Terceiro e último western de Fritz Lang, Rancho Notorious foi filmado mais de dez anos depois dos anteriores filmes do género. E se, com The Return of Frank James e Western Union, Lang tinha assinado alguns marcos míticos do género na sua fase “pura” (ou seja, nos anos 40, quando só o Oeste era mítico e o western film ainda o não era) com Rancho Notorious inaugura-se o que nos anos 50 se chamou “western impuro”, ou seja o filme que já tem a consciência da carga mítica que agita.

reviews.author: Catherine Stebbins
reviews.text: The definition of an undiscovered jewel. Patricia Gozzi, looking like a gamine teenage Juliette Binoche, is uncut, honest, and raw as the troubled Agnes. Everything feels like a highly fractured fairy tale; delusional, grand, and run-down. It’s keyed into French New Wave sensibilities but isn’t led by them. The isolation and family dynamics sit somewhere above us, slightly inexplicable and unconventional but visible all the same. Dean Stockwell is sort of impossibly good-looking in the 60’s, something I wasn’t aware of until now. Seek this out when you can (PS; it's on youtube). It’s sumptuous, troubling, and off-kilter in equal measure.

reviews.text: What an odd film this was! In fact, I'm still sorting out my complicated reaction to it. On the one hand, it has moments of beautiful lyricism bordering on fantasy, set on the turbulent coast on Brittany. Yet at other times, it's deeply unsettling in its portrayal of a teenage girl with clear psychiatric and perhaps cognitive challenges who's dealing with her sexual awakening as she enters puberty. All of which is set aflame when she and her father shelter a handsome fugitive who brutally beat a police officer, with both father and daughter projecting their fantasies upon him.

Plus the impact of familial struggle on existence - a fuzzy similarity to a wife that tore your heart out, the enigmatic stranger who finally gives one the love they’ve been craving for - “you never refused me anything”. Paternal oppression manifests into the only genuine connection being with a scarecrow built from rags, and then believing it’s come to life since that improbability seems the only thing that will possibly allow escape. Patricia Gozzi’s Agnes is an emotive, expressive presence, giving the film a tangible quality and someone to truly root for in what’s otherwise a tragic, regretful film. But a beautiful one. The time limit for this fantasy (when people turn back into who they truly are) brings in the Cinderella story influence. It’s also interesting to me that the narrative is told here from a male protagonist’s perspective. I guessed how the film would end at its midpoint. This could have gone in many different directions tho… it’s a well written & produced short, which would hold its own as a feature film.

reviews.author: ThisIsBigCat
reviews.text: Much like Howard the Duck, Red Tails is yet another George Lucas pet project that failed miserably. Lucas intended to make a film about the Tuskegee Airmen for years, even envisioning it as a three-hour epic. He even got Boondocks creator Aaron McGruder involved as co-writer. The problem with Red Tails is that it intends to honor the sacrifices of the Tuskegee Airmen, but it ultimately trivializes them. It's like the filmmakers tried desperately to appeal to modern audiences, but all that effort fell flat on its face. The excessive use of CGI is distracting, and the tone is corny as hell. The movie throws in all the Hollywood cliches you can think of to the point of cringe.

reviews.text: After switching gears to try to catch up on some TV for the last couple of weeks (No, I was not captive in a Russian Gulag for my last Military Monday documentary review, that was a joke as I noted with the "satire" tag, which it does seem most of yall caught) I figured I'd hit this title for Military Monday this week. There's nothing particularly exciting or unique about it; it's another WW2 propaganda documentary which I've found plenty of on these Mill Creek collections. This one, as the title suggests, focuses on the scraps against japan in the Aleutians, which were fairly minor skirmishes compared to the greater war effort in the South Pacific at the time. It's a bit of an interesting watch if you enjoy period documentaries since this is another one filmed during wartime in during WW2.

Strategically Adak is one of the most important locations in the world.”

reviews.text: This is the first film in the series to feel almost entirely artificial, with lots of unnatural landscapes peopled by CGI automatons alongside people acting like automatons. In retrospect, the Army of Millas (one of the top five coolest things in cinema this decade) is the pivot point of the entire series, the moment at which we go through the looking glass from a real world beset by technological-biological catastrophe to the overwriting of our now dead planet by ever-fungible technological-biological simulacra.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Of the three Resident Evil films Paul WS directed, this is probably the least interesting - save for a scumbag movie producer, it's virtually apolitical. Yet, there's still an astounding formal cohesion & furthermore a rueful melancholy which to my eyes seem unmatched before or since. In many ways it's the most similar film to the original - where that film was set almost entirely in one location, this one brings it up to two! This structural tightness however also allows WS to diverge/experiment formally - nothing in WS's films prior (or movies in general?) has looked quite like this - action sequences become a complete sensorial overload - total digital cinema! Two of my favourite action sequences ever: Redfield fighting…

reviews.text: I watched this movie purely based on casting. Linda Cardellini is maybe the most underrated actress in Hollywood, her performance here was top notch and certainly the best part about the movie. Michael Shannon did great as well, and it was nice to see him in yet another film. Speaking on the character development though, it's as if our Lindsey from Freaks And Geeks has all grown up! Linda plays Kelly, a simple but genuine individual who returns home from being deployed. When she arrives, nothing goes as planned and rightfully so, as one would expect from coming home after being deployed. The deeper roots of this film, though, show what it's like to deal with trauma... and more importantly,…

reviews.text: Damn, this was tough. That ending packs a special kind of wallop. There’s certainly honor in doing what you have to do, even if that path is downright nightmarish, I just don’t even know how you muster the strength to accept it. However, I do know that Linda Cardellini rocked the fuck out in this thing. The weight she carries in her performance makes all this circumstantial hurt hit so hard. Especially during the “I have to go back” sequence, that weight seems unbearable. That moment completely consumed me. Ugh, and the smile on her face as she says “I’m fine” feels so broken it’s hard to stomach. Dammit, this performance is amazing. And Liza Johnson is the real deal

reviews.text: Sony Chiba is as lethal as ever in this sequel, but it's missing plenty that the original had. There's no shocking graphic mutations here. The cinematography in the climax was way too dark which largely was absent from the original featuring a fight in a rainstorm at night at the end. Act one is actually largely absent the star with it showing simple karate demonstrations for over ten minutes and proceeding to focus on side characters. The tag-a-long doofus wasn't as good here either. Then what's good about this one? Well, practically everything Sony Chiba did here was fantastic. From taking on cops in the station while his hands were bound to that climax against a building full of mafia, this one still thrilled plenty. It just clearly falls short of the original.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: A sly piece of pop subversion, this irresistible satire of Reagan-era materialism features Tom Cruise in his star-is-born breakthrough as a Chicago suburban prepster whose college-bound life spirals out of control when his parents go out of town for the week and an enterprising call girl (Rebecca De Mornay) invites him to walk on the wild side. While Cruise boogying in his briefs yielded one of the most iconic pop-cultural moments of the 1980s, it is the film’s unexpected mix of tender romance (enhanced by a moody synth score by Tangerine Dream) and sharp-witted capitalist critique that remains fresh and daring.

reviews.text: Luchino Visconti is one of my favorite Italian directors, and Rocco and His Brothers has solidified that sentiment for me. There’s something about the way he handles emotion, scale, and character that just clicks with me. This movie is very melodramatic, but what makes it land for me is that it’s rooted in the lives of people who have nothing. Set in a post-WWII Italy still recovering from the scars of fascism, the movie reflects how uneven that recovery was, especially for the South. These were rural, agricultural areas where opportunity was scarce and the economy was practically lifeless. So when this family (a mother and her five sons) move north to Milan, there’s this immediate sense of hope mixed…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Luchino Visconti’s epic melodrama of social migration and moral decay was first released in 1960, when it was met with great scandal (a prosecutor threatened to charge the director with “disseminating an obscene object”) and even greater success. Today, distanced from ridiculous controversy and dislocated from the provincial politics that drive its story, this immaculately restored classic of post-WWII Italian cinema often feels like a new experience altogether.

reviews.author: Henry
reviews.text: Being from Michigan makes this hit a lot harder, especially when members of my family used to work in the auto industry. Looking at how capitalism and the people in charge of these huge corporations can just tear down an entire city without any consequences is always hard to watch, but it something that always needs to be seen. It’s amazing that Moore can arrange these clips of horrible things to create comedy that is both funny and painful. I’m very excited to watch more of Moore’s work because the level of provocation he brings to a documentary is exactly what I find impactful.

reviews.text: I've lived in southeastern Michigan for the past year, which definitely added some weight to my experience with this movie. A widening area around Detroit is still experiencing the economic desolation that Moore chronicles here, as well as the generalized pity and sometimes contempt that accompany it. Decades old though the footage may be, it remains woefully salient. Candid interviews juxtapose laid-off auto workers with Flint's clueless elite, who themselves satirize the wealth gap better than most fiction. Thoroughly, systematically, Moore traces the fallout of the factory closings: from new jobs for the unemployed (Amway, Taco Bell) to the nonstop evictions (in which you can see how heavily Flint's poverty is inflected by racism) to city officials' short-sighted attempts to…

Roger & Me is the prototype of what would come, and it's far less potent in its obnoxiousness. Moore is in the sidelines. The intensity of his persona toned down. The story is interesting and it's told well. That said, his manipulation is still there. There's scenes that are there purely for sensationalist impact. reviews.text: Despite both this and NIGHTCRAWLER employing some pretty well-worn ideas to say not much that's particularly fresh, Gilroy's certainly making some idiosyncratic stylistic and narrative moves here. This is like his own version of his brother's MICHAEL CLAYTON but without the self-satisfied portent, and it's as full of tics as Denzel's performance (which is great, maybe the best thing he's done since Demme's MANCHURIAN CANDIDATE). I like that this reverses the boilerplate "crisis of conscience" throughline, having a guy realize that his pristine ideals really aren't worth compromising, even though the beats sort of remain the same, which leaves room for a lot of welcome digression (like the vacation, or the way this noticeably takes place in a very recognizable sphere of runaway capital, institutional failure, and gentrification).

reviews.text: "Rover Dangerfield" is a 1991 animated film directed by James L. George and Bob Seeley. Following the infamous persona of comedian Rodney Dangerfield, the film inserts him in animated dog from as he ventures from the streets of Las Vegas to an adventure down on the farm. Ironically, this film was never intended to be the G rated film that it turned out to be. Rather it was a product in development within the late 1980s and was intended to be a R rated animation with adult based humor. Certainty this all flew over my head as a child but upon rewatch I can absolutely see the intent and that this was drastically changed in mid process.

reviews.author: Ed Küpfer
reviews.text: Well, now we know what First Blood would have looked like if it was directed by Hal Needham and starred Face from the A Team. What's interesting is not so much that the premise of the movie—Vietnam vet with PTSD gets hassled by the police in a small town and fights back—predates Rambo's debut by more than a year, but that such stories were in the air to begin with. This is a very PG version of the story, so there isn't a lot of thrills or action, but in keeping with the hicksploitation aspects of the story there are a ton of car stunts and explosions.

reviews.text: A simple, direct, vaguely political magical realist film that spins three good yarns out of a fairly conventional flashback structure. The biggest speed bumps are the seams between the episodes, the connective tissue isn't very artful, but the clumsiness quickly fades away while the plot moves relentlessly forward. Overall a skilled and beguiling distillation of the feeling of a time and place, made with openness and authenticity. We were told that in the Ivory Coast, where this film was made and truly needs to be seen, there are a total of three theatres. I hope it sells out at every one.

Sylvia Sydney really shined in the 3rd act (which I wish was longer). Oskar Homolka is a dead ringer for someone I know & I don’t know if it made it scarier or took me out of it

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Sabotage is an interesting early Hitchcock film that showcases the director's flair for causing a shock. The film focuses on an evil menace lurking in a London community. Cinema owner Karl Verloc has a lucrative little sideline in conducting sabotage, but the local greengrocer (also a Scotland Yard detective) is hot on his tail. It's all about secrets - people acting in the shadows and unknown danger lurking behind everyday life. Sabotage is deceptively simple, but draws its suspense from a well crafted plot and set pieces. The film is most famous for one particular scene that sees a young boy unwittingly carry a bomb onto a packed London bus. Hitchcock really ramps up the suspense here - made even…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: The further I delve into the Western genre, the more I tend to focus on actors that intrigue me. Robert Taylor wouldn't be everyone's idea of the traditional Western star, but it would appear that Taylor had an eye for a good script, worked with seasoned directors who knew their stuff, and ultimately, so far, has delivered time and time again for everyone from William A. Wellman to John Sturges, Anthony Mann to Michael Curtiz. Taylor had a natural screen presence, a strong jaw, and looked the part on a horse, and although more suited to possibly romantic roles where his movie-star looks seemed to work wonders with the ladies, his Westerns have been of a very high standard.

reviews.text: This pretty good forgotten western would be memorable just on the basis of the weird radical contrasts of laid back leading man Robert Taylor, a retired gunmen, and the nervous tics of his trigger happy brother John Cassavetes. Robert Parish directs a fine anti-western script by Rod Serling with no patience for the sort of major rhetorical gambits and bloat that often sink those, but it is the Taylor/Cassavetes dynamic and the radical disparity between old/new Hollywood that carries the film.

reviews.author: Jenna Ipcar
reviews.text: Oh, interesting! Weird! Fun! A straight almost classic western that hates violence! Not even just unjust violence, but all violence. (Not a big surprise for Rod Serling but a welcome change in the genre for sure.) Usually the movies end with the gunslinger settling down, but this one starts off with him already settled until his trigger happy and emotionally stunted younger brother comes back to town and starts to shoot up a storm. That that brother is young, high-voiced John Cassavetes makes the whole thing even weirder.

reviews.text: Cassavetes digs deep to find the unhinged asshole within. It's weird to see him do it in this classical Hollywood context instead of in his self-produced films where he has his entire cast doing it. It sort of works and it sort of doesn't. He definitely keeps the movie from being just another routine Western, but I found I was always relieved when he wasn't on the screen. Royal Dano might actually make MVP as the desperate Yankee trying to farm in cattle country and the Rod Serling script has its share of good ideas, even if the backstory isn't always convincing.

The film has the standard gunslinger with a vendetta against the hero but here it is only to serve as the catalyst for the descent into villainry of the hero's brother. The farmer vs rancher storyline is also told in an interesting way. But the most notable part is the death of the villain. I can't recall seeing that before in a western.

reviews.text: Spaghetti Western from Mattei & Fragasso. Set in Texas after the Civil War. A sleazy Southern commander seeks to buy the beautiful daughter (‘Yarin’) of Native American chief ‘Black Eagle’. He is killed and his community is slaughtered when he refuses - and Yarin is kidnapped. Yarin manages to escape, and encounters a rancher / former confederate soldier. The duo reluctantly ally and attempt to get even. Stylish, grim and downbeat. A macabre tale of revenge and morality. Cheap, rough around the edges, and suitably nasty in spots - boasting an array of scalpings, traps, and torture scenes. Farnese and Galan are good, though the supporting performances are generally weak. The make up effects and set pieces are good, and Luigi Ceccarelli's rip off synthy score is fine. A surprisingly decent Mattei & Fragasso joint.

reviews.text: Incompetent Z-grade movies from sixty years ago are generally more engaging than incompetent Z-grade movies made today. It’s not the time-capsule factor; it’s because the mechanics of shooting 35mm with slow lenses on the cheap necessitates a lot of narrative snipping and quirky decision-making. Here, that means long takes, solid-color sets, and circular, drawn-out dialogue (“But whhhyyy, Laura? Whhhyyy are you opposed to the baaandaaage? Does it re-mind you of something, perhaaaps?”).

He knows that because they're human they're driven by animal desires that will corrupt any sense of decency or morality to which they may have previously clung. His sandbox is devoid of real love, just a dead sea of unhappy marriages, misguided obsession, abuse, theft, and manipulation. Everyone's trying to put one over on everybody else. It's grim, adult stuff which makes the "Jeepers!" and "For cat's sake!" exclamations seem especially quaint compared to the deep black in which everything else is cast. reviews.text: One great type of Lang shot. You can pan or truck to show a person moving towards another person, but if you arrange them diagonally, you can do it with a push-in, and eliminate lateral movement. In this way, moving towards someone is not a form of progression in space, but is tantamount to becoming trapped with them in a shrinking frame.

reviews.author: Jane Firehorse
reviews.text: Perhaps I was in the mood for a little gothic melodrama mixed with stunning film noir cinematography. Perhaps it was the "Bluebeard" myth that got to me. Or maybe it was the mystery, the doubling, or even Joan Bennett's gorgeous wardrobe. But whatever it was, I truly enjoyed watching Fritz Lang's "Secret Beyond the Door" for the first time. It has a lot going on, including Freudian elements that predate Hitchcock's "Psycho" while riffing on his depiction of The Gothic genre in "Rebecca"; it's a love story, a mystery, and a horror story all rolled into one. As a result, the film might come across as jumbled, but that weirdness is part of the appeal, for me at least. It's also well acted, beautifully shot, and captivating. Well worth the watch!

reviews.text: As the third entry in the original Shaft trilogy, Shaft in Africa also feels like the most different of the three given the drastic change in location despite also keeping a lot of the Blaxploitation touches that makes these three notable films. Honestly however, I don't really love the way that this movie completely removes Shaft from the New York dwellings of the first two and it seems to make a conscious effort to shift him into being a James Bond-type action hero (complete with silly gadgets) rather than a private detective. In those terms, it sort of works but it's still the weakest of the three for me since it's a fairly formulaic adventure that compensates for the thin story by throwing in more action. Still, Richard Roundtree is great again and Shaft in Africa overall is a pretty fun Blaxploitation film, if one that's an unnecessary departure for the character and series.

reviews.author: MichaelEternity
reviews.text: There's always something fraught about John Hughes movies; not the story tension, that's just part of any movie's DNA. It's how capricious they can be from moment to moment, given his unique perspective on conventional teen comedies, rom-coms, feature-length sitcoms..and it's how real their hearts throb underneath. Clearly "The Breakfast Club" is an open dissection of high school-age emotional warfare, but even his bubbly fountains of mirth like "Ferris Bueller", "Sixteen Candles", "Planes, Trains and Automobiles", and "Uncle Buck" have gobsmacking undercurrents of deep pathos and existentialism. That ardor, that glowing bonfire in his soul that loves and engages in life, is what made his work so special.

reviews.text: Opens as a bureaucratic farce, with lanyard nerds moving from boardroom to slightly bigger boardroom while civilian lives are being lost--most interesting is how Anno and Higuchi capture their futility in the filmmaking, very few compositions in each of the setups match so that the visual information is always slightly shifting (not dissimilar from the dialogue, a bunch of contributing voices not really saying much of anything) while the off-rhythm rapid cuts don't allow you the proper time to even process any information of any kind, putting us in lockstep with the characters' sense of overwhelming panic--and then slowly transitions into an optimistic ode to our ability to collectively overcome our fears. Mankind is a chaotic, impractical mess of lone wolves, nerds, troublemakers, outcasts, academic heretics and general pains-in-the-bureacracy... but together, we're capable of some pretty extraordinary things.

reviews.text: The only Mel Brooks movie I’d never seen is ... pretty consistently hilarious? reviews.text: Sister Street Fighter was exactly what I wanted: violent, action-packed, and a story that may have been written by a ten-year-old. Even the way some characters die seem like something a kid would come up with. Oh! Let's have a guy get his head twisted around backwards! And then he can stagger around looking like Tom Green as the Backwards Man in Freddy Got Fingered! Haha! Etsuko Shihomi (aka Sue Shiomi) is an excellent lead and kicks a whole lot of ass. Sonny Chiba isn't in the film much, but his few scenes were a nice reminder of his incredible martial arts skills. There's explosive geysers of blood. There's an absurd amount of villains who hang out together by a poolside. There's a guy with nunchucks who blurts out non-stop high-pitched screams. There's a funky-as-fuck score. There's even a mid-air fight. Sister Street Fighter is awesome.

reviews.text: Goddamn this was a fucking blast. These 70s Japanese exploitation movies scratch a very specific itch for me with their constant assault on the senses and nonstop funky 70s music. reviews.text: Quite simply, I wanted to see some Dudes Get Wrecked ™ last night, and that itch was scratched. Soon enough they break up and Jacqui has an affair with Al's best mate who happens to be a local cop. Things get…

reviews.author: Wilson
reviews.text: Roger Donaldson's Smash Palace is a remarkable piece of work. It shows the best of Donaldson's work, the down to earth action of the car racing sequences and the bitter raw emotion of the relationship separation, the grim violence of the sex and tough, precision of the car scenes. The brutality of the rape scene, haunting propulsive score, the third act terror. Smash Palace is practically a domestic horror. Fathers for Justice taken to their natural, insane conclusion. Horror, in its way, but mostly a drama.

reviews.author: Bandy Greensacks
reviews.text: Certainly the most relatable story of a man taking his young daughter and an innocent woman hostage. It's amazing that a film with subject matter this ugly - a disintegrating marriage, a cheating spouse and a non-molestation order taking a child away from a parent - could be so god damn beautiful to look at, with so many picture perfect magic hour shots, overhead helicopter shots, action shots from inside a race car, etc. And the balance between quiet moments and explosive, angry moments is nearly as perfect.

Imagine HUNT FOR THE WILDERPEOPLE, only instead of Sam Neill, you have Charles Rane headed up into the woods with his kid, the entire affair climaxing in a grim, fatalistic final reel. Even love is a form of trauma.

reviews.author: RivoliPalace
reviews.text: Australian born New Zealand Director Roger Donaldson put himself on the cinematic map with his relationship drama “Smash Palace” in 1981. Making it available in the States throughout 1982 in a reverse logic manner of distribution. Thinking perhaps if there was a film made in New Zealand that was garnering buzz in America but not yet available down under or in Kiwi it would gin up interest in the property that otherwise might just come and go. The gamble paid off as U.S. critics sang Donaldson’s praises and heralded “Smash Palace” as a breakthrough in New Zealand’s growing film industry.

The beauty is that everything is translated in pure action, everything a matter of another form of behavior. The spacedock flyby of the refitted Enterprise lasts almost six minutes! Unheard of now, and in fact I can't safely say that if such a thing were to occur in a modern studio event feature like this that I wouldn't be bitching about it being excruciatingly boring. reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: Deathly serious movie about an intergalactic destructive cloud that features long stretches of people politely speaking in Naval command instructions on a flight deck. Almost entirely action-free and unusually philosophical about the nature of existence, even by Trekkian standards. WRATH OF KHAN is the standard-bearer in my mind, but this has a methodical, almost religious approach that is shocking for such a high-budgeted post-STAR WARS science fiction feature. You can feel the weight of CLOSE ENCOUNTERS OF THE THIRD KIND on it. The big reveal, when the crew discovers what “V’ger” stands for, is downright hilarious. But the conclusion foretells the same A.I. anxiety that animated a lot of Kubrick’s work. The production design and tech has aged poorly, but the intent never expires.

Technically, the movie is solid; especially the perfectly fitting dramatic musical score. Russell Crowe puts on a strong show. Additional credits to his stylish long hair for raising the bar on coolness. Rachael McAdams and Ben Affleck were good. The movie on the whole carries a compelling aura and ends up an enjoyable thriller.

reviews.text: Jim Jarmusch's "wherever you go, it's all the same" movie may feel a little cynical about the joys of the world — here, the joys are mostly a stolen pack of cigarettes, an old cartoon on TV, and a win at the racetrack — but it's a terrific moody character study and it feels like the Rosetta Stone to understanding Jim Jarmusch's film rhythms, the way he lingers on shots and lets his characters sit around so viewers can study and understand them. This is a film about people fighting to define themselves in spite of other people's expectations, but the fights are so subtle that they get summed up in the way the characters stand, and sit, and look at each other, and listen to music.

reviews.text: I'm not a huge fan of documentaries or films focused on a single crime and the subsequent fight for justice, but I was pleasantly surprised to find that Strong Island was more than it initially seemed. Its examination of an injustice reached out into broader topics about race, and also more intimate revelations about a family history. It reveals deep regrets and also deep flaws in society. Yet Strong Island doesn't really congeal into a singular purposeful text, instead partially being an essay, a memoir, and a tribute without really committing to any single one. With so many strong American films (and especially documentaries) discussing race in the last couple of years, Strong Island just lacks the bite and overview to sit among…

reviews.author: Movie Good or Movie Bad?
reviews.text: Yance Ford delivered an extremely powerful documentary about the questions surrounding his brother’s death and his family’s challenges to process the grief of this death in an unjust world that never gave him a fair chance. I have many thoughts about those being challenged by the editing or the pacing or the fact that this film moves in a way that doesn’t provide as much information as others are used to when watching “true crime” and I think that’s a flawed way of looking at this documentary. Grief is cyclical and we see that as this family experiences it over and over again until some of these family members die without answers, which is how we as the audience are left by the end. Powerful filmmaking that I wish more people saw the way I did.

Instead, what Suburbia does is effectively demonstrate the obvious but frequently unacknowledged notion that society is constructed to give the benefit of the doubt to some, while always assuming the worst in others. It's about whom we choose to hold accountable as much as for what. And what's doubly impressive is that Spheeris gets it done via a narrative framework that's incredibly compelling…

reviews.text: Two older adults who are discreetly in a parallel relationship with a younger man, both fulfilling themselves with dissimilar occupations yet use this man as a source to reclaim their youth and elation. It’s not exactly a film about desperation and pain but rather jealousy and spiritual obligations, emphasizing one's desire to feel accepted. Sunday Bloody Sunday showcases homosexual affection in a way I’ve rarely seen on film: normal. The screenplay doesn’t shift focuses unprecedentedly, utilize certain characters’ storylines over others, misrepresent sexuality and, mostly importantly, it doesn’t try to act “clever” or “witty” as much as it is authentic and truthful. Absolutely stunning.

reviews.text: Criterion 2025 challenge movie #18Sunday Bloody Sunday is a pretty revolutionary film of the period and throws the viewer into a quiet study of love and loneliness in middle-class London and revolves around a love triangle and a gay relationship, which obviously at the time on screen was pretty groundbreaking stuff, but ultimately it's not a film that landed for me. I like the depictions of loneliness, and the way it looks into a homosexual relationship feels respectable and complex, and Peter Finch is really great here, but I just think it's all been done better since this film, unfortunately. It's got a good, restrained approach though, and it is ultimately new at the time, but it just didn't hit me the intended way, but I don't know, maybe on a rewatch it will; it's worth a watch though.
