reviews.text: since my friend passed away in december, i don't think i've watched a single movie without thinking about her. i don't know if i've read a book or poem without thinking of her, either. i wouldn't say my grief has consumed me, and i'd like to think i'm not obsessed with it, but perhaps i'm hyperaware of loss in art. it's the absolute inevitable, the big cliche, the ultimate truth: we cannot control or change death. i'm interested in how that dictates the ways in which we process loss. how we make something immutable more malleable so we can learn to not just move past it, but live with it.

reviews.author: Patrick Pryor
reviews.text: A movie that totally lives up to its premise of Gary Busey, F. Murray Abraham, Rutger Hauer, Charles S. Dutton, and John C. McGinley riding ATVs through the PNW to hunt Ice T with automatic weapons. What a cast, and they do not disappoint! I especially loved Gary Busey's gripping and disturbing long take monologue about his dear old bulldog, Prince Henry Stout. And a 30-year-old man playing F. Murray Abraham's tween son left me screamin'! Surviving the Game plays like a relentlessly entertaining caravan of stars at the top of their alt-right cartoon villain game packed with taught action and a (chillingly) poignant theme of America's rich sighting us poors in their crosshairs. Lightning really struck with this'un! TOO FUN!

reviews.text: The Jonathan Demme-Goldie Hawn fight over the editing aside, what remains here is still pretty lovely, probably because Demme’s focus is in period depiction and the world of war time US comes alive with care and insight. Some of Hawn/Russell material, particular in the late going, is awkward, but everything to do with her friendship with Lahti is top Demme. Of note, this was Demme’s first big studio movie and he would only do another one with Philadelphia 9 years later, so maybe the mess here did help us to get another few years of very good Demme movies. Very underrated and on par with Demme’s other work from this period, but if you are one of those happy few that have the bootleg VHS director’s cut please DM through Twitter.

reviews.author: pirateneckbeard
reviews.text: I feel this is very much a Jonathan Demme movie and also not. He captures moments but doesn't let them stagnate and lets them play out more organically without demonizing the bad elements of humanity just showcasing it for better or worse. I really wanted to see this film for Demme's style and the cast that he was working with. This captures a unique time with a story that has an importance and seldom told about and I enjoyed that aspect. While I don't think it is a solid piece of work I did enjoy it and think that there is a better version out there possibly in the directors cut.

reviews.text: "Sylvio" is a 2017 comedy directed by Albert Birney and Kentucker Audley. In tandem with the film's name, the central character of the film is a gorilla named Sylvio Bernardi who is generally soft spoken in his general approach. As the only phrases that come out of his mouth come from the robotic voice of a computer that he types words into, most of the film is a comedic observation on his deadpan approach to the world. Although his comedy is muted and surmised of irony builds, there are often implanted inflections of the heart by his routine, usually when he introduces his hand puppet Herbert Herpels into the equation.

reviews.author: Arlo Wiley
reviews.text: Taking Chance follows the week-long journey of LtCol Mike Strobl (Kevin Bacon) as he escorts the remains of fallen soldier Chance Phelps back home. There's a good movie here; a scene where one of Chance's war buddies (played by the fantastic Enver Gjokaj) recalls the day Chance was shot down is affecting, and the ending works up some palpable emotion. Bacon gives a good, buttoned-down performance as Strobl, a Desert Storm vet who's left the battlefield behind for a cubicle and feels enormous guilt over it. Alas, the film is so stately and respectable that it often feels generic. A bland release from the usually adventurous HBO.

reviews.text: According to the historical docudrama Taking Woodstock, three days of peace and music circa 1969 was preceded with uproar by community members who believed the concert would prompt dangerous riots. Organizers attempted to calm those fears by saying there wouldn’t be more than 50,000 in attendance. By the end of the first day, the City of White Lake was declared by the New York State Governor as a disaster zone as an estimated 450,000 showed up for what became a free concert. Uptight townspeople protested on street corners to kick the hippies out by decrying a national emergency. Brighter townspeople decided to cash in on the foot traffic.

reviews.author: Maria
reviews.text: Despite its scale, it's a minor Ang Lee film. But it's not as bad as people make it out to be. It's really funny and it has some sweet moments. It's less for those interested in Woodstock and more for those interested in Lee's filmography. It's really not about the festival at all, but rather about themes that are found in each of his films—family, self-repression, desire, moving on (whatever that may mean). It feels like the hazy, joyful memory of its central character. Cultural events are defined by the people who lived them, and we never once see the concert but we still live through the festival, through this one perspective. Jonathan Groff was the real highlight for me; there's an otherworldly quality about him here that I never previously associated with him. And Paul Dano is always a joy to watch, even if it's only for a short scene.

Each character is a subject of an emotional cornerstone but they don't all necessarily embody that emotion rather they are chasing it. Some of them can't even achieve it and the implications are horrifying to witness. This makes the narrative work more than it should, adding more nuance to a simple concept. While there are some spots that could've been toned down, I think this is one of the most underrated films of the 2000s. I expected people like Forest Whittaker, Kevin Bacon, Andy Garcia, and Julie Deply to give great performances, but I was surprised to see Sarah Michelle Gellar and Brendan Fraser give such dead on portrayals of such damaged characters. The script felt poetic and I thought it was smart the way the characters connected, except the ending. The "Love" segment fell below expectations from the really exciting previous segments. The last segment also felt too predictable and stuff happens that I feel is to convienent to believe. Nonetheless, I thought this was a unique, thoughtful, passionate and visually stunning film. I'd recommend it because you can "love" it despite it's low budget, feel "sorrow" for each character's pain, find "pleasure" in it's breathtaking visuals and soundtrack, and feel "happiness" after deciding to watch this beautiful gem.

reviews.text: Hate to sound all “Vanderpump Rules,” but a babysitter is not the same as a nanny! A tempting/tame TV thriller from Peter Medak (“The Changeling”) teasing the nefarious nanny nightmare of “The Hand That Rocks the Cradle” (with John Houseman in the Julianne Moore role), “Leave Her to Heaven” (“accidents” on the water) and most notably “Poison Ivy,” as our abandoned orphan torments a fractured family by escalating a mother’s illness, seducing distant daddy William Shatner in her slinky dress, and bludgeons an animal for the onlookers. Some fairly solid visuals thanks to the setting and a eurohorror-style score, dependable 70’s (technically 80's) domestic drama from Patty Duke, and generally tried and true tropes that still satisfy me despite zero surprises. BTW this babysitter/NANNY Joanna would be so fantastic on “Vanderpump Rules.” (Scheana needs her, we need her).

reviews.text: Despite the lack of T&A, this is a very entertaining Made-for-TV film by Peter Medak. A young and enticing Stephanie Zimbalist is the ultimate home wrecker and this film serves as a template for the interloper thrillers that would become a nineties trend. I was particularly surprised with how much Poison Ivy seems to have borrowed from this. Some creepy and effective little scenes and we get both John Houseman and William Shatner together. Zimbalist's fully clothed seduction of Shatner is sexier than anything Teri Hatcher did in The Cool Surface with her clothes off. Good little potboiler.

They mock conventions while openly embracing them in a method that may read as far too subtle only to be punctuated by a non sequitor or particularly odd character trait that goes unaddressed. (ie never addressing the giant penis in Wanderlust, and Michael Ian Black being in his underwear and women's tank tops in this). The weird thing is, a lot of the same people had tried the same thing almost ten years earlier, with a much more satisfying result.

I mean… Rain Man fkn slaps, so seeing the American director lend his talents to my favorite genre was just too intriguing a premise to pass up. The Bay navigates a fairly simple yet gruesome bio-infection horror setup infused with a whole lotta atmospheric tension, told through a faux-documentary format. And while it doesn’t add too many new wrinkles to its subgenre, it’s a very well told story in a space full of not-well-told stories.

reviews.text: Battle Creek Brawl is a film that is nowhere near as cool as its title. Jackie Chan's first attempt to break into the US market is a rather stale affair. It's not surprising that it didn't deliver the Enter the Dragon style returns that Warner Bros were hoping for. The film is set in 1930's America and sees Jackie cast as the son of a restaurant owner who is coerced by the mob to take part in a fighting competition. The main problem with this film is that it doesn't capitalise on the things that made Chan's Hong Kong films such good fun. It's a mix of action and comedy, but the comedy feels rather forced and often doesn't fit…

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: It’s like they took everything great about peak Jackie Chan, threw it out the window and went ‘confusingly 1930s set gangster roller-derby is where the fun is at.’ I get that this was Chan’s first attempt to break into America, so I wasn’t expecting it to be amazing. But I don’t think I was prepared for just how dull it would be. The story is dumb, the comedy doesn’t work and the attempts at action are just underwhelming. They’re so flatly filmed, and Chan does not appear to be in his element, I swear you can see him pulling punches. The only time I didn’t spend being bored was when I was busy being baffled by how the cars and costumes were period appropriate and yet everything else…was not. If you can’t tell, I really disliked this.

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: I love how Robert Clouse was able to inject a real Hong Kong sensibility into this film, by seeming to have no sense at all of American history. The mob subplot, the men's hats, and the cars all want to suggest that we're in the 1930s, but everything else - the helmet wearing roller derby competitors with the emcee shouting "We're BREAKING BONES over here!", the spandex-clad WWE style wrestlers, the polyester-clad spectators, absolutely screams the 1970s. Probably in Asian markets, audiences simply assumed that it took place in modern Chicago. I remember when I traveled around Southeast Asia in the 90's, whenever I said I was from Chicago, the response was usually, "Oh! Al Capone!" and machine gun fingers…

Appearing in the two Cannonball Run movies as a JAPANESE man is unfortunate by today’s standards, plus he wasn’t able to do much in all-star ensemble pictures. reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Raymond Chow's first attempt at breaking Jackie Chan into the international market tapped Robert Clouse (Enter the Dragon) to give it that Bruce Lee star turn. A reasonable success, Golden Harvest deemed the film a disappointment for not seeing Enter the Dragon box office returns, ultimately going back to the drawing board on Chan's American introduction. This failure to launch narrative is further promoted by Chan, disappointed that the action sequences fail to represent his style. With studio and star deriding it, The Big Brawl is resented as one of those reasons it took another fifteen years for many to enjoy Chan - when the truth is its a surprisingly enjoyable film.

Even worse Danny trades in his Dad's beloved 1963 (but deeply unfashionable) Nissan Cedric. "Cedric? Sounds more like a Qantas steward." reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Beyond charming Aussie John Hughes analog - the reductive quick take is "Ozploitation PRETTY IN PINK with teenage Ben Mendelsohn in the Molly Ringwald role" - that's one part coming of age comedy, and another part teen caper picture. However, the dude who steals the entire movie is Steve Bisley's scumbag used car dealer, who'll not only sell you a vintage lemon Jag, but then sic his thuggish associates on you once you attempt to reclaim your property. And despite this being a YA fantasy, complete with vintage early '90s Down Under synth pop, the hard edge of Oz cinema shines through, with odd instances of sleaze (such as a scheme involving naked mud wrestling) and even a full-blown car chase. Why this has zero North American presence is a mystery to me, as it's a total delight that I'm probably undervaluing when all's said and done.

reviews.text: Whilst no Malcolm, Tass/Parker's 1990 film The Big Steal is still a solid genre caper with its heart in the right place, if nothing particularly outstanding. It's a fairly simple film done right that always feels like it is on the cusp of something more magnificent (i.e. the Coen-esque parents who always threaten to walk off with the film, but never really manage it). Still, this nearly-there very tongue-in-cheek comfort film is a lot of fun, demonstrating the Tass/Parker ability to mine a cliche, generic realm and find something very original.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: More imaginative than “Coco,” more soulful than “Moana,” more everything than “Despicable Me 3,” Nora Twomey’s “The Breadwinner” cements Ireland’s Cartoon Saloon as an animation powerhouse worth mentioning alongside the likes of Pixar, Laika, and the great Studio Ghibli. A deeply anguished story that’s told with the same vivid style as Cartoon Saloon’s two previous features, “The Secret of Kells” and “Song of the Sea,” “The Breadwinner” triumphs with a sense of emotional sobriety that strikes far deeper than anything that passes for children’s entertainment in this part of the world — it may be aimed at (older) kids, but it’s certain to hit their parents twice as hard.

reviews.text: This was a solid war film depicting the ending of WW2. It dealt with all the tragedies of both sides being demoralized yet forced by powers greater to finish out the ill parts of a forgone conclusion to push faster or hold on longer and herein lies the crux of the title. I get to se my Segal and plus Gazzara being weathered men forced to advance on the front line with accolades going to the hire ups counterpoint seeing Robert Vaughn entrusted to defend a bridge that at some point must be blown to impede the Americans encroach on to Germany whilst very little help from the top brass. Bleak but yet I found myself very invested with the material and how it is dealt with. A very solid war movie with a smart story that pays dividends the more you get into it.

Art Hindle’s blank face is the perfect foil to such dissection and the film has some of the most effective horrifying images put on film particularly when they are the most simple (as a 15 year old those little deformed hands coming from under the bed really did a number on me). Even the pure little girl sight is disturbing. And then there is the moment in which the ex-husband arrives in the school to murdered body of the teacher and all those little children crying. When it comes to psychological damage, The Brood has something for everyone.

reviews.text: The Butler is a Forrest Gump-like fly-over of 20th century American history. Trying to tell two stories at once, we get the tale of a poorer than dirt kid who became a white house butler for thirty years, and also, the entire chronicle of American civil rights. Forrest Gump did not explore American problems; instead it milked humour from the protagonist’s obliviousness. The Butler, conversely, dives into America’s muck. The protagonist Cecil Gaines is starkly aware of, and victimized by, African-American oppression.

The director is Lee Daniels of “Precious,” who comes up with stirringly evocative images of re-created images, but also includes inert scenes of too much domestic babble. reviews.author: ThisIsBigCat
reviews.text: The Butler (or should I say Lee Daniels' The Butler) has an intriguing concept behind it, chronicling 30+ years of American history from the perspective of a black White House butler. It's loosely based on the life of Eugene Allen, who worked as a White House butler from 1952 to 1986, but of course, the film embellishes tons of details for dramatic effect. There's also a side plot involving his son, who's pretty much the Forrest Gump of the Civil Rights movement. The film has an incredibly stacked cast, featuring actors you all recognize (although some of the Presidents don't look their parts at all). You can tell this was Lee Daniels' attempt at Oscar glory, but my main issue…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A very gracefully-stylized haunted house movie/conspiratorial unsolved murder procedural crossover with impeccable control over its eerie, lonely, grief-stricken atmosphere. So many fantastic slow zooms/pans/dollys, shadowy corridor compositions, creepy handheld POV tracking shots, and Victorian architecture observed in beautiful and strange wide-angle, low-angle and overhead images. All of this further complimented by the intentionally quiet, windy sound design and spare piano score that has this ghostly twinkling lullaby quality to it emphasizing the feelings of emptiness and loss that overwhelms these characters and the generational history they're investigating. Really spectacular feel-bad revenge climax as well. Completes the George C. Scott trilogy (including Hardcore and The Exorcist III) of religious grandpas from the Midwest or upstate NY going detective mode over a history of violently abusive American behavior.

Left unacknowledged or covered up the stain of the act itself seeps into the walls of the place where it happened like the pores of your skin and seeks to replay its trauma over and over again.

reviews.text: Fantasy setting, extravagant transformation scenes, bright colors draped in shadow, and fairytale atmosphere combine to make this heavy-handed sexual metaphor much more interesting. The metaphor is very upfront--coming of age mixed with sexual predation--but still gets mixed in a way only possible under patriarchy. Part of this is because the stories told are used to show shifting perspectives between characters and stages of their development, but partly it's the filmmaker's problem. The final moments of the film could be taken a few ways; the fear of wolves and the acceptance of them could be seen as an acceptance of sexual violence or as an embrace of sexuality, and that (especially being tied so heavily to coming of age) seems off. Still, despite the muddled message, it's a gorgeous dark film.

reviews.text: Set in the aftermath of World War II and Hungary's transition to communism but styled very much in the late-'60s student movements rocking Europe, The Confrontation is as moddish as it is analytical. Jancsó turns his long takes into loping circles to show communist youth fanning out over the countryside to spread the good word about the new way of things via shifting forms of direct action. In many respects, this is a deconstructed musical of kids dancing around and singing socialist anthems in ways that can be as inviting as they are threatening.

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: The long opening take is a great one, exhibiting Miklós Jancsó’s trademark visual grace, formal rigour and fascinating narrative ambiguities in a bravura sequence. What begins as a confrontation, as young protesters blockade the passage of military vehicles, transforms into a communal festival as the civilians are joined by the militia in high spirited singing and dancing.

reviews.text: The prowling widescreen camera of Miklós Jancsó, the closely choreographed movements and contributions of his cast, the long uninterrupted takes plucking meaning from mise en scène - all the director's hallmarks are present and as enthralling as ever. The content however, as a group of Communist youths descend on a monastery not long after WW2 and attempt to re-educate the priests and students there, is less gripping and gets bogged down in didactic arguments about the tactics of Communist uprising, amid frequent bursts into revolutionary song. The visual pleasures of Jancsó's first film in colour remain undimmed.

reviews.text: Western PA GOD George Romero's nastiest and funniest film features a small town put under an incompetently run military quarantine after a biological weapon taints their water supply. A supremely bleak satire of the depleted and demoralized late-Vietnam era military, where it's never really clear what is being caused by the contagion which drives people insane and what's due to the overall panic, hysteria and the baseline violence people are capable of when put under pressure. So much high quality ownage in this one, as dumb-ass slob troops and yinzer townsfolk kill each other in very high numbers. An absolute blast that has absolutely ZERO contemporary relevance.

reviews.author: Brett Wright
reviews.text: Released only a few years before he made his two greatest films, 'Martin' and 'Dawn of the Dead,' 'The Crazies' is an odd entry in the George A. Romero canon. The film concerns a small Pennsylvania town where a plane carrying a top secret biological weapon has crash landed in the nearby mountain range. The chemical seeps into the water supply causing infected citizens to go mad, murder each other, destroy their homes, and rampage through the streets. The military is sent in with little information as they try and fail to contain the situation. A few locals escape the government’s jurisdiction and do their best to maintain their freedom before one-by-one succumbing to the all-around toxic atmosphere.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: This is how you do fast-editing: overwhelming but lucid, a montage of faces locked in horror, rage, fear, bewilderment. Romero's rough but composed style ducks the potential Body Snatchers paranoia of seeing who is infected as opposed to those who simply erupt against government forces in favor of overwhelming but carefully ordered brute strength. Well, ordered on Romero's part, as one of the most fun aspects of THE CRAZIES is how over their heads and sloppy the government is even as they descend upon a time with shocking speed. It's a giant clusterfuck of a scene, all the more compelling for being so.

His 1973 military-infected-horror film The Crazies isn’t one that gets brought up much as part of Romero’s upper echelon, but it’s one that I would love to see continuously reevaluated over time. The Crazies is a surprisingly deep horror film highlighting the inefficiencies of bureaucracy and government in crisis situations, while offering a wonderful blend of genre punch and social subtext to chew on.

reviews.text: Alfonso Gomez-Rejon, director of the perceptive and unjustly maligned “Me and Earl and the Dying Girl,” is a young, thoughtful filmmaker with an inventive visual imagination and a very bright future ahead of him. That being said, something clearly went very, very wrong during the making of “The Current War.” A lifeless period drama about the rivalry between two of America’s greatest geniuses, Gomez-Rejon’s lavish third feature unfolds like a more historically accurate riff on “The Prestige,” albeit one lacking even a trace amount of magic (Nikola Tesla factors in, however, and Nicholas Hoult’s performance pays tribute to David Bowie).

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: After premiering almost two years ago, The Current War now arrives into cinemas with a supposed re-edit managed by the director. Unfortunately The Current War is a mess in its current state. The editing is actually quite awful, obsessed with being showy rather than flowing at a reasonable pace. The opening five minutes instantly signal the problem, as so much text - the film title, exposition, location signifiers - are thrown on the screen in quick succession, not even in an order that seems logical. From there, The Current War continues to be too fast and too excited to ever settle down and grapple with its themes.

reviews.text: The Current War is solid but drags a bit— pacing’s a slog at times. Editing and scoring grab you from the start; sharp cuts and an epic vibe that hold it together. Cumberbatch’s Edison starts as someone you’d root for, only to turn into a sly, ambitious mess (and I kept seeing Sherlock in him lol). Meanwhile, Michael Shannon’s Westinghouse feels flat and sneaky— totally miscast for a calm, good-hearted guy. I legit thought he’d be the villain, but ended up loving him more than Edison 😭

reviews.text: The Dance of Reality is so many things at once. It is musical, fantastical, surreal, historical, satirical, and autobiographical. In a way it is the kind of surrealism I find hard to like, since it is just random pieces. Well I guess it's more just Alejandro Jodorowsky's feelings and memories in a metaphorical form, but as with anything that only has a personal meaning, it is basically impenetrable. Nevertheless The Dance of Reality is filled with powerful, provocative images. Plague is cured by piss, donkeys are ripped apart, penises are tortured. The Dance of Reality certainly provides the edgy, satirical tone that one appreciates from Jodorowsky.

Emphasis is placed on how Michael’s autism is “hurting the family”, with it being blamed for the weird thing’s happening around the house, and the story legitimately connects being autistic with demon possession. Loath as I am to repeat the majority verdict, this is indeed no Threads. A lot of it feels like a very corny TV movie, which isn't necessarily a problem - part of the fascination of doing something like this on television lies in subverting the domestic cosiness of the medium. But I just don't have enough investment in or knowledge of the style and feel of American TV movies from this era, so it doesn't feel as impactful for me as something like Ghostwatch.

There's something about how those incoherent parts go together. For instance, it doesn't quite seem to know if Ford is around to offer a moral compass or to get a lesson about how his black and white morality doesn't work. There's actually a surprising amount of good scenes, particular the quieter ones, and some real good…

So what? A subplot involving Ruben Blades shooting an unarmed dude. Why? Whatever. Pitt's whole mission is so wildly imperfect. Cross the Atlantic on a boat, reaching the shores of Ireland with rockets and shit? That plan gets an F. But I still like it! That whole American ending to an American story always gets me, that boat slowly turning with a crying Ford steering it inland. I don't know why I like it so much.

reviews.text: It's A Nightmare On Elm Street with bathtubs instead of beds. While there's undoubtedly a gap in the market for a new horror franchise villain, this one was just too ridiculous a concept and didn't work for me at all. A boogeyman who materialises through puddles and running water, dragging his victims into a nightmare realm of liquid based torment, a sort of supernatural waterboarding if you like.Frankly, I found the central premise so idiotic I spent most of my time pondering the fact that if the heroine of the piece had such a feverish phobia of water, she must have serious personal hygeine issues, which nobody seems to notice. So oddly here's a movie which seems to have an aversion to bathing and cleanliness - could it possibly be the first pro-crusty horror film? A complete damp squib.

John Sturges's directing style, while grand and classic, was most definitely of an era and seems much more a product of the very early 60's. I had fun watching it and because of the high concept plot, I was engaged the entire 2 hours and 15 minutes. But damn, the casting and refusal of some of the actors to attempt accents really tested me. To cast English actors to play Germans trying to go undercover as Polish in Britain just isn't the best idea. Caine's cockney accent constantly took me out. Sutherland, playing Irish, was truly charming though.

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: Like all men-on-a-mission movies in theInglorious Basterds DNA strand, this is packed with stars. Michael Caine and Robert Duval as noble Germans. The ever anachronistic Donald Sutherland (cf. The Dirty Dozen) as an IRA lothario, a delicious Donald Pleasence giving us maybe the best Himmler ever. And Larry Hagman, who apparently prepped for his role as a US Colonel by watching Dr Strangelove. Of course there’s an improbable plot, a fluidity of tone and plenty of sturdy Sturgess action sequences. But what separates this from its genre peers — and makes it so much fun — is the dissonance of Nazi commandos swarming an idyllic English village where we’d expect to encounter Miss Marple or a menagerie of Wodehousean eccentrics.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "The Eagle Has Landed" is a 1976 WW2 adventure film directed by John Sturges. The narrative of the film focuses on a do or die suicide mission from German forces all in an attempt to kidnap Winston Churchill. All based in a book in 1975 by Jack Higgins, which was purely fictional as the events that both the book and film portray did not actually occur. Working under the guise as Polish paratroopers, the film gives us a heist narrative where eventually everything goes wrong. Packed full of notable actors and directed by John Sturges who works well at making character driven adventure movies, the film is something of not direct strategic war to be taken seriously. It really is…

reviews.author: Brian Hammons
reviews.text: Probably one of the more overlooked entries into the "mumblecore" movement. Lead Zoe Kazan is remarkable as Ivy, a college student who suffers from epilepsy returning home on break to Brookyln. Like the best works in the genre it's not always about what happens (in so much that not a lot in the traditional narrative sense happens, walking, lying in bed, talking on cell phones, quietly thinking, etc.) but the pregnant silences that hold such weight and dramatic import. Complicating matters is Al, a long-time friend who's room at home has been rented out by his parents, leading him to crash with Ivy and her mom. Their feelings about each other are still evolving and are yet to be defined. Nicely shot with a naturalistic touch and anchored by sensational work by Zoe Kazan this is worth seeking out.

reviews.text: De forma similar a otras obras como Nausicaä del Valle del Viento (1984), El castillo en el cielo (1986), Coral Reef Legend (1986) o Green Legend Ran (1992), The E.Y.E.S. of Mars aborda la cuestión ecológica del carácter autodestructivo del ser humano respecto a su entorno natural, tratando de incidir en la importancia de que el ser humano se transforme desde un punto de vista espiritual en lugar de aferrarse a la comodidad de la ciencia. Aquí el problema es que el desarrollo argumental resulta bastante accidentado, con caracteres superficiales, escasos momentos para que la protagonista procese la información y madure para adoptar su misión, múltiples conveniencias y huecos argumentales (¿Qué onda con que los padres se pregunten por ella, les respondan satisfactoriamente y luego se unan a la resistencia de repente?). De todas formas, el entrenamiento psíquico resulta interesante y la contraposición ciencia y espiritualidad no está presentada con maniqueísmo (aunque la película tiene claro por quien se decanta).

reviews.text: This movie contains my favorite scene of any movie. If you’ve seen it, it’s the one between Parry and Lydia on the sidewalk. Over the last few years I’ve revisited that scene over and over, I’ve probably watched it 50 times if not more. It incapsulates a love I have for somebody special in my life who I’ve missed dearly like nothing else. After many years I reunited with this person and we watched the movie together, they hadn’t seen it. When the scene came up, that made me think of them for years, they turned around and held me. I didn’t tell them about the scene, they just felt it too. We paused the movie and cried for an hour. I missed them so much. I love movies.

It may be a mystery hinging on the death of a man who has become a monster, but, at its core, the film is a whodunit and why. The film's appeal, however, comes from its ability to take that core mystery and layer it with genre trappings. It is this layering of science fiction, horror, and drama that makes "The Fly" an understated 1950s horror classic.

The plot begins with an IRA bombing, which kills the daughter of a humble restaurateur - who then vows revenge on the perpetrators. The film features two standout lead performances. An aging Jackie Chan is great in the lead and gets good backup from Pierce Brosnan in a Gerry Adams inspired role. reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: i was worried while watching this that martin campbell would have lost his formalist chops over the years (especially after the disaster that was green lantern), but i'm very glad to say that this totally rules, it's this fabulously lean mediation on the usual action movie notion of cyclical revenge, with pierce brosnan playing a nicely complex badguy foil to jackie chan's hyper-fixated bomb-happy vigilante. despite any expectations, they make a surprisingly amazing pairing, and jackie chan gets to have some of the most emotionally poignant acting that i've seen in his whole career! the foreigner evokes the best serious-minded and entertaining action thrillers of the 80s and 90s that had awesome workhorse directors who knew their craft back-to-front along with great screen performers giving it their best. a superb showing for all parties involved, i'd eagerly recommend this to any fan of old-school action, it seriously delivers the goods over and over again.

reviews.text: In a 20-year career that ended with his murder by the Irish Republican Army in 1994, Martin Cahill (Brendan Gleeson) and his gang stole money and property with an estimated value over $60,000,000. John Boorman’s sympathetic portrait of the Irish gangster presents the essence of Cahill’s character as a sense of working-class outrage at being relegated to the margins of society. Boorman shows the young Cahill (Eamonn Owens) stealing both to provide for his poor family and as an act of rebellion. A 60s style of anti-establishment attitude runs through many of Boorman’s films and is clearly on display in The General, which also resembles British films of the 60s in its visual style and its mixture of violence and…

reviews.author: Albie Hay
reviews.text: John Boorman has a terrific eye, and his decision to shoot the film in black-and-white yields some stunning images (especially when he gets to use hard lighting dramatically), but I'm inclined to think that most of the credit for making this as good as it is belongs to Brendan Gleeson. His performance is what keeps the film from lapsing into rote biopic solemnity, making real-life gangster Martin Cahill so ceaselessly funny and charismatic that the film effectively plays like a heist film that happens to be based on a true story, complete with Danny Ocean-style lovable rogue in the lead. Boorman's screenplay has some smart dialogue to help Gleeson and the other actors (including an oddly cast but nonetheless effective Jon Voight) along, but the story is rather confusing and scattershot.

reviews.text: Not sure if police corruption or institutional racism has ever seemed so casually insurmountable. Burnett has a deft, sardonic touch that likens this more to a nightmarish Sam Fuller picture than a movie like L.A. Confidential. And the casting is perfect: Michael Boatman, who I only knew from Spin City and Arliss, plays the rookie with an alert, acerbic edge; Ice Cube, whose likeness was slathered all over the film's confused marketing, gets to toy with his post-NWA rap image; and character actors like M. Emmet Walsh and the blithely sinister Michael Ironside populate the margins. Sad that Burnett never quite broke big in the 90's like he should've.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: This has a nebulous, overcomplicated plot (convoluted enough to be based on true events), but Burnett does his level best to make it work cinematically. His compositions are just immaculate, every closeup feels exciting and urgent, and he saturates the screen with reds, blues, and silhouettes. Probably not exciting enough to serve as the true antidote to police propaganda that its comic pop art title sequence seems to be positioning it as but still engaging and with an insane supporting cast -- hard to believe M Emmett Walsh could still be alive almost 30 years later, that's Hollywood for you.

reviews.author: jrhovind
reviews.text: Charles Burnett trades his characteristic poetic naturalism for slightly bigger budget high pulp; the opening burst of comic-book imagery announces both something of the film’s ironic gallows humor, but also its mostly cartoonishly simplistic moral vision (though, that said, when making a film about cops, cartoonishly evil is of course its kind of naturalism). A bruised morality play about the cost of trying to fit in with a crowd that’s never going to want you anyway (“Oh, it’s not a question of the leopard changing his spots. It’s the animal”); one naïve cop’s disorienting awakening to the cruel intractability of insidious systems. Occasionally broad movie-of-the-week strokes feel like a good filmmaker overwhelmed by studio expectations, though at least he takes the Kafkaesque sense of defeatism all the way to its logical endpoint. “What happened to rescuing innocent people from the bad guys?”

reviews.author: Matheus Fiore
reviews.text: O maior mérito desse filme do Charles Burnett é assumir as contradições do protagonista. O jovem negro que entra para a força policial cheio de sonhos e acaba errando muito no caminho, perpetuando o racismo sistêmico sem perceber, se contentando com tapinhas nas costas. JJ é um dos melhores policiais que o cinema americano entregou nos anos 90, porque as expressões inocentes e joviais de Michael Boatman corroboram tudo que o texto e as câmeras querem nos dizer sobre ele. O sujeito que quer fazer diferente dentro de um sistema planejado para fracassar. Em um filme que começa nos detalhes, até que ganha um grande escopo e se debruça sobre os novos detalhes por ele revelados.

reviews.text: Completely blown away by this and my lack of presumed period drama knowledge. I had no idea that Merchant Ivory's style could be traced so directly to something from the early 70s. 60s historical pieces are so distinctly 60s, but The Go-Between is less tied to the period that it was made in than the period in which it was set, which generally became the go-to stylistic choice of all the period pieces that followed. Not only did this capture a time and place so perfectly, but it's also one of the most immaculately shot movies I think I've ever seen. Plus, it plays with that Pinterian relationship between the past and present, the same way he does with the past/present and fiction/reality in The French Lieutenant's Woman. I'm a wee bit in love with Alan Bates, too, who I had no idea could be a complete hunk. Don't text.

reviews.text: After Mountain of the Cannibal God, director Sergio Martino decided to head back into the jungle...for a much less satisfying adventure. This time, the focus is on a giant alligator that is terrorising a local tourist resort. Honestly the film is a complete mess. The plot makes little sense and it's really just an excuse to feature a giant fake alligator. But don't get me wrong, I'd much rather a giant fake alligator than a giant CGI alligator! The film is part Jaws rip off and part cannibal exploration movie though it doesn't have the strong characters of the former or the guts and gore of the latter. Barbara Bach and Claudio Cassinelli make for perfectly fine leads but neither one seems completely on board with their characters or the project. The fact that it's all shot on location lends some realism at least; but It's nowhere near as good as it's title would suggest!

reviews.text: "The Great Alligator" is a 1979 Italian nature horror film directed by Sergio Martino. Intermixed in the repetitious fashion of various "Jaws" (1975) clones, this film considerably comparable to other releases. It's got that Italian exploitative blend of things, complete with the tonal sexuality blend of eroticism contained within exoticism Italian films just often inherently contain, especially because it involves a modeling tour going to Africa for a photoshoot. Also throw in the other trope of local tribal people who wreak havoc as both antagonists and protagonists, flipping sides about every 20 minutes depending on if a big goofy fake Alligator is attacking or not. I always have an underlying noticed energy that much of Italian exploitation efforts still have…

reviews.text: I've been listening to "The Harder They Come" soundtrack for years now, so to finally watch the accompanying movie is a great companion piece to the phenomenal album. It's a raw and stylish film which put reggae on the map in most of the world while delivering a politically charged film embedded in that period. It follows Ivan's descent into crime after running into exploitation by the music business, the police, and the broader social system. It's a great transition from outsider to outlaw antihero and is equally earned and tragic. Its authenticity beams through every shot of this film and doesn't romanticize poverty or violence, presenting an unpolished story which feels increasingly documentary-esque at points. Jimmy Cliff is also…

reviews.text: Starts out as a neorealist ramble following a man named Ivan as he arrives in Kingston and tries his best to make ends meet while aspiring to become a famous singer, the film preoccupied with taking in the surroundings and the texture of life and seemingly not at all in a hurry to get anywhere, before the pressure inevitably drops and this becomes a very different sort of movie. All I'll say is that it's not an accident that Ivan goes to a theater to watch Django near the beginning. This is a seemingly rough-hewn but subtly artful film that always has more on its mind than it lets on, choosing to let its ingredients slowly simmer through much of its runtime until the point at which everything comes to a boil. And of course the soundtrack is incredible.

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: Films like The Harder They Come are perfect examples of the power of shooting real locations. The natural and built environments of any place carry within them a sense of history and culture that no CGI or studio shoots can ever hope to perfectly capture. The beaches, roads, homes, and gathering places all have their own stories to tell if you so desire to observe and listen. Now more than ever before, we are starting to see much more "imagined cities." Depictions of cities that are trying to appeal to so many different people and locations that the end-product becomes overwhelmingly homogenous and lacks any recognizable or resonant cultural identity.

reviews.author: solstrale
reviews.text: "The Insult" is a heavily political movie. It is about clash of ideas of Lebanese Christians and Palestinian Muslims which is represented by two leads. It is about refugees and civil war victims. It focuses on ego, bias and hatred. The film basically tells us words can be as dangerous as actions. At first, things seem personal, but then everything becomes political and national as things start to escalate and spin out of control. I was surprised how thrilling and suspenseful the courtroom scenes were. There weren't any dull moments, at all. I had no idea about how politics worked in Lebanon before watching it. Thanks to this movie, I got to learn about different attitudes emerging in Lebanon. I need to get it out of my chest that it was really heartbreaking to see how people did side against each other because of their nationality and religion though.

reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: A small dispute between a Lebanese Christian and a Palestinian refugee turns into an intense legal case of national interest that exposes the social fractures resulting from the Lebanese Civil War. The Insult presents a reflection on hatred, pride, resentment, and differences that divide humankind whilst revealing the open wounds of a nation that is also embedded in the complex and visceral reality of the Middle East that is constantly exacerbated by religious and ethnic conflicts. Although this is a parable with a fluid pace and moments of tension, as well as the commendable intention of opening a dialogue that leads to reconciliation; in the end, it may be a little too simplistic, not very subtle, rather melodramatic, and it loses strength in the last act.

reviews.text: Michael Winterbottom's The Killer Inside Me is extremely well-done technical filmmaking – but overall it’s not very good. It’s a period-set noir in 1950’s Texas, with Casey Affleck (as Lou Ford), a blasé, placid deputy sheriff with a natural zing for double-murders. The first murder of the film is so grisly and revolting that you want to scream out “anti-entertainment.” Morbid curiosity might keep you watching, the faint of heart should avoid. Jessica Alba is bare and tantalizing as the disreputable town whore. Kate Hudson is Lou’s regular girl, the one he’s supposed to one day begrudgingly marry. Simon Baker and Elias Koteas do most of the film’s best secondary acting within a large cast that also includes Ned Beatty,…

reviews.text: Look I'm on record as deeply anti-Gilliam, yes, I even really hate that one you like a lot, but even by that metric this is a disorganized, self-satisfied mess made by a guy who still thinks he's an underappreciated genius tilting at everyone else's failures of intellect and imagination. It's long past tiresome for me. An emblematic moment: Driver's tortured director character, who's in the midst of a Quixote-inspired commercial shoot, is confronted by his former star, a man driven so mad (or is he the only one who really gets it, etc, boring) he still thinks he's the Man of La Mancha. When the guy attacks a windmill thinking it's a giant, Driver seems to have no idea what's going on, this delusion apparently having no context in his mind whatsoever.

The Mechanic stars Charles Bronson as a hitman with a modus operandi that involves making his kills look like accidents. But he's getting old and therefore decides to take on a protégé in the form of Jan-Michael Vincent. The film starts with a very steady and deliberately paced kill scene that sets the character well. The central conceit; that of a hitman wanting to…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: The silent opener sets the tone: tense, pragmatical, wary and very much occupied with filling in the hired killer's life details. With the possible exception of Hill's Hard Times, no film has put Bronson's best quality - the way he carries himself like he has lived a whole shitty life before the camera rolled - to better use. His hired gun is a classic Hawksian pro set against Jan Michael Vincent bland psychotic son of privilege – sometimes Vincent non entity presence bogs the movie down, but when it is well employed it contrasts nicely to Bronson’s presence. The methodical approach serves Michael Winner’s usual heavy hand. Monte Hellman reportedly worked in the script early on the development which might explain why this is far more thoughtful than most Winner films.

reviews.text: the nihilism of the soured youth culture funneled into the cold-blooded professionalism of their elders. i wasn't expecting this to have the existential flavor it does, it is a good deal closer to boorman's point blank than the straight-shooting pulp that i associate with bronson. the anonymous, stripped-back depiction of assassination gives the mechanic a compressed atmosphere that lends itself well to this slightly homoerotic mentor/mentee character study. like most assassin films it is concerned with 'the code', but michael winner's sturdy conservatism emphasizes that bronson's teaching is an imbalance that upsets the self-denying materialism of the criminal organization he belongs to -- his unstated desire for companionship after years of solitude belies the apparently 'mechanical' way that the film is constructed, yet the zero-sum nature of contract killing makes it so any relationship is 'til death do us part'.

There is a disturbing scene which involves a young lady (Linda Ridgeway; this was her only role although she is best known as one of Bill Cosby’s many accusers) slitting her wrists and the two leads not caring if she dies. To be frank, that is the sort of scene I expect in a Michael Winner picture. If that isn’t too upsetting to you and the plot otherwise sounds intriguing, then the movie is…

I recall it having a just okay storyline but a certain charm and I totally loved the classic noir style. I also loved Michael Shannon as the depressed sudsy detective, a role he fits easily. This director has a real way with quirk and cinematography and I must say that I like the cut of his jib; I'll be diving into his filmography shortly. reviews.author: Kurdt
reviews.text: Michael Shannon plays a private detective tasked with following an unknown middle-aged man in this indie neo-noir that feels about as close to one of those 70s 150-page gumshoe paperbacks with faded lettering and dog-eared corners as a modern film could. Except the interesting twist on this is how it weaves recent real world events into its narrative - it’s best to go in pretty blind with this. Shannon's melancholic and vaguely grumpy detective holds the film together when the plot is sparse before it takes a couple of unique turns I haven't seen in the genre before. It riffs on grief, loneliness, isolation and the desire for escape while retaining an interesting atmosphere. Really great, wonderfully shot ending. Hard to believe this is so underseen.

That seems like a terrible idea, but then Mission: Impossible and Charlie's Angels had much commercial success doing the thing around the same time. Silver's Mod Squad, though, was so bad that to date he has never directed again, not even an episode of television.

reviews.text: I always knew I'd probably enjoy this one on some level, but I'd avoided it because I thought it would be a straightforward courtroom drama. While there is of course a courtroom element, the mood of this film is closer to a Dashiell Hammett Continental Op story than And Justice for All (1979). The direction in this film, with its elaborate staging, brilliant use of lighting and vignette, is some of the best in any film ever; As I watched, I felt like this film was the Harlem Globetrotters, and I was the other team, just sitting there slack-jawed as they passed the ball around me, and dazzled me with amusing tricks. I'd heard this film mentioned in the context of John Sturges' filmography, but never as a classic noir, or great film, both of which it deserves recognition for being.

reviews.text: Let me start this review by giving The Poseidon Adventure the credit it deserves. Ronald Neame's film is a spectacular piece of entertainment, and the accomplishment is even more impressive because, back in 1972, filmmakers couldn't rely on CGI or digital effects. To recreate the nightmarish setting of an upside-down boat with such gritty realism elevates The Poseidon Adventure, on a pure technical level, to a milestone in the same vein as Star Wars or Who Framed Roger Rabbit. But the risk with special effects is that they are often taken for granted as the sole pillar of a film's success, instead of being exploited for the sake of the story.

reviews.text: Simultaneously lacks the Jodorowskian tendencies I find insufferable (the faux-thoughtful attempts at commentary and themes, in particular) and the Jodorowskian tendencies I love (the cheeky humor, his acting, his gonzo stylization), leaving a strange thing behind. I don't mean to suggest that this movie lacks personality or visual panache (it has plenty of both), or even that it isn't Jodorowskian, simply that it's a muted sort of affair. It's honestly quite charming, albeit a bit of a plotless ramble, the kind of thing that, had I seen when I was much younger, I might have a ton of nostalgia (and perhaps an extra half-star or so) for. Seeing it for the first time today, though, it's just quite nice.

For far too long a time, we just have a few men walking into the facility and lots of men walking out of the facility, all carefully saying goodbye to the security guard. I probably should have watched it in 2020 also, it wouldn't have been a great film then either, but it might have earned a small bump for feeling timely and relevant. The Satan Bug was adapted from an Alastair MacLean novel, and features all those trademark MacLean-isms: confusingly dense plotting, manly men doing manly things, double agents and double crosses and a near total absence of woman. In fact I'm surprised Anne Francis was even allowed on set and was probably only there as she knew the director. She'd been in a previous John Sturges film, the…

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: John Sturges was one the greatest action directors of his generation. Sadly, this, his follow up to The Great Escape, doesn’t offer much proof of his skill. I’ve seen it before, and I was under the impression it ran over two hours. It doesn’t, but it feels like it does. It’s not bad, exactly; it just lacks the sense of urgency that a film about a stolen biological weapon should have. Sturges fared better with another Alistair MacLean novel three years later, when he made Ice Station Zebra. The Boulting Brothers’ Seven Days To Noon is a much better take on the holding-a-city-hostage plot line.

reviews.text: 'The Serpent And The Rainbow' is a frustrating film to both watch and review. Based somewhat loosely on Wade Davis' non-fiction account of ethnobotanical exploration in Haiti in the 1970's and 1980's, and his research into the psychopharmacological and cultural roots of zombi-ism in Haiti, 'The Serpent And The Rainbow' was sold to Hollywood as a film project with the original understanding that Peter Weir would direct and Mel Gibson would star (thanks Wikipedia!), which would have been a pretty different movie. Wes Craven was a somewhat more left-field choice but a good one in that he had a scholarly background himself and an enduring interest in folklore. The film was shot in the U.S., Haiti and the Dominican Republic,…

Very enjoyably weird (features a scene where Bill Pullman gets a nail shoved through his scrotum) but much prefer Fulci's attempt to revive this exact same genre.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: "The Serpent and the Rainbow" is one of Wes Craven's best films, and, for much of its running time, it is one of the horror director's most restrained films. Telling a story based on actual events, Craven eschews gore and token exploitative touches for authentic fear and effective imagery. With most of his narrative grounded in realism, it is only until a finale that runs away from this realism that Craven's film loses a step and becomes something less impressive than what it had been building toward.

reviews.text: I'll have to get back to you all on this one. In Cimino's cut (the only one I've seen) there's like, a billion things going on here. It seems like the most the most economical Cimino I've seen. In his previous three films, Cimino seems to be interested in either abstraction or spectacle...or both at once. So we get enormous crowds or a shot following a gust of smoke billowing through a street. But here every shot seems to have a fixed purpose or idea, a car busting into a church, the garish red flags after the massacre, like the betrayal of an ideal.

reviews.text: It seems like destiny that Michael Cimino became a cause célèbre beyond his time. What tarnished him as a filmmaker while part of the industry are often the kind of things that age into period styling. If one doesn't watch a few dozens silent films from the 1910s, it can be hard to differentiate Mary Pickford performance from any Mary Sue thrown into a melodrama. Meanwhile, what often does outlive an era—the bread and butter of directing, for example—is what has become clear in the 30 years from Cimino's heyday.

His Alice obsession is in full swing here: visual references to the Red Queen; a lawyer named Charles Dodgson, Esq.; Hatter's Hotel, where the menu includes Mock Turtle Soup and a special called Rabbit in the Hole. Probably too goofy to serve as an introduction to his work, but a treasure trove for fans.

reviews.text: Kind of a bummer nobody talks about this, because it’s a delight - certainly this unsold pilot is Anderson at his lowest-rent and most rote (which ain’t to say it’s not stylized to hell and back), but if you’re sincerely gonna tell me you wouldn’t rather be living in the timeline where we got like 5 seasons of a PWSA-helmed show about an architect turned amateur paranormal detective, well, I’m sorry, we’re just fundamentally very different people. Also - and I swear on my life this does not constitute a meaningful spoiler (it sounds like it does! It doesn’t! I’m serious!) - features a climactic image of the destroyed twin towers??? After all but opening with a carefully-blocked match overlay where one of them is superimposed with an opening door... it’s got me wondering if Mr. Anderson has touched the monolith!

reviews.text: Com certeza a coisa mais adorável aqui é como o Paul W.S. Anderson não consegue se segurar. O elemento mais simples precisa soar o mais histriônico. É quase um laboratório pra esse maneirismo limpo de estúdio que ele foi concebendo ao longo dos anos. E de alguma forma isso acaba se adaptando muito bem ao filme, até porque mesmo a relação entre espaço espiritual e espaço físico aqui é sempre muito ambígua, já que basicamente tudo é estilizado da mesma forma. A coisa toda vira esse limbo gótico azulado pseudo-noir onde apesar de existirem sombras, o que obviamente domina é uma luminosidade frontal sempre característica do diretor.

reviews.author: Christian
reviews.text: This is a true use case for auteur theory because the uniformly dopey acting performances wash off me like an ocean wave breaking against a smooth rock in favor of me eating up PWSA's deranged texturing - which includes psychic visions shot like the scary bits in digital-era Shinya Tsukamoto movies, an extended CG sequence where the camera goes inside the tumblers of a lock as ghosts unlock it, riffs on shots from Don't Look Now and The Changeling, and especially the last two minutes of this 2000 (!) release, which contains an image of the destroyed Twin Towers.

reviews.author: Auteur
reviews.text: The Sight is a filmed pilot for a supernatural television show that was never picked up, headlined by Andrew McCarthy and Kevin Tighe (I can't imagine why), and a final gasp of awfulness from PWSA before he found success and consistent, relative critical acclaim with the Resident Evil franchise. I can't even begin to appreciate Anderson's unique visual strategy for the film, and supposed future filmography Easter eggs, or the score by Eyes Wide Shut's Jocelyn Pook, because the screenplay and the dialogue and the acting are so atrocious. As most of Anderson's nineties output has betrayed an inability to overcome the restrictions of basic narrative templates, perhaps the rigorous structure of a television pilot was not the best fit for him.

reviews.author: David Jenkins
reviews.text: I would like to say, for the record, that this may be one of the very worst films I've ever seen. Not a single idea, image, motif, theme, joke, performance or shot connected with me. Irritating, reactionary and incoherent, this is, in a best-case scenario, a 3 minute short hammered out to an excruciating 140 minutes (reportedly cut down from 160!!). The film's intended scathing critique of art world arrogance is reverse engineered on to characters and situations that are so unbelievable and insubstantial that it ends up as a bloated manifestation of the titular Square – a vapid, experiential conceptual art piece whose purpose is justified by abstruse double-speak. I watched this film and wondered whether Ruben Östland ever had contact with another human being. If he has, there is no doubt in my mind that he was revolted by them. Since seeing it, this film has stayed with me like a weeping boil. Burn the negative.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: In this intriguing short film, what’s important is the questions it asks, rather than any answers it may or may not contain. We’re given pieces of information both verbally and through body language and facial expressions and are left to decide for ourselves what is actually going on between these two characters. The possible dark and sinister implication is disturbing but I don’t know—I said some fucked up, wild, out of pocket shit when I was a kid, so maybe there’s a bit of that going on. The Strange Ones racked my brain and I’m still thinking about it hours later. I went into it blind, with modest expectations and was pleasantly surprised. It’s ambiguous atmosphere reminded me slightly of both Weir’s Picnic at Hanging Rock and Altman’s 3 Women. I’ve no intentions on seeing the feature anytime soon. This works perfectly as it is and doesn’t really call for a full-length adaptation, in my opinion.

reviews.text: Who's the liar? A young man and a boy break down on the side of the road, and stop at a nearby hotel. Are they brothers, as the older of the two claims? Or is something much darker going on, as the younger one confesses to the hotel clerk? THE STRANGE ONES never answers our questions, leaving us with an unsettled air of mystery. The film's final moments gives clues, but only the fleeting clues of a passerby, leaving us with little to no tangible information.

Also, there's some really really interesting tension building that never really blows up as much as it implodes. This is a heavy movie. reviews.text: Lyrical, deliberately ambiguous, methodically paced character study has some highly effective scenes, and subtle, nuanced performances from leads James Freedson-Jackson and Alex Pettyfer. The presentation is reminiscent of early David Gordon Green and Debra Granik. It treads dark thematic territory, revealing the true nature of the story bit by bit until the whole macabre mosaic reveals itself. The dialogue is confidently written, and executed with a natural, raw immediacy that really works, so that when we reach the end it makes you look back on everything in a new light, forced to question assumptions made as a viewer, much like Lodge Kerrigan did with Clean Shaven. While maybe it meanders a tad too much for its own good, there’s still a ton of atmosphere and effective storytelling in this unorthodox, subtly disturbing road movie.

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: Highly entertaining 'copsploitation' drama from Shaft director Gordon Parks, with a manic lead performance from Ron Leibman. New York is at its gritty and grubby 70s finest.Based on the 'true' story of New York cops Dave Greenberg and Robert Hantz who were known as 'The Super Cops' or 'Batman & Robin' due to their extremely high conviction rate. Apparently they were the inspiration for Starsky & Hutch.The film opens with actual footage from a news conference where Greenberg and Hantz are being commended. And the two real-life cops have bit-parts as other cops in the film. They also both served as 'technical advisors' on the film. They were certainly riding the crest of a wave at this time but, unfortunately, both were later convicted of crimes - Greenberg for mail & insurance fraud and Hantz for possessing marijuana - which sullied their reputations somewhat.The film may not be historically accurate but it is great fun.

The Super Cops stands apart from the rest because it’s a comedy… an unflinching, realistic comedy directed by (famed photographer) Gordon Parks. Parks brings to it the same authentic urban sensibility he showed with his 1971 hit Shaft.

reviews.text: The Tiger's Tail certainly is an interesting, dark, satirical drama which takes place during Ireland's Celtic Tiger boom and follows Liam as his life begins to unravel after a doppelganger starts stalking him. At the core of the film, it's going for a psychological thriller with a strong social commentary undercurrent throughout, and Boorman uses this strange plot to critique the greed and hollow prosperity of this era, and it shows throughout. Brendan Gleeson is also incredible here in dual roles, and his constant change from role to role is effortless, and Kim Cattrall is no Samantha here but still entertaining. Visually, it's intriguing too, but arguably it's a bit heavy-handed with its commentary, and it never feels like it fully comes together, but it still remains an ambitious, intriguing film and an exploration of greed and morality, and it's certainly an underrated one.

reviews.text: Military Monday roars back with another really solid wartime documentary from World War 2. In the last act there are several disturbing sequences shot regarding the discovery of the Nazi prison camps. It's chilling to think this level of Fascism could return to the world a century after our grandparents rejected it with live fire. This documentary is particularly effective at showing the atrocities of Nazi policy, and the determination of The Greatest Generation in eliminating their ability to harm others, for a time at least.

You can sense this was handle with a little more care than your average keeping-you-up-to-date-with-the-war documentary and is quite easy to digest.

reviews.author: Gabe Rodríguez
reviews.text: THE TWELVE CHAIRS is one of the smartest and most enjoyable films in the Mel Brooks canon. I once heard Brooks say in an interview that THE PRODUCERS and TWELVE CHAIRS were the types of movies he had really wanted to make: small little comedies. But after BLAZING SADDLES was such a hit, he found himself typecast into making the same type of large bombastic parodies over and over again. TWELVE CHAIRS then feels like a nice glimpse into the type of work Brooks could have made had he gone in a different direction.

reviews.author: Zeeneaste (Christian)
reviews.text: A favourite entry for many fans of the Gaulish duo, and I get why that is. It has Astérix and Obélix at their most anarchic and anachronistic. At points they operate almost like Bugs Bunny and his cohorts. By design, the film is very episodic. The chapters are varied, colourful and range from adventurous to creepy. It is debatable if fewer quests would have been advantageous. They do get a lot fun moments out of our protagonists, though. Astérix uses his mind and courage while Obélix shines as the sensitive giant that he is. The film is even respectful to its antagonist, Julius Caesar, and doesn't just turn him into the evil bad guy - his retirement epilogue is earned and adorable.

The funny thing is, and we've mentioned it before, why is this known with two different titles? It's know as both Chino, and The Valdez Horses, and has a chequered production history as original director John Sturges apparently disowned the finished film after a bust-up with Bronson over the casting of his wife Jill Ireland. The film was then mothballed for several months before co-producer Dino De Laurentiis reassembled the cast and hired Duilio Coletti for reshoots. I'm not sure what Sturges' film would have looked like, or…

reviews.text: This is a strange one: De Laurentis filming a serious western novel in Spain with Charles Bronson during that short period he was a big star in Europe but not in the US with an aging John Sturges at helm. Bronson is half indian wild horse breeder and good chunk of it is really just moving between Bronson and his kid assistant (who is there so the movie isn't half dialogue free) working on the horses and he looking his silent manacing number. Lots of talk comparing men and horses. Marcel Bozzuffi is around as big landowner so one knows some third act fireworks are in place, but this is as far from either an Eurowestern or old Hollywood western as possible. Sort of a sad character piece, but not self conscious arty in the way New Hollywood westerns usually get. It is certainly one of the greatest uses of Bronson screen persona.

reviews.text: A nifty little horror film, Dan Bush's "The Vault" combines ghost story and heist flick to admirable results. Revolving around a bank robbery gone awry when the thieves run headlong into the terrors of the bank's past, the story provides a mix of low-wattage crime-picture thrills and effectively chilling jolts and atmosphere. The production is appropriately small-scale and features a committed cast. In the end, there may not be much to "The Vault;" but it is solid enough to neatly engage.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Director Jung Byung-gil insists that “The Villainess” was made without any reference to preexisting films; that all of its gonzo action was hatched directly from his own demented imagination (with assists from stunt coordinator Kwon Gui-duck and cinematographer Park Jung-hun). And yet the very first scene of the movie busts out of the gate like a female-driven remake of “Hardcore Henry,” Jung immediately launching us into a prolonged first-person sequence in which our avatar slaughters dozens of men in a dingy crystal meth lab. Imagine the hallway fight from “Oldboy,” but three times as long and incalculably more violent (eek, another reference).

reviews.author: LeSchroeck
reviews.text: Fantasy Filmfest 2017, die wilde 13: The Villainess ist genau mein Kino. Es beginnt mit einer Plansequenz, die von der Ego- in die 3rd-Person-Perspektive wechselt, nachdem ihr Zentrum, Killerin Sook-hee, mit dem Kopf gegen einen Spiegel geknallt wird. Und es zeigt ein Schlachtfest, das mal eben in 10 Minuten mit allen John Wicks, Atomic Blondes, Hardcore Henrys oder Kingsmen den Boden aufwischt. Was folgt, ist tatsächlich nicht mehr wirklich originell: die koreanische Antwort auf Luc Bessons "Nikita". Aber es geht für mich deutlich tiefer, weil Regisseur Byung-gil Jeong das Seelenleben dieser Auftragsmörderin auf gleich drei (Zeit)Ebenen aufsplittet und dem "Hitgirl lernt die Liebe kennen"-Prinzip ein paar mehr Fallhöhen verschafft. Und weil er die Action, die Inszenierung und den (auch CGI-)Blutzoll einfach in neue, formschöne und kinetisch ungeahnte Höhen schraubt. Wer "The Raid 2" liebt, darf auch dieser tragischen Kampfmaschine sein Herz schenken. Ich hab es definitiv getan.

reviews.text: This is a 1986 Canadian sci-fi flick that is firmly in B-movie territory. Carl Lehman is a scientist who gets blown up by his shady boss at ARC, only to be reborn as a rage-fueled cyborg in a discount spacesuit. His quest for vengeance and reconnection with his wife is chased by Pam Grier’s badass bounty hunter, Hunter. It’s a messy mix of heart and cheese, with Stan Winston’s effects as the highlight.It’s basically RoboCop’s rough draft, minus the budget, satire, or polish. Released a year before Verhoeven’s 1987 classic, The Vindicator shares its DNA: dead hero, corporate evil, cyborg identity crisis. But where RoboCop soars, this stumbles with a flimsy script and a suit that screams cosplay clearance. Pam Grier and a synth-heavy vibe save it from disaster, making it a fun, flawed time capsule for 80s sci-fi fans.

reviews.text: The whisperer in darkness is quite something. I loved the acting, the visuals and the ways the mystery unfolded and concluded. It has a few parts that are a bit hokey, and once the creatures are shown it does lose a bit of its mysticism, but that's only in the very final scenes. The craft and attention to detail that went into this is impressive. It's clearly made by passionate craftsmen, and that always shows in the end result. It makes for a compelling watch because of it. It's a visual tour de force full of beautiful shots and meticulous use of camera placement. The use of black and white adds to its old fashioned vibes and the score enhances the uncanny, otherworldly mood and tone. If speaking of hidden gems, this truly is one. It's a must see for fans of Lovecraftian horror.

reviews.text: Aside from the fantasy, apart from the supernatural and mythological love story, this film manages to do something that no other in its genre (that I've seen) has done. That is, to properly show the immensity of imperial China: its sprawling bureaucracy, its complex social system, its incredibly advanced technology. It is awe-inspiring to see the massiveness, the completeness of such an ancient society brought to the screen in such a captivating way, especially given that this is not historical film. And as it should, it also portrays the necessary cruelty that such a system would require to be functional, and the violence that a feudal society must wreak on itself to become as advanced and sophisticated as ancient China…

The confusingly fast paced plot, set during the final years of the Ming Dynasty, is composed of an endless series of predictable betrayals and assassinations. Furthermore, the story suffers from having one too many forgettable supporting characters who wasted the precious camera time of the main cast. It’s like an over-plotted, wuxia version of Game of Thrones,…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: In The White Ribbon, director Michael Haneke seems to ask us: where does evil come from? This is a story told as a parable, to show us a world we deeply know. It is an inhuman look at humanity, showing us the root of an evil that is (and, more crucially, was) powerful. There is sharp black and white photography, accompanied by static camerawork, and this colourless, slow portrayal of life makes no comment upon it, instead just showing us the festering evil. The White Ribbon is cold, cerebral, and calculated, calmly deconstructing things and presenting them bleakly. It's an uncompromising masterpiece.

Sadly, our female protagonist doesn’t transform into a Medusan enchantress who rises out of the waves to entrance and decapitate her victims with a scythe. In fact, there is very little gore to speak of here at all (though it does feature in small doses). Instead, this is very much a psychological affair, built around Millie Perkins’ character, Molly—an alcoholic, sexually repressed bartender who struggles to deal with the traumas of her past. Molly seems to be in an almost permanent half-daze; prone to short-term memory loss and long bouts of daydreaming—her mind often conjuring up depraved, sadomasochistic encounters between her…

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: For one of the few directors who successfully transitioned from the silent era to sound, Fritz Lang seems like he has almost nothing to do in the disappointingly talky The Woman in the Window. It's one of the films which helped inspire the French New Wave to create the term "film noir," but while all the visual coordinates of the genre are definitely here (nighttime, dark shadows, sharp contrast), it's hard to imagine that this is the film that inspired a generation.

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: It might not have the most original mind-blowing noir story, but, man, this got me. I was in it, totally invested in wanting everything to work out okay. Proper edge-of-my-seat behaviour, which I’m not even sure was warranted, but like I said, I was in it. Maybe it was the whole small-misstep spiralling into ever increasing doom. Or maybe it was the disastrous body dump. Or the relatable slump of Edward G Robinson’s shoulders. Or Joan Bennet’s absolute panic when the blackmailer called her on spiking the drinks. But whatever it was, I was so relieved for that ending. Yes, it’s a cop out one and no, I don’t care. I was just happy.

reviews.text: Supposedly this low-budget exploitation film about the Zodiac Killer was made with the intention of capturing the Zodiac. The director, Tom Hanson, rented a theatre for the premiere and invited audience members to write the best answer to the question "I believe the Zodiac kills because..." Hanson apparently thought that by analyzing these cards he'd be able to find the real killer. Hard to believe this wasn't just ballyhoo, but the reporter Paul Avery (played by Robert Downey Jr. in the David Fincher film) was actually involved in this crummy little movie: he is credited as a consultant and wrote an on-screen forward ("The motion picture you are about to see was conceived in June 1970. Its goal is not to win commercial awards but to create an 'awareness of a present danger'..."). Despite Avery's involvement, this movie is mostly fiction.

reviews.text: We may never run out of movies to make about World War II, the people who lived through it, and the people who didn’t. It may seem a bit obvious given the global scope of the conflict, but the sheer number of narratives that have emerged from the period is truly mind-boggling, bordering on the infinite, and it often feels as though most of them have made their way in front of a camera. The Holocaust alone offers more stories than we could ever hope to pass along — in Niki Caro’s beautifully realized and occasionally stirring “The Zookeeper’s Wife,” even the animals have their own tales to tell.

reviews.text: If we want to be vague and reductive, we can compartmentalize the notion of "indie" cinema—as a designation of style rather than means of production—into two general sub-categories: the quirky character-piece or the subdued slice of life. Naturally, these categories aren't mutually exclusive, as most films hitting the Sundance/Cannes circuit tend to cherry-pick ideas from both sides of the fence, and in the broadest sense, a film like Things You Can Tell Just by Looking at Her can be observed as just the sort that aims primarily to hit one side while glancing longingly at the other every so often.

As if the words being spoken are wholly symbolic, not meant to be taken as literal conversation. Something very captivating about that. & performances were just fantastic. Going on my rewatch list so I can get a bit closer to the characters. Especially holly hunter’s, rebecca, who is the queen of stoic self-flagellation, cornering herself into pitiless relationships and choosing to undergo a surgical abortion all by her lonesome, which proves to be more physically painful & emotionally taxing than she’s able to stomach.
