reviews.text: The latest output from filmmaker Nathan Silver (Stinking Heaven, Actor Martinez) is a neon-lit, psychosexual thriller about an American flight attendant named Gina (Lindsay Burdge) who, following a recent tragedy, inserts herself in the life of a Parisian man named Jerome (Damien Bonnard), eventually becoming obsessive to the point of extreme consequences. On the exterior, viewers are provided with a classic downward spiral of a character arc but, upon closer investigation, Thirst Street is more so a genuine examination of the places that the mind takes the body when attempting to deal with post-traumatic stress.

reviews.text: America misadventures abroad. At the face of trauma, a flight into fantasy. An afternoon at the movies, a cruel Fassbinderean window intro power and obsession. Sean Price Williams usual exquisite cinematography keep Gina’s action in the realm of the symbolic while Lindsay Burdge compassionate performance takes her trauma serious while allowing the film to keep at a remove. Silver has been flirting with leaving naturalism behind for a few years already (he always had a taste for brushes of excess most other low budget American directors lack) and this is by far his most successful foray into that yet. Also, as usual he has a great taste for cruel comedy of misunderstanding.

reviews.text: An erotic thriller farce of escalating obsession, rendered gorgeously retro-lurid by Sean Price Williams and alternately hilarious, heartbreaking and terrifying by Lindsay Burdge's wild performance. She places manically wide eyes on top of frozen smiles, a look perched in a nebulous fog between deluded affection and some social awareness in the back of her brain screaming bloody murder. There's a particularly perverse comedy to the way that she knowingly exploits the French custom for kiss greetings to subtly make her crush kiss her, and you can track the overall flow of this film by the increasing dismay on his face every time politeness obligates him to peck her on the cheek.

reviews.author: Siân
reviews.text: This wasn't quite what I was expecting, but for what it was (a bio-pic), it was incredibly well-crafted. Basically Barbara Kopple is a goddess no matter what sort of documentary she's making. And, overhwhelmingly, we need more trans stories (non-fiction and narrative) on screen and I'm happy this is one of them. This is Everything documents the life of Gigi Gorgeous, from her early life as Greg to using Youtube as a platform to express herself, to finally coming out as transgender. The doc gets amazing home video access to her transition process, particularly how it affected her family. There's no denying that Gigi is blessed with privilege, particularly in being able to afford to transition, but having a supportive family is never a guarantee in these situations. The best thing that Gigi has isn't her Youtube fame or career success or ability to transition—it's her immensely supportive family. That's what this doc is all about, really.

reviews.author: Ken Rudolph
reviews.text: For over a decade now, YouTube has made and enriched several international vlogging celebrities. Even an old codger like me has followed the lives of some of these millennial extroverts. However, I missed out on the young Gregory Lazzarato's activities as over the years "they" transitioned on-line from Canadian high school diving champion and femme oriented gay boy, to ravishing, transexual woman and celebrity, Giselle Loren Lazzarato (aka Gigi Gorgeous). This film, artfully edited and directed by the superb film maker Barbara Kopple, tells her story, emphasizing the transition process and her supportive family (two brothers and her father.) It's a fascinating story, well documented with YouTube video extracts and interviews. It is above all a heartening, entertaining, and relatively non-judgmental story of a courageous individual who embodies one aspect of the 21st century GLBT+ sexual revolution.

reviews.author: Calvin Kemph 🤠
reviews.text: Watch out for Clyde Petersen, who animates and directs their autobiography without dialogue, but sometimes with Godzilla roars. This is a story about transitioning, which finds beautiful metaphors for the trans experience and confronts head-on, the difficulty of having a parent who struggles to stabilize, when you’re just trying to become who you really are. Beautiful animated art, utilizing stop motion and multimedia to tell an authentically personal story in a very moving way.

reviews.author: Osvaldo Escalante
reviews.text: Siempre es difícil juzgar una película tan personal, pero la propuesta de Clyde Petersen es sumamente cálida, humana y llena de imaginación. Excelente decisión el utilizar el stop-motion como técnica de animación (además de que todo fue realizado y cortado a mano). El que no haya una historia fija vuelve más confrontante este coming-of-age. Pero la gran capacidad de su director para contar subtramas y llevarnos por la mente de su protagonista, hace que este largometraje de apenas 60 minutos sea muy disfrutable.

reviews.author: SpaghettiNoir
reviews.text: This British procedural splits the difference between a noir and a whodunnit as a detective superintendent from the Yard investigates the murder of a young woman in a small town. While the mystery and reveal are just so-so, Town on Trial's approach feels fresh and proto-Lynch, abandoning the stuffy Agatha Christie drawing room for a more hard-boiled approach that focuses on the lurid world beneath the cozy village: the posh tennis club becomes a hedonistic dancehall at night, the "benevolent" local doctor looks and behaves like a gangster; even the dutiful detective isn't above getting involved with a potential suspect/witness.The B&W photography is stellar, featuring some early slasher/giallo POV stuff too (just look at that poster).

reviews.author: MushiMinion
reviews.text: Much like the three-part structure to a magic trick, all murder mysteries rely on a variant of the same three events: the crime, the investigation, and the reveal. The crime is the hook, and the investigation should tantalize us until everything culminates in the reveal. If any piece of this act falls apart, the whole thing crumbles. Town on Trial is a textbook example of an ending ruining everything that came before it. This movie is beautifully shot and surprisingly well executed, but the final reveal is so unsatisfying that it ruins all the effort that went into the previous 75-minutes.

reviews.author: Wilson
reviews.text: Town on Trial is a solid British mystery, a whodunit in the style of an Agatha Christie, directed by future Death on the Nile director John Guillermin. John Mills is great value in the lead role, as the working class detective dropped in an upper-class town, with secrets, determined to solve the murder of a blonde sex symbol. He spits out the dialogue and even ends the film with an action scene. It is John Mills, doing a little bit of noir styling in a British setting, looking at murders that have a tinge of giallo to them. Strangulation by stocking, there is nothing more giallo than that.

reviews.text: Nice little mystery about a murder in an uptight british community. Lots of tut-tuts and sexual repression. It is interesting watching a working class superintendent investigate a young lady who was killed but lower class. Dealing with people with their noses up in the air. Plenty of leads and red herrings. Nothing really outstanding but solid as can be. The flawed superintendent is fun as he ruffles feathers. The suspects all have some dirty on them. So it could be any of them. Although you might be able to figure it out rather quick.

Directed by John Guillermin, Town on Trial clearly has its eye on the American market and rightly surfaces, flailing, soggy, and exhausted, somewhere in the Mid-Atlantic (the same territory Mills' accent bizarrely strays to on occasion) for such flagrant importunity. Still, at least Guillermin caught the eye of Hollywood, even if this film didn't, and it's nice to see Harry Locke get more to do than usual in the role of Mills' sidekick.

Есть классно снятые сцены (например, на танцах и когда включается POV убийцы), Джон Миллс в роли следака убедителен, есть и волнительная попытка залезть на шпиль церкви, которую режиссер Гиллермин потом повторит в "Кинг Конге", но видели мы британские детективы и поизящней. Забавно тут копы ведут себя с подозреваемыми, "с увожением", даже когда на них буквально набрасываются с кулаками. Вот она, матушка Англия.

reviews.text: What sticks out here the most is actually Breaion's refusal to submit to authority or take any responsibility for her actions. Was the force used on her excessive? Possibly. Since she fights and screams and will not comply it becomes difficult to tell. I don't doubt that racist behavior happens in the police force, but this was not compelling evidence of it. This felt like a very manipulative documentary that spends only a portion of its 30 minutes showing actual events and the rest trying to make us empathize with Breaion outside of her actions during the arrest.

reviews.author: Matthew B.
reviews.text: Traffic Stop, an Oscar-nominated documentary short from HBO Films and director Kate Davis, tells the story of Breaion King, an African-American schoolteacher from Austin, Texas. Through police car dashboard cameras, viewers see how a routine traffic stop quickly escalated into a violent encounter between King and Officer Bryan Richter, where the much-smaller King is harshly thrown to the ground with force and taken into custody for (allegedly) resisting arrest.

I was not aware it was Oscar nominated. Watch this, it’s short (about 30 minutes) and not only socially relevant but well made as well.

Being stupid teenagers didn't help our image either to be honest. So we got pulled over for "routine traffic stops" a lot. Every weekend. reviews.text: One of the better Frank Capra wartime documentaries I've seen so far. This one, as the title suggests, focuses entirely on the war effort in North Africa. There are plenty of shots of tanks in the desert, and a simplified explanation of how the war in Africa went. I've enjoyed these wartime documentaries more than average tonight. I don't know if it's because these tiles, being left off my 36-DvD America at War collection from the same production company, Mill Creek, are somehow slightly higher in quality, or if I've just been burnt out of old Horror flicks I've been bingeing. The scores on these few documentaries have actually supported the former seeing that they're all highly rated, especially this one. These haven't been bad. I'll be looking forward to next week's Military Monday after this.

reviews.author: Isaac Williams
reviews.text: Twenty people of various backgrounds sit individually in a closed room with a camera on them & twenty cards laid out on a table with questions ranging from “Why do you litter?”, “How will you die?”, “TV preachers?” to “Anal sex?” & “Shoes?”. They select cards at random & answer them. This hour-long experimental documentary is fun, emotional & sometimes thought-provoking. I think it’s an experiment that could be done over & over again. Bechard’s set-up includes a TV monitor with random footage playing, including sexy stuff, violence & Ronald Reagan. Anther monitor has a rotating selection of words & a third is the profile view of the subject. The director of DISCONNECTED & PSYCHOS IN LOVE shot this in ’87, assembled it the following year & released it for public consumption in 2017.

Most of this movie is watching them learn to work together and Eastwood realizing how in control of the situation…

reviews.author: legolas
reviews.text: As far as Eastwood's iconic "Man with No Name" persona from the Spaghetti Westerns is concerned, Two Mules for Sister Sara feels like a more fleshed-out and satisfying elaboration. His character here isn't just a silhouette of stoicism, but he's more permitted more depth, more personality, and a more defined emotional arc, and as such, he feels considerably more three-dimensional. Honestly, when Eastwood is in a Western, I don't for a second doubt that he'll see it through, because he always does. That gritty assurance, the quiet resolve, the unassuming strength, it's all there.

reviews.author: Brian Saur
reviews.text: Not for everyone I suppose but has become something of a personal favorite of mine. I call it William Castle meets Live Action Disney (due in no small part to the casting of Dean Jones). Connie Stevens is heir to her weird magician fathers (Caesar Romero) fortune and old spooky house but she must spend 7 nights there to get it. Jones is a reporter who starts off looking for a story but ends up falling for her. Well directed by actor William Conrad.Would double interestingly with William Castle’s own THE NIGHT WALKER (1964) with Barbara Stanwyck. Could also pair with THE MAD MAGICIAN (1954) with Vincent Price.**Tangential David Lynch connection: Connie Stevens sings the song “Sixteen Reasons” used in this memorable scene from MULHOLLAND DRIVE: https://youtu.be/AnZKD-EqMQA

It is campy and fun in the right ways. It couldn't be anything other as it involves a magician leaving his house full of tricks to his long lost daughter.What put it over the top is the casting. Here we get Connie Stevens and Dean Jones and the wholesomeness of this pairing, playing it straight…

reviews.author: Scarecrow88
reviews.text: Nowhere near as macabre as you'd think from the title, this is more or less a romantic drama as Connie Stevens (daughter of wacko magician Cesar Romero) could stand to inherit her father's fortune if she can stay in his eccentric house gradually while bonding with secret reporter Dean Jones (pre Disney). In the wreckage of Romero's death is his long-term aid (Gregg) and agent (Baer), both of whom are pitiful drunks left with basically nothing despite their years of dedication and service. Stevens didn't know what happened to her mother (said to have "disappeared"), later realizing that Romero's claim of eventually returning from beyond the grave might just be true.

reviews.author: Boof65
reviews.text: The title of this fluffy yet enjoyable romp is far more foreboding than the film itself turns out to be. Prior to taking Herbie for a spin, Dean Jones stars as a reporter who wheedles his way into the life of an heiress (Connie Stevens) who must stay in the spooky old house left to her by her father for seven consecutive nights in order to claim a large inheritance. Initially Jones is just there for a story and the way that the two hook up is frankly quite bizarre, but of course love ends up rearing its ugly head.The house is full of tricks (literally) and when you throw in Cesar Romero as the enigmatic magician father who has vowed to return from the dead, all of the elements are there for an entertaining (if not particularly challenging) evening's viewing!

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Interesting to note that while it's not an exploration of race or gender in any way, it also doesn't fuck up with the two non-white male characters with major roles in any significant ways. Both are stories of grief--and they're not exactly deep or nuanced--and that grief (regret, guilt, frustration, loss) overwhelms all other narratives. Her love for her lost fiance certainly defines her story here, but in a way that reveals things about her. His need to be part of his team, his desire to honor his lost teammates isn't predicated on any racial basis; just pure loss. Everything else is pushed to the side. reviews.text: 100-word review: Capturing the historic 1974 Rumble in the Jungle between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman, When We Were Kings portrays sporting greatness and cultural significance. At its heart is Ali's magnetic charisma, which shines through as he prepares for the iconic boxing match. The film portrays Foreman in an unfair role as the villain, juxtaposing his formidable presence against Ali's poetic bravado. One of the documentary's standout features is its seamless integration of live music performances, notably B.B. King's soulful contributions. However, the title song feels oddly out of place amidst the historical backdrop, disrupting the film's otherwise authentic vibe.

reviews.text: It's not the counterculture disaster that Otto Preminger's Skidoo is, but this naive and strident John Boorman movie (which he wrote with his daughter) feels like a misguided vanity project. It treads the same whimsical waters as depression era social comedies like Hallelulah, I'm a Bum and My Man Godfrey, but the comedy here is wincingly overplayed and amateurish. reviews.text: A revolutionary revisit as I had only previously seen it in very poor condition on one of those public domain style horror compilation DVDs. Turns out this film is gorgeous, dripping with hanging shadows and drifting through dusty caverns with a visual style that uses architecture to create something that feels like silent film framing, which is something horror was moving away from at the time. The angular German expressionism tells where the genre would go and where it had been. The slow creeping transformation of lost humanity and bodily autonomy is lingered on to an uncomfortable degree. Lugosi is also one of a handful of guys who can evoke the mood of horror in the way he carries himself…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Bart Freundlich ("Catch That Kid") isn’t known for making particularly subtle movies, and "Wolves" — for all its virtues — won’t do much to undo that reputation. A clunky but compelling coming-of-age saga about a prep school basketball phenom (Taylor John Smith) whose future is threatened by his father’s (Michael Shannon) gambling addiction, this is the kind of film that milks every metaphor until its dry and then eats the cow for dinner. And yet, while "Wolves" sometimes strains even harder than his 2005 relationship drama, "Trust the Man," Freundlich’s palpable connection to this story breathes it full of life. That vitality didn’t come easy ("Wolves" finds the filmmaker reviving characters that he first conceived for a high school writing assignment more than two decades ago), but the personal touch makes this by far the best of his six features to date.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Kim Ki-young's Housemaid (1961) frequently has "best Korean film" praise thrown at it - a predecessor to the erotic thriller, about the title character bringing a family to ruin. The runaway success meant that Kim would revisit the collateral damage of extramarital affairs for a "Housemaid Trilogy" - while making a number of other efforts in a very similar vein (i.e. Insect Woman). Woman of Fire (1971) is the second film in the trilogy, and features Oscar winner Youn Yuh-jung (Minari) in her feature film debut, as our femme fatale homewrecker. This is not a spiritual sequel, but rather the director remaking his work a decade later.

reviews.text: Kim Ki-Young's decadal The Housemaid update, in which he tries to be more grand, experimental and scandalous than in the original. Granted, he does succeed, though at cost of subtlety, which incidentally was my favorite part about the original. To not subject it to endless comparisons though, because this absolutely works as a stand-alone picture, Kim Ki-Youg, on a stylistic note, is at his peak here. There is something about the specific ways he utilizes the many shades of red, presumably to mirror Youn Yuh-jung's intensity, that is remarkably mesmerizing, and almost inexplicably macabre. His camera placement and movement, both present to evade governmental restrictions and to make himself stand out even further, is also impeccable. So many shots that i previously hadn't seen in any other films.

reviews.text: Second time around, it’s easy to spot all the ways Bong Joon-ho cribbed from peak Kim Ki-young: the family house here, in particular, appears a direct inspiration for Parasite, the production design evoking the same note of extravagance that never quite crosses over into the unreal. There are parallels with Minari too, though, in the slightly peculiar amount of time spent on the raising of chickens, and the ‘smell’ of Youn Yuh-jung’s character (Namkoong Won holds his nose the first time he encounters her). This was her debut performance, and it has to be said that it shows: she has this habit of jutting out her teeth in every reaction shot, and it’s distracting as hell.

reviews.text: This imaginative sci-fi drama-western has a lot of complex themes, but it’s not glued together well—thankfully, its climax saves it. Set in a dystopian future with limited water resources, it stars Michael Shannon and Kodi Smit-McPhee as Earnest and Jerome Holm, a father and son working a supply route while trying to revive their drought-stricken land. But Earnest’s daughter Mary (Elle Fanning) is caught up in a scheme devised by her boyfriend Flem (Nicholas Hoult) to take over their land. The film unfolds in three acts, each focusing on a character study of the male leads. Visually, it’s stunning, and the robots are impressive. The acting is solid across the board, but some parts feel disjointed. While the ending delivers excitement, by that point, the film has lost a lot of its momentum. It’s a decent film, but that’s about it.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: Every time you watch an Amir Shervan movie, you can't help but compare it to his masterpiece final film, 1991's Samurai Cop. Yet that tasteful classic of cinema didn't appear out of thin air, my friends. Every previous film Shervan sculpted was a small step, an incremental accumulation of refined dialogue, skillful hand-to-hand combat set-pieces and extended stripper scenes. Young Rebels may be that most important step on the way to Samurai Cop. This one has it all - thongs, helicopters, seduction of the innocent, a shirtless Robert Zdar drinking red wine, a smokin' hot synth soundtrack and more action than Tango & Cash could ever dream of.

Слишком много персонажей, среди которых теряется неброский герой, а интерьеры арендованных для съемок домов опять намного интереснее экшена. reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: Amir Shervan and Andy Sidaris were born two years apart on opposite sides of the world in Tehran and Chicago. Somehow they absorbed the exact same inspirations and aesthetic style - Russ Meyer cartoon boobs, mullets, thongs, long butts, spray tans, helicopters, synth scores, drug scores and permanent sunshine. Sidaris had a better budget and better actors, but their intentions were the same. They just go for it in some kind of 80’s hairspray and Jolt Cola frenzy. Young Rebels would have been Shervan’s masterpiece until he blew it out of the water with Samurai Cop a few years later.

reviews.text: The deeper and deeper I dig into film history, my appreciation for Hollywood polish declines further and further, and the more I crave the liberty of the zero budget, quasi-professional film-making of the fringe industry. reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: A boy's own adventure story of American soldiers behind German lines where they discover a crashed spaceship and its furry alien passenger. The men from Trancers are back - Tim Thomerson as "Sarge", Art Lefleur as "Mittens", and Biff Manard as ace reporter Dolan - sorry, no women allowed. This is a great movie because Thomerson, and only Thomerson, can deliver lines like, when asking for a cigarette, "Butt me, Mitt." Meanwhile Aliens pull out their disintegrator pistols and trade fantasy make out time with the girl of your dreams for a smoke, while Lefleur punches Hitler right in the face. It's a lot of low budget nonsense that might sometimes test your patience, especially in the middle. But looking back, it only brings a smile to my face. Kind of a classic. Another great Danny Bilson/Paul De Mao script (of Rocketeer and Da 5 Bloods fame).

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: Decided to follow "Trancers" and "The Rocketeer" screenwriters Danny Bilson & Paul DeMeo from the "Trancers 1.5" short film "City of Lost Angels" to this 1985 effort from Empire Pictures. Bilson actually steps behind the camera for "Zone Troopers," one of the rare films that offers a blend of boots-on-the-ground World War II action with far-flung space science-fiction. It's a terrific example of two great tastes tasting great together; and the zippy, period accurate dialogue tells you that Bilson and DeMeo must have ingested dozens of old black-and-white war movies growing up. It's no wonder that these two would go on to a write a high-concept throwback film as well realized and executed as "The Rocketeer" just five short years after…

reviews.author: Demdike
reviews.text: A cracking war, sci-fi epic from Charles Band starring Tim Thomerson, an actor who lights up any low budget production and turns it into a sparkling gem, as the grizzled sergeant of a platoon (Do four men constitute a platoon?) lost behind enemy lines in Italy 1942 who discover an alien space craft crashed in the woods, it's pilot captured by the SS.

reviews.author: Saint_Hooligan
reviews.text: During the 80’s and early 90’s, Tim Thomerson’s movies were some of the best B-movies out there. When you watched his movies you knew you were going to have a fun time. This one is a campy combination of WWII action, sci-fi, and comedy. It reunites actors Tim Thomerson, Art Lafleur, and Biff Manard from the classic Sci-Fi movie Trancers. Kitschy, and with cornball dialogue right out of the 50’s and 60’s, this movie transports you back to when movies could make you forget about the world for awhile. Has that great old comic book feel to it. This could have been lifted right out of DC Comics’ Weird War Tales series from the 70’s and 80’s. Zone Troopers proves that likable characters and interesting story can overcome a low budget. In this case, the limitations add to the old-fashioned sci-fi charm.
